title: What to know about Falcons – Packers on Thursday Night Football
summary: We barely have time to digest the Week 2 loss to the Carolina Panthers before the Atlanta Falcons suit up to take on the Green Bay Packers in Week 3. Perhaps that’s for the best, or perhaps we’re going to we’re going to get rocked by this team twice in less than a week. Who’s […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - SEPTEMBER 17: Green Bay Packers running back AJ Dillon #28 runs the football as Atlanta Falcons cornerback A.J. Terrell #24 defends during the NFL game between the Green Bay Packers and the Atlanta Falcons on September 17, 2023 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Jeff Robinson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We barely have time to digest the Week 2 loss to the Carolina Panthers before the Atlanta Falcons suit up to take on the Green Bay Packers in Week 3. Perhaps that’s for the best, or perhaps we’re going to we’re going to get rocked by this team twice in less than a week. Who’s to say? I am. The Falcons are facing off against a tired, vulnerable Packers team but may not have the wherewithal to take advantage of that fact; the return of Michael Penix Jr. to the starting lineup should at least give them a fighting chance. In what’s likely to be a confusing, deeply irritating slopfest from two very tired teams, who will prevail? Let’s try to figure that out. How these two teams stack up Both have been disappointing, but one only mildly and the other very much so. The Packers are 19th in points scored and 24th in points allowed thus far, which is what happens when you get stomped by the Vikings 39-22 in Week 1 and go to overtime with the Jets in Week 2. Jordan Love has been quite solid and this team still has a gifted set of top receiving options, but their ground game has been mediocre and Love’s completed a concerningly low 52% of his passes thus far. The dismal pass protection of Week 1, aided by Brian Flores summoning blitzes from his hands all day, led Green Bay to lean heavily on a quick passing game in Week 2 that Jeff Ulbrich is going to have to effectively counter. As Justis Mosqueda notes in the writeup I just linked from Acme Packing Company, Love is getting rattled by pressure, and the Falcons can provide that. Defensively I don’t think the Packers are at all bad, and in fact Edgerrin Cooper and Lukas Van Ness are extremely scary for a team that hasn’t blocked all that well and is about to roll Penix out there, with the 39 points they allowed to Minnesota swinging on short fields provided by special teams miscues and turnovers. They don’t have Micah Parsons yet but are quite stout without him, though Bijan Robinson will sorely test them. Special teams coverage was shaky in Week 1 for Green Bay but quite good in Week 2, and rookie kicker Trey Smack has been a perfect 5/5 with a long of 59 yards. Like Green Bay, Atlanta’s great weakness thus far has been the offense. Unlike Green Bay, they have a terrific ground game that hasn’t even begun to get untracked yet because of the weakness of the passing game, though that may change if Penix is able to at least restore competence and the threat of an explosive play through the air. The Falcons offense has been so dismal thus far under Cooper Rush and (briefly) Jack Strand that it’s virtually impossible to say what form it’s going to take Thursday night, though we should be able to bet on it looking better than it has. Defensively, the Falcons have mostly picked up where they left off last year. Ulbrich and company are getting more juice out of their pass rush with fewer blitzes thus far and have been solid stopping the run, which is a major victory. A.J. Terrell potentially being out and the secondary looking a little wobbly thus far—zero turnovers, some bad lapses in coverage, etc.—is a cause for concern if Love does get untracked. And on special teams, the Falcons have struggled a bit in coverage, which is a problem with Skyy Moore capable of breaking one. Nick Folk’s dismal start to the season needs to change fast, too, if this should come down to a field goal arms (legs?) race. How the Packers have changed in 2026 Not a whole lot. Jonathan Gannon landing on his feet as the new defensive coordinator after he was bounced as Arizona’s head coach is a good thing for both the coach and the team, as his defense has looked quite good thus far. Javon Hargrave was one of the headline additions in free agency and has gotten off to a quiet start, and they did trade for linebacker Zaire Franklin. Otherwise, they lost quite a few contributors of yesteryear in free agency and ended up with just a six man draft class after trading their 2026T first to Dallas in the Micah Parsons deal. To be fair, second round pick Brandon Cisse is already starting at cornerback, Smack has been excellent, and rookie reserve guard Jager Burton has already had to jump into game action and held his own. They also just lost Jayden Reed, one of their promising and productive young receivers, for a bit after a scary back injury in Week 2. Otherwise, though, this is a familiar cast of characters for a team that’s typically among the NFC’s better squads. What to expect on Thursday Night Football I think it’s fair to anticipate the defenses ruling the evening. The Falcons will be— have to be—better offensively against Green Bay with Penix under center, but this is not an ideal matchup for them with a tough front that already has seven sacks and a frisky secondary that will punish mistakes. Similarly, the lackluster Green Bay ground game and Love’s shaky play under pressure are not exactly ideal when you’re facing off against an Atlanta defense that can bring pressure, at least theoretically has a cast of playmakers in the secondary, and has been solid against the run in its own right. Barring something stunning from Penix or a major return to form from Love, then, this shouldn’t be a high-scoring affair. What it will be is a game of attrition where the team that makes fewer mistakes will likely win, which is once again not exactly great news for either team. The Falcons have had some really poorly timed offensive line penalties and secondary miscues, adding up to 15 penalties for 135 yards, but the Packers have had an incredible 26 penalties called through two games. If the Falcons can get a couple of Love turnovers and give this overmatched Green Bay line enough fits to force multiple false starts and holds, they’ll give the offense a real chance at pulling this one out in primetime. Of course, the offense has to hold up its end of the bargain. Penix will open up the field for Atlanta and should ensure that Kyle Pitts and Drake London are not non-factors the way they largely have been the first two weeks—Pitts in particular—but also has a track record of shaky games against tough defenses in his short NFL career that includes a 135 yard effort against Minnesota and 12/28 and 177 yards against Indianapolis. We just don’t know what he’s going to look like in his first game back since his ACL surgery, and much will hinge on whether he’s rusty, solid, or great. It’s worth noting that over his final six games of 2025, Penix had thrown six touchdowns against zero interceptions, and if he can be careful with the ball it will go a long way toward this team earning a victory Thursday night. We do know that Bijan and Brian Robinsons can run effectively against this front, even though it’s quite stout, because they’re a quality duo and Bijan in particular is hard to bottle up for an entire game. Leaning on play action heavily and giving the Packers a heavy dose of Bijan to try to ease Penix in is a solid game plan that Tommy Rees is likely to prioritize, but at some point the Falcons are going to need to take those big shots to win. We’ll see what Penix can offer. If it’s close, as it’s likely to be, all eyes will be on Nick Folk. Smack’s looked very dependable for Green Bay early on and has hit kicks from range, where Folk’s vaunted accuracy has evaporated as he’s missed three of the six attempts he’s taken thus far, including one in the cozy confines of Mercedes-Benz Stadium. The Falcons really can’t afford to have missed kicks define this one. I see no reason to assume this will be a lopsided game, both because Atlanta should be better with Penix and Green Bay is still…

title: Ravens news: Lamar Jackson could run all over Cowboys defense
summary: Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover Lamar Jackson’s major rushing opportunity against the Cowboys, early-season results of past Super Bowl champions, and first-round pick Vega Ioane’s Week 2 grades. Let’s dive in! Lamar Jackson could run all over […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 22: Quarterback Lamar Jackson #8 of the Baltimore Ravens runs against the Dallas Cowboys during the fourth quarter at AT&T Stadium on September 22, 2024 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Ron Jenkins/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover Lamar Jackson’s major rushing opportunity against the Cowboys, early-season results of past Super Bowl champions, and first-round pick Vega Ioane’s Week 2 grades. Let’s dive in! Lamar Jackson could run all over Cowboys defense On Sunday in Brazil, the NFL’s worst rushing defense against quarterbacks will go up against the most dangerous rushing quarterback in league history. Hammer, meet nail. Lamar Jackson has gashed the Cowboys on the ground before. In their previous two matchups, he has racked up 181 yards and two touchdowns on 23 carries (6.7 yards per carry) – not to mention a 120.44 passer rating, 9.03 yards per attempt, and three more scores through the air. Dallas, meanwhile, allowed Jaxson Dart to rush for 54 yards on 11 attempts in Week 1 and surrendered 69 yards to Jayden Daniels in the first half of Week 2. The two-time MVP has yet to take over a game with his legs this year. New offensive coordinator Declan Doyle has prioritized an under-center rushing attack with play-action looks that get Jackson on the move as a passer. This is part of an intentional effort to keep the Ravens away from the shotgun-based hero-ball trap the offense has fallen in for years. But…that big red button is always there. On an international trip, while dealing with injuries, and against a defense that has struggled against mobile quarterbacks, Doyle may want to consider breaking out his not-so-secret weapon this week. Kenny Clark, Donovan Ezeiruaku break down facing Lamar Jackson, Ravens offense – Tommy Yarrish (DallasCowboys.com) Ravens QB and two-time league MVP Lamar Jackson awaits in Brazil, a difficult challenge for any team because of his ability to break contain and make explosive plays with his legs. The Cowboys defense understands the task that lies ahead in containing Jackson. “We all know what it is,” Cowboys OLB Donovan Ezeiruaku said. “You guys know. We know as players the type of guy he is. Somebody who can throw the ball, but also run the ball at a very high level. It’s easier to say than to do, but our job is to go out there and go do. That’s what we’re tasked with.” Past Super Bowl champs rarely defined by early-season loss Super Bowl odds: Bills now clear No. 2, plus what history tells us about 1-1 Ravens – Scott Phillips (The Athletic) Of the 14 teams currently carrying Super Bowl odds shorter than +2500 on BetMGM, eight of them hold at least one loss, including the favorite Rams at No. 1 and the Ravens at No. 3. Although it might feel like a September dud would deflate Super Bowl chances, recent history shows it’s fairly normal for future champions to lose early in the season. Six of the last 10 Super Bowl champions started the regular season 1-1 — including the last three winners… Week 2 grades for 1st-round pick Vega Ioane Grading all 32 NFL first-round rookies after Week 2 – Dalton Wasserman (Pro Football Focus) Overall Rookie Grade: 61.1 (Rank: 5/12) Principal Opponent: Vernon Broughton Week 2 Snaps: 58 Week 2 Grade: 47.7 Ioane took a slight step back from his solid Week 1 performance, earning a 47.7 PFF grade that was the lowest along Baltimore’s offensive line this week. He allowed four pressures, all hurries, in pass protection, which brings his total to six for the season. Ioane still flashed his potential as a run-blocker as he generated four positive, but also four negative, grades in that department.

title: Ravens Week 2 film study: RT Roger Rosengarten making Year 3 leap
summary: The Ravens’ Week 2 matchup against the New Orleans Saints may not have produced the home-opening result Baltimore wanted, but there were still several encouraging individual performances in the team’s first loss of the season. Right tackle Roger Rosengarten continued to show signs of a Year 3 leap, displaying the technical refinement and improved play […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - SEPTEMBER 20: Roger Rosengarten #70 of the Baltimore Ravens defends against the New Orleans Saints during an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Ravens’ Week 2 matchup against the New Orleans Saints may not have produced the home-opening result Baltimore wanted, but there were still several encouraging individual performances in the team’s first loss of the season. Right tackle Roger Rosengarten continued to show signs of a Year 3 leap, displaying the technical refinement and improved play strength that could make him a stabilizing presence along Baltimore’s offensive line. Linebacker Trenton Simpson showcased the athleticism and physicality required of a modern NFL linebacker, particularly when playing in space and attacking screen concepts. And with Zay Flowers sidelined, wide receiver Rashod Bateman stepped into the No. 1 receiving role and became Baltimore’s primary source of explosive plays through the air. Here’s what stood out from that trio in Week 2: RT Roger Rosengarten 58 snaps | 40 pass blocking | 18 run blocking | 0 pressures allowed | 78.2 true pass set grade Rosengarten has been excellent to start his 2026 campaign at right tackle with zero pressures allowed through two games and 73 pass-blocking reps. The biggest development has been his growth as both a technician and a run blocker. Rosengarten’s initial strike carries noticeably more strength and conviction than it did earlier in his career. His hand placement has become more deliberate, and he is doing a better job controlling defenders once contact is established. That improvement has carried over into pass protection, where Rosengarten consistently gave Jackson enough time to operate. There were several reps where Rosengarten either won his pass set outright or, just as importantly, ‘lost slowly.’ Even when a defender gained an initial advantage, Rosengarten remained attached and forced the rusher to take a longer path to the quarterback, buying Jackson the additional fraction of a second needed to get the ball out. Roger Rosengarten has allowed 0 pressures on true pass sets this year (excludes plays with less than 4 rushers, play action, screens, short dropbacks and time-to-throws under 2 seconds) Strong grip strength in the run game to create gap displacement, MMA like pass set usage… pic.twitter.com/rQ7xYp7et5 — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) September 22, 2026 One particularly interesting addition to his pass-protection toolbox has been the snatch-and-trap technique. Rosengarten used the rusher’s forward momentum against him, pulling the defender downward before finishing on top of him. Adding counters like this is an encouraging sign of the technical development taking place entering his third season. His movement ability was equally noticeable in the running game. On one rep, Rosengarten climbed roughly seven yards beyond the line of scrimmage, located the linebacker at the second level, and sealed him away from the running lane for Derrick Henry. On another, he was able to engage a defensive lineman, flip his hips, and establish positioning to create another lane. Rosengarten’s development could have implications beyond right tackle. If Baltimore can consistently trust him to handle one-on-one assignments without additional protection, the Ravens can allocate chips, slides, and other forms of protection help toward weaker areas of the offensive line. That makes Rosengarten’s Year 3 leap potentially pivotal to the offensive line’s ability to improve as a unit. Through two games, the combination of improved play strength, movement ability, and a growing pass-protection toolbox has made him one of Baltimore’s most encouraging early-season developments. LB Trenton Simpson 42 snaps | 21 run defense | 8 pass rush | 13 coverage | 2 pressures | 5 tackles | 10 yards allowed on 3 receptions Simpson’s performance against New Orleans offered another glimpse at the type of modern NFL linebacker his athletic profile could allow him to become. What stood out most was his ability to operate in space without sacrificing physicality at the point of attack. On a screen thrown to his side, Simpson worked through a block in space, stayed square to the ball carrier, and secured the tackle for a minimal gain. It was a good example of his athleticism translating into functional pursuit ability rather than simply testing numbers. His physical development also showed up against the run. On another rep, Simpson met an offensive guard at the point of attack, absorbed the contact, disengaged, and finished the play in the backfield. That ability to take on offensive linemen and work through contact has been an important part of his development. Trenton Simpson had a impressive week 2 performance Block deconstruction, attacking in space and dropping to his landmarks to take away passing lanes pic.twitter.com/GjqgdwItpg — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) September 21, 2026 Simpson also made his presence felt as a blitzer. On one pressure, he crashed downhill before recognizing the quarterback preparing to throw. Simpson used his high-end athleticism to time his jump and take away the throwing lane, forcing the quarterback to pull the ball down and ultimately contributing to a sack. The athleticism has always been there with Simpson. The encouraging development is how much more controlled and functional that athleticism looks within the structure of the defense. His ability to process, play through contact, and impact passing concepts in space will be worth tracking as the season progresses. WR Rashod Bateman 9 targets | 7 receptions | 88 yards | 1 touchdown | 2.44 yards per route run With Flowers unavailable, Baltimore needed someone to assume a larger role in the passing game. Bateman answered that challenge with seven receptions for 88 yards and a touchdown while accounting for several of Baltimore’s most explosive plays through the air. One of my criticisms of Bateman in the past has been his ability to consistently get ‘friendly’ to the quarterback. There have been instances where he could have shortened routes against zone coverage, settled into open grass, and gotten his head around earlier to give Lamar Jackson an easier throwing window. That wasn’t an issue Sunday. On several reps, Bateman recognized the soft spots in New Orleans’ zone coverage, adjusted his route accordingly, and presented himself to Jackson. Rather than simply running the route as drawn, he showed a better understanding of how to manipulate space and make himself available to his quarterback. Rashod Bateman 7 receptions for 88 yards Stemming off at the top of his routes, head fakes and selling his cuts. Finding soft spots in zones and sitting down. Got friendly to the qb. pic.twitter.com/xY3f0LDtqc — Yuri (@Yuri_Ravens) September 22, 2026 His route-running ability also showed up against tighter coverage. On two separate plays, Bateman snapped off his route at the breakpoint, combining quick feet with head fakes to manipulate the defender and create separation. Those are the subtle details that have always made Bateman an intriguing route runner when healthy and involved. The biggest question coming out of this performance is what Bateman’s role looks like once Flowers returns. Flowers remains a major part of Baltimore’s passing attack, but Bateman showed against New Orleans that he can handle additional volume. Rather than simply functioning as a complementary option, this performance strengthened the case for keeping him consistently involved even when the receiving corps returns to full strength. Advanced metrics via Pro Football Focus.

title: Ravens news: Lamar Jackson among NFL’s most-pressured quarterbacks
summary: Welcome to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of all of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover Lamar Jackson’s way-too-high pressure rate through two games, a few mitigating factors for the team’s offensive collapse vs. the Saints, and Let’s dive in! Lamar Jackson begins 2026 season among NFL’s […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - SEPTEMBER 20: New Orleans Saints defensive end Chase Young (99) holds onto Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson (8) for a sack during a NFL football game between New Orleans Saints and Baltimore Ravens September 20, 2026 at M&T Bank Stadium in Baltimore, MD (Photo by Charles Brock/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Welcome to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of all of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover Lamar Jackson’s way-too-high pressure rate through two games, a few mitigating factors for the team’s offensive collapse vs. the Saints, and Let’s dive in! Lamar Jackson begins 2026 season among NFL’s most-pressured QBs Pass protection has been the undoing of the Ravens offense for multiple years, and the first two weeks of the 2026 season prove that old habits die hard. The unit has been excellent in the run game, ranking first in ESPN’s win rate and second in PFF’s grading , but they fall to 30th and 32nd in each service’s respective pass-blocking metrics. Plenty of other teams have disparities of their own, but none are nearly as severe as Baltimore’s. As a result, Lamar Jackson has been feeling the heat to start the season. He has faced pressure on 41.2% of his dropbacks ( via Next Gen Stats ), the sixth-highest rate in the league. And despite different collection methodology, Pro Football Focus also ranks the two-time MVP as the sixth-most-pressured quarterback in the league: NFL quarterbacks facing the highest pressure rates through Week 2 – Mark Chichester (Pro Football Focus) 6. Lamar Jackson, Baltimore Ravens 42.6% pressure rate | 47.1 PFF grade under pressure | -0.280 EPA per play under pressure Jackson has faced pressure on 42.6% of his dropbacks, the sixth-highest rate among qualifying quarterbacks. His results in those situations have been mixed: His 8.6 yards per attempt under pressure ranks sixth among 32 qualifiers, but he has taken five sacks and produced two turnover-worthy plays. Jackson’s 6.5% turnover-worthy play rate ranks 10th-highest at the position, helping drag his production down to -0.280 EPA per play despite his ability to generate yardage when pressured. Next Gen Stats has Jackson producing -0.31 EPA/play under pressure, again aligning with PFF’s numbers and indicating a major drop-off in his performance in such situations. He struggled last year due to his injuries, but in 2023 and 2024, he ranked among the league’s best passers against pressure – and that is without accounting for his scrambling ability. There are schematic elements at play here. The Saints countered the Ravens’ under-center offense with linebacker blitzes that closed the distance to Jackson while his back was turned and disrupted Baltimore’s rhythm. Offensive coordinator Declan Doyle and offensive line coach Dwayne Ledford can be better-prepared for similar strategies in the future, while Jackson and his blockers will have to sharpen up their pre-snap adjustments at the line of scrimmage. If center Jovaughn Gwyn continues to struggle in pass protection, the Ravens may consider inserting veteran Ethan Pocic into the starting lineup to stabilize the middle of the unit. What is your biggest concern coming out of the Ravens' Week 2 loss to the Saints? | Baltimore Beatdown Derrick Henry won’t solve all of the Ravens’ late-game problems Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 3 – Ben Solak (ESPN) The Ravens never entered salt-the-clock mode against the Saints because they never got to that game state. They weren’t up by two scores in the fourth quarter. They lost Zay Flowers (and Ja’Kobi Lane ) at wide receiver, and left tackle Ronnie Stanley left the game in the third quarter (toe) after struggling against Chase Young . The Saints were also run-blitzing in the second half in an effort to take Henry out of the game plan, and coordinator Declan Doyle had some good calls to beat those looks, but pass protection failed across the board… …Could the Ravens have funneled more runs to Henry? Sure. The larger issue is that they never put the Saints to bed in the bulk of the game; the Ravens were too lacking in talent on offense, and defensively, their dam burst as the Saints made second-half adjustments. I still like the Ravens from a season-long perspective, but this is a growing team. The Ravens get an unbelievable soft stretch of defenses over the next three weeks (Cowboys, Titans and Falcons) with a potential return of Flowers. This is good soil from which to grow confidence and cohesion on offense. Are you confident the Ravens are headed in the right direction? | Baltimore Beatdown Rio field conditions still under question NFL intends to proceed with Ravens-Cowboys in Brazil, but field will look bad on TV – Mike Florio (Pro Football Talk) On Sunday, the Ravens will face the Cowboys at Maracaña Stadium in Rio de Janeiro. Despite concerns regarding the quality of the field, the NFL does intend to proceed. It’s our current understanding that the game is “likely” to happen as scheduled. If/when it does, expect the field to not look great on TV. Also, it will be very important for the teams to get early access to the field so that the players will be able to make the right decisions about footwear for the game.

title: Buffalo Bills fans might be shocked to learn Los Angeles Chargers are elite in one key area
summary: When diving into opponent previews each week, I find it helpful to scour the relative rankings across a variety of stats to see opponent strengths and weaknesses. The Los Angeles Chargers are 0 – 2 losing both games with the exact score of 14 – 26 which is a fun fact. They’ve had a slew […]
full_text: When diving into opponent previews each week, I find it helpful to scour the relative rankings across a variety of stats to see opponent strengths and weaknesses. The Los Angeles Chargers are 0 – 2 losing both games with the exact score of 14 – 26 which is a fun fact. They’ve had a slew of injuries and well… No one is really expecting much from them anymore. Are they good at anything? Across the board on most major offensive stats, they’re mediocre to pretty bad with a relative high point being the 14th best passing yards per play with 6.85. Yes, the high point is firmly “meh.” What if I told you they had one stat so far that was not only elite, but best in the league? And if it holds true, would actually be a pretty big deal against the Buffalo Bills? Well, you might want to find out if it was a legit concern or mirage. No one is better at stopping the run Yeah, that’s right. At 2.75 yards per rushing attempt allowed, no one is better at stopping the run game than the Los Angeles Chargers. Per game they’re 7th best, allowing 86.5 yards per contest. Are they truly excellent, or is it an early season mirage? pic.twitter.com/3SRjZgCkjU — Kuebiko (@Kuebiko_Kami) September 24, 2026 I’m not going to dive into each play specifically, but do want to suggest these are pretty representative of what I saw in the 63 snaps from the Chargers’ run defense. For the short version, I don’t think the run numbers are entirely a mirage. I don’t know if I’m confident they’ll retain the number one spot all season, but based on current information I would say they’ll likely wind up with good numbers. There’s no single reason which is honestly a bigger compliment. The defense for Los Angeles seems to do well maintaining their assignments and acting as a single unit. No one player stood out as a true game wrecker (Khalil Mack is still doing some really nice things). As a group though, everyone is capable of winning a matchup and making a play. There are some good stats to also back that this isn’t a fluke. With 63 rushing snaps and the Chargers losing both games by double digits, I wondered if part of their statistical dominance was due to “negative” rushes also known as “kneel downs” by the opponent. And indeed; between the Arizona Cardinals and Las Vegas Raiders, they’ve faced six kneel downs all for -1 yard. That’s 9.5% of their total volume. How big of an impact is that? If you remove the kneel downs, the Chargers held the Cardinals to 3.6 yards per carry and the Raiders to 2.3 yards per carry. Overall their adjusted run defense rate would be 3.03 yards per rush. That would still be fourth best in the NFL. Furthermore, while still an admittedly small sample size, both Arizona and Las Vegas performed worse against Los Angeles in the run game than they did in their other matchup this year. On the surface, Arizona had more yards against Los Angeles than the Seattle Seahawks, but on average they were held to 3.4 yards by the Chargers while the Seahawks allowed 4.1 yards per run. Las Vegas had a looooooowly 1.97 yards per rush against Los Angeles. While the Raiders didn’t exactly establish themselves as a dominant running team against the Miami Dolphins, the 3.51 yards per carry is a lot better than what happened against LA. Two more thoughts on their run defense not being a fluke. At the end of the first quarter vs. the Raiders a turnover gave Las Vegas the ball at the Chargers’ three-yard line. The results were a loss of two, gain of three, gain of one, and gain of zero. That’s right, a goal line stand of four running plays. My final thought is on their consistency. Through two games, the Chargers have five tackles for a loss. To compare, the Bills have 13. The Chargers allow the lower rushing rate which means they’re more consistently getting a quick stop. Is the run defense unbeatable? No. They have allowed a few explosive runs which to my eyes were shiftier runs to the outside. That’s something James Cook could certainly do. The Bills know how to support him too, with the fourth-best yards per carry in the league right now. Josh Allen is also second in the NFL in yards per attempt at 9.7 right now. The Bills have the firepower to beat the Chargers, and I’m not remotely trying to downplay that message. If there’s one matchup where Los Angeles would have an edge on paper though, run defense would be it.

title: Bills Mafia weighs in on Buffalo’s defense through 2 games of 2026 NFL season
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bills fans and fans across the country. Through two games, it’s fair to say that the Buffalo Bills have leaned quite heavily on the offense while building an unblemished record. That doesn’t mean […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 17: Amon-Ra St. Brown #14 of the Detroit Lions runs with the football during the second half of the NFL game against the Buffalo Bills at Highmark Stadium on September 17, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bills fans and fans across the country. Through two games, it’s fair to say that the Buffalo Bills have leaned quite heavily on the offense while building an unblemished record. That doesn’t mean the team’s defense has simply watched from the sidelines, comfortable taking a back seat to the party. Despite the incredible play by quarterback Josh Allen and the rest of Buffalo’s offense, it’s also true that without a few key plays on defense things might look different in the W-L column. Defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard is in the midst of transforming a defense group that, by and large, played instinctual football under the direction of former head coach Sean McDermott. Now operating out of a base 3-4 system, many players have been asked to alter their roles a bit. That naturally leads to a learning curve, but it sure seems as though the defensive front seven have been quick to pick up the changes. Notably, outside linebacker Greg Rousseau has taken a shine to playing a role he’d never manned before in the NFL. He currently leads the NFL in sacks with four, doing things he’d struggled to consistently produce even against similar opponents in years’ past. It’s a much different story with the defensive backfield, where the level of play has noticeably regressed. Before, cornerbacks Christian Benford and Maxwell Hairston were put in position to succeed as predominantly zone-based outside corners. While that changed slightly in McDermott’s final season, the difference in how they play and their results are stark. It’s not all bad, of course, but there have been enough plays that cause a person to wonder what’s going on with the defense. Apart from the household names on defense, new additions at defensive back in C.J. Gardner-Johnson and Dee Alford simply haven’t yet brought an improved level of play to the field. It’s early, of course and expecting anything would be 100% ready even by now might have folks asking if you’ve been drinking some strange Kool-Aid . Bills reporter Sal Capaccio with WGR 550 shared Buffalo’s overall rankings , which may surprise readers. Currently, the Bills’ defense is ranked as follows out of 32 NFL teams: Yards/game Week 1: 23rd Week 2: 28th Yards/play Week 1: 14th Week 2: 20th Rush yards/game Week 1: 20th Week 2: 12th Rush yards/play Week 1: 11th Week 2: 8th Pass yards/game Week 1: 25th Week 2: 30th Pass yards/play Week 1: 16th Week 2: 20th Sacks/pass attempt Week 1: 15th Week 2: 10th Red zone defense Week 1: T-21st Week 2: 25th Third-down defense Week 1: 21st Week 2: 19th Points/game Week 1: T-23rd (31.0) Week 2: T-28th (31.0) All that considered, how are you feeling about the defense through two games against quality offenses? Are you concerned about the yards given up and their official league rankings? Or are you optimistic given the improved play up front and the on-the-fly learning process elsewhere to this point? Vote now, and be sure to also weigh in with our weekly poll asking if you think the Bills are or are not headed in the right direction. How are you feeling about the Bills’ defense? title: Updating Buffalo Bills early-down pass frequency entering Week 3 game vs. Chargers
summary: This is an offensive tendency for the Buffalo Bills worth monitoring throughout the season. Early-down passing. A week ago, I presented the philosophy — and explained the thought behind it — mostly because the Bills came in sixth in the early-down (neutral situation) passing metric after all of Week 1’s action concluded. While just one […]
full_text: This is an offensive tendency for the Buffalo Bills worth monitoring throughout the season. Early-down passing. A week ago, I presented the philosophy — and explained the thought behind it — mostly because the Bills came in sixth in the early-down (neutral situation) passing metric after all of Week 1’s action concluded. While just one game, it was a stark contrast from Buffalo’s 20th-place finish in what was an overtly ground-game centric attack in 2025. Therefore, I’m likely going to be providing an update on this topic, with some commentary, every week. I think it’s that important for the Bills offense (every offense, really). Here’s where the Bills sit through two weeks in early-down passing frequency in non-garbage time situations: Still pretty darn good! Buffalo is eighth in early-down pass frequency in non-garbage time situations at north of 55%. A year ago through Week 2, the Bills were 28th in early-down pass frequency in these scenarios. I will continue to push for the Bills to inch closer to — and even eclipse — the 60% mark, but I also realize game script has its impact each week. The Bills led the Lions 27-7 at one point in the first half and 34-17 in the third quarter, so it was reasonably sensible for the offense to drain clock with the ground game. However, Detroit’s valiant effort that inched the score to 34-24 in the fourth quarter should serve as a reminder that — within reason — teams can’t take their proverbial foot off the gas in the modern NFL. Essentially no lead is safe. Not in this day and age of the sport. Anyway, Buffalo looks well on its way to staying in the upper fourth of the league in this advanced metric. With Josh Allen at quarterback, that is precisely where the Bills should live offensively all season.

title: Bills-Chargers history: Championships and weirdness
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers don’t see each other all that often anymore. There was a time, however, when they couldn’t seem to get away from each other.  When the Chargers make their first trip to Orchard Park since 2020 on Sunday, it will be the 42nd meeting between two franchises whose history together stretches all the way back […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers don’t see each other all that often anymore. There was a time, however, when they couldn’t seem to get away from each other. When the Chargers make their first trip to Orchard Park since 2020 on Sunday, it will be the 42nd meeting between two franchises whose history together stretches all the way back to the beginning. Buffalo and the Chargers were both original members of the American Football League in 1960, and by the middle of that decade, they were meeting with championships on the line. Yes, those championships – the ones the Bills have banners hanging for. The ones before the Super Bowl Era began. _____________________________________________________________________________ Back-to-back titles — both against the Chargers Buffalo has won two league championships in franchise history. Both came against the Chargers, exactly one year apart. On Dec. 26, 1964, the Bills hosted San Diego at War Memorial Stadium for the AFL Championship Game. Buffalo came away with a 20-7 win in front of a standing-room-only crowd of 40,242, giving the franchise its first championship. One year later, the teams did it again. This time Buffalo traveled to San Diego for the 1965 AFL Championship Game. The Bills didn’t just repeat — they shut the Chargers out, 23-0. Butch Byrd returned an interception 74 yards for a touchdown as Buffalo’s defense held San Diego to 223 total yards. ___________________________________ San Diego gets one back It would take another 15 years before the teams met in the postseason again, and this one went the other way. The Bills went 11-5 and won the AFC East in 1980, earning a trip to San Diego for the divisional round. Buffalo carried a 14-3 lead into halftime behind a Roosevelt Leaks touchdown run and a Joe Ferguson touchdown pass to Frank Lewis. Then Dan Fouts and the Chargers came back. San Diego pulled within 14-13 before Fouts connected with Ron Smith for a 50-yard touchdown with 2:08 remaining. The Chargers won 20-14, ending Buffalo’s season and accounting for San Diego’s lone postseason victory in the series. Buffalo still owns the playoff edge, 2-1. But the Chargers own the overall series, 25-14-2. _____________________________________________________________________________ The day the lights went out in Orchard Park Not every memorable Bills-Chargers game involved a championship or playoff berth. Sometimes all it takes is three helium balloons. The Chargers visited Ralph Wilson Stadium on Oct. 19, 2008, and the afternoon quickly became one of the stranger games played in Orchard Park. Three balloons became tangled in a power line outside the stadium, knocking out electricity and causing a delay during the first quarter. The scoreboard and play clocks went dark, the CBS broadcast disappeared, and officials eventually had to resume play while keeping time on the field. The Bills handled the weirdness better. Trent Edwards completed 25 of 30 passes for 261 yards and a touchdown, Marshawn Lynch scored the go-ahead touchdown in the third quarter, and Kawika Mitchell intercepted Philip Rivers in the end zone late in the fourth. Buffalo won 23-14 to improve to 5-1. But maybe we should leave the balloons at home on Sunday. _____________________________________________________________________________ The one we’d rather forget Of course, there is another Bills-Chargers game from the not-so-distant past that Buffalo fans probably remember for entirely different reasons. Nathan Peterman. Sean McDermott made the decision to start the rookie over Tyrod Taylor when Buffalo traveled to Los Angeles in November 2017. Peterman’s first NFL start lasted one half. He threw five interceptions on 14 attempts. The Chargers turned those mistakes into a 37-7 halftime lead. Peterman was replaced by Taylor for the second half, but there was no undoing the damage. Los Angeles won 54-24. Maybe we can just put that one back in the capsule and close the lid. _____________________________________________________________________________ The Allen era has belonged to Buffalo Things have gone considerably better against the Chargers since Josh Allen took over at quarterback. The teams have met twice during Allen’s career, and Buffalo has won both. The first came in Orchard Park in November 2020. Allen threw a touchdown and ran for another, while Cole Beasley got in on the fun by throwing a 20-yard touchdown pass to Gabe Davis. Buffalo’s defense intercepted rookie Justin Herbert, sacked him three times, and helped the Bills to a 27-17 win. Allen’s second Chargers meeting was considerably tighter. Buffalo traveled to Los Angeles on Dec. 23, 2023, and found itself trailing 10-0 in the second quarter before Allen connected with Gabe Davis for a 57-yard touchdown. Allen added two rushing touchdowns, but the Chargers took a 22-21 lead with 5:26 remaining. That left Buffalo needing one more drive. Allen and the offense moved the Bills into position for Tyler Bass, who connected from 29 yards with 28 seconds remaining to give Buffalo a 24-22 win. _____________________________________________________________________________ So, what does 66 years of Bills-Chargers history tell us about what to expect Sunday? Absolutely nothing. If this series has taught us anything, it’s that things can get weird in a hurry.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Josh Allen wins FedEx Air & Ground Player of the Week for second straight week
summary: Josh Allen is two games into the 2026 season and already has two FedEx Air & Ground Player of the Week awards. The Buffalo Bills quarterback won the Week 2 honor after leading Buffalo to a 41-31 victory over the Detroit Lions in the first game at the new Highmark Stadium. He also won the […]
full_text: Josh Allen is two games into the 2026 season and already has two FedEx Air & Ground Player of the Week awards. The Buffalo Bills quarterback won the Week 2 honor after leading Buffalo to a 41-31 victory over the Detroit Lions in the first game at the new Highmark Stadium. He also won the award for Week 1 against Houston. Allen completed 20 of 31 passes for 248 yards and three touchdowns against Detroit. He added 69 yards and two more scores on 14 carries, accounting for five of Buffalo’s touchdowns. That performance earned him AFC Offensive Player of the Week award, too. Allen was selected from a Week 2 FedEx field that also included Bills running back James Cook, quarterbacks Brock Purdy and Patrick Mahomes, and receivers CeeDee Lamb and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Smith-Njigba joined Allen as this week’s other winner after catching nine passes for 155 yards and three touchdowns for Seattle. The FedEx awards carry an impact beyond the field. Each week, FedEx donates $2,000 to Feeding America in honor of each winner, for a $4,000 weekly total benefiting local food banks in the winning players’ cities. With Allen winning in both Week 1 and Week 2, that means two donations made in his honor to a local food bank to start the season.

title: Bills news: Assessing Buffalo’s 2-0 start
summary: The Buffalo Bills are off to a 2-0 start for the sixth time in the last eight seasons, and Josh Allen and the offense are off to a dynamic start, averaging 38.5 points per game in wins over the Houston Texans and Detroit Lions. Despite the fast start, the Bills are not without their issues, […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills are off to a 2-0 start for the sixth time in the last eight seasons, and Josh Allen and the offense are off to a dynamic start, averaging 38.5 points per game in wins over the Houston Texans and Detroit Lions. Despite the fast start, the Bills are not without their issues, especially on defense, where Buffalo became just the third team in league history to begin a season 2-0 while allowing at least 30 points per game (along with the 1991 Bills and 2000 St. Louis Rams). After two weeks, today’s edition of Buffalo Rumblinks leads off by assessing what has gone right and where the Bills can still improve following their 2-0 start. Check out the assessments below and then let us know your thoughts in the comments section. Bills offense has been explosive, defense has work to do Among the reasons for optimism among Bills fans: the red-hot starts from quarterback Josh Allen, defensive tackle Deone Walker, running back James Cook, pass rusher Greg Rousseau, and tight end Dalton Kincaid; how well Buffalo’s offensive and defensive lines have played through two games; how efficient Allen has been directing a dynamic offense; and how vastly improved Buffalo’s third-down defense has been so far. Among the causes for concern: Buffalo’s secondary has been picked apart in the first two games of the season; the depth along the defensive line beyond Rousseau, Walker, Ed Oliver and Bradley Chubb has been inconsistent at best; and the defense has allowed opponents to convert on 53 percent of their late-down chances when a stop would clinch a victory. title: Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes laying the lumber as blockers for Buffalo Bills
summary: Nowadays, if you’re writing about a Buffalo Bills tight end, it’s probably Dalton Kincaid. But this piece is dedicated to shedding light on the occasionally overlooked aspect of… blocking at the position. While Kincaid has improved in this area, his fellow tight end mates, Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes, have blocking savants through two contests. […]
full_text: Nowadays, if you’re writing about a Buffalo Bills tight end, it’s probably Dalton Kincaid. But this piece is dedicated to shedding light on the occasionally overlooked aspect of… blocking at the position. While Kincaid has improved in this area, his fellow tight end mates, Dawson Knox and Jackson Hawes, have blocking savants through two contests. James Cook has seven runs of 10-plus yards through two games. That’s tied for the third-most in football. Knox has been on the field for all of them. Let’s dive into the film to highlight the dirty work done exquisitely by both of now veteran blockers. Here’s the first 10-plus yarder of the season for Cook, a run not possible without two second-level blocks from Knox and Hawes: pic.twitter.com/G7xXbvFCTl — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 That’s a reach block from Hawes on Sheldon Rankins, who’s been one of the more unrated backfield disruptors in football for a while now. On Cook’s 12-yard scamper that ended with a fumble and an O’Cyrus Torrence recovery against the Texans — yes, that run — Hawes stood up and stayed engaged with Danielle Hunter at the point of attack at the line of scrimmage. pic.twitter.com/tBDuhmmKTl — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 No easy task there. Hunter is one of the most physical imposing edge rushers in the NFL. Against the Lions, when Cook had five 10-plus yard runs, the tandem was sensational. First, check this reach and hook from Knox on defensive end D.J. Woonum, in space, to clear a clean cutback lane for Cook to accelerate through the second level. pic.twitter.com/l6rBAde8ye — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 The combination of Hawes and Knox’s blocks were essentially done in perfect rhythm here, just how it’s drawn up, on this long Cook run later in the game. Hawes washed down linebacker Derrick Barnes while Knox ascended to the second level to get a hat on 2025 All-Pro Jack Campbell, one of the largest off-ball linebackers in the game. pic.twitter.com/wsCzrxqpw2 — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 As if the Hunter assignment wasn’t difficult enough, Hawes later took on Aidan Hutchinson crashing inside and handled himself admirably. The subsequent block as Cook started to knife through the line of scrimmage was another Knox stick of Campbell in the whole. pic.twitter.com/KySPe6Uif9 — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 Another sizable gain for Buffalo’s rushing attack. Watch that one again, the cutback lane for Cook was gorgeously paved on that play. Late against the Lions, watch as Hawes cut off Malcolm Rodriguez as the linebacker over pursued, but I urge you to pay attention the snatch-trap utilized by Knox on Hutchinson at the left side of the screen. It ultimately became precisely where Cook ran with the football. And he nearly scored. pic.twitter.com/RFE8f1XB2A — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 No, that’s not a flag on Knox. Hats off to the refereeing crew for not calling a penalty there. Hawes has been especially sturdy as a pass protector too. He’s been credited with zero pressures allowed on 10 pass-blocking snaps, reps that many of which have looked like this (watch him on the right side of the screen): pic.twitter.com/86TFsZExcV — Chris Trapasso (@trapassofilm) September 23, 2026 Kincaid has been a receiving wizard through two games… and frankly, since the start of 2025. His yards-per-route-run figure is 4.69 through two games after leading all tight ends in YPRR at 2.70 last season. Knox has three catches for 12 yards entering Week 3. Hawes is still looking for his first catch of his second professional season. But we mustn’t forget about the serious value Knox and Hawes are adding to Buffalo’s offense as blockers. Because they’ve been sensational in the trenches, moving defensive lineman, clearing linebackers, and locking down the edges of Josh Allen’s pocket. No wonder t he Bills are second in the NFL in 13 personnel usage right now.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Jadan Baugh
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: OCTOBER 4, 2025 Florida running back Jadan Baugh (13) was a joy to shoot this season. Unfortunately his future at Florida is uncertain. Florida running back Jadan Baugh (13) leaps over Texas defensive back Graceson Littleton (29) during the first half an NCAA football game in Gainesville, FL on Saturday, October 4, 2025. [Alan Youngblood/Gainesville Sun] | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Florida Gators running back Jadan Baugh. Bio Baugh (6’1”, 230 lbs.) is the rare recruit to see substantial playing time as a true freshman in the SEC. Originally committed to Arkansas, the four star recruit out of Decatur, GA flipped to the Florida Gators late in the process. Not only did Baugh see the field a lot, he actually led the Gators in rushing during his true freshman season, racking up 673 yards and eight total touchdowns that season. Last year, still just a true sophomore, Baugh toted the rock 221 times for 1,168 yards and eight touchdowns and added a modest 210 yards and a couple scores through the air as well. Baugh has exploded in three games this season, already rushing for 458 yards and eight touchdowns on 8.5 yards per carry. Two of those three games have been against relative cupcakes, but that production is undeniable. Strengths/Weaknesses Baugh has the frame of a bell cow back in the NFL. He’s still a young player as a true junior but has the patience and technique of a much more seasoned player. He consistently runs behind his pads, rarely getting knocked backwards and routinely breaking arm tackles to extend runs. What could be his biggest strength in some coaches’ eyes is his ball security: Baugh has been credited with a lone fumble throughout his entire collegiate career. While he isn’t exactly Christian McCaffrey in the receiving game, he is a good enough receiver out of the backfield to make teams pay attention to swings and checkdowns. At the next level, teams will want him to do more in the passing game, especially with modern NFL offenses. He’ll also need to be coached up on his pass blocking technique and decision making in order to be a true three-down back. Baugh is not the type of back to win “in a phone booth,” relying more heavily on vision and patience to hit larger holes. Projection Baugh is exploding up draft boards, with some mock drafts having him as a first round selection (a couple even mocking him to the Panthers in the 20s). With his combination of workhorse durability, size, explosiveness, and ball security, it’s no wonder that he’s in the first round conversation. The Panthers could definitely use some young depth at running back, especially now that Jonathan Brooks is on IR with another surgery (this time a groin issue). Chuba Hubbard is not getting any younger, and Trevor Etienne has not flashed as a true number-one back type of player. Baugh would be a reliable backfield battery mate for Bryce Young, adding another element to the offense. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Jadan Baugh is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: Chicago Bears Pass Protection Analysis on the Sacks Allowed vs Vikings
summary: It’s not just the actual blitzers from Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores that get you; it’s also how they present themselves pre-snap to confuse a pass-blocking scheme and create favorable one-on-one matchups. All afternoon against the Chicago Bears, the Vikings showed multiple threats on the line of scrimmage; the Bears set their pass protection; […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - SEPTEMBER 2026: Minnesota Vikings linebacker Andrew van Ginkel (43) sacks Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams (18) on the last play of the second quarter at Solider Field in Chicago, Illinois, on Sunday, September 20, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) It’s not just the actual blitzers from Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores that get you; it’s also how they present themselves pre-snap to confuse a pass-blocking scheme and create favorable one-on-one matchups. All afternoon against the Chicago Bears, the Vikings showed multiple threats on the line of scrimmage; the Bears set their pass protection; then the Vikings dropped defenders off, leaving some Bears blockers unoccupied. Flores’ overall 75.9% blitz rate through two games is the highest in the NFL by far, with the second-highest coming from the Carolina Panthers at 48.1%. In case you were wondering, the Bears blitz the sixth most at 40.3%. But again, it’s not just the frequency of the blitz; it’s the design. Flores is really good at his job. Chicago didn’t know who was rushing or from where, and no stat showed that better than this. Here's a crazy stat from Brian Flores' defense that I just ran across: On Sunday vs. Chicago, 15 different players had at least one pass rushing snap. That is wild. — Matthew Coller (@MatthewColler) September 22, 2026 Now let’s move on to the Sackwatch! Sack 3: 2nd Quarter: 2-3-CHI 41 (:15) (Shotgun) C.Williams sacked at CHI 24 for -17 yards (A.Van Ginkel) Last play of the half, and the Bears were just trying to get a big chunk. The Vikings were showing 6 threats, and the Bears elected to slide protection left, leaving outside linebacker Dallas Turner (#15, circled) unblocked off the Bears’ right side (and Caleb Williams’ responsibility). The Bears must have figured Minnesota would drop one of the four inside defenders out, but they didn’t know who. On the snap, right tackle Darnell Wright got in position to cut off Turner while watching the man in front of him, linebacker Eric Wilson (#55). Check out the end zone view in the GIF below. If Wilson dropped, then Wright would try to quickly shift focus to Turner. But Wilson blitzed, so Wright had to stay. Linebacker Blake Cashman (#51), who was lined up over right guard Jonah Jackson, was the defender who dropped, but he did it after engaging, ensuring the Bears would keep Jackson and Wright exactly where their pass-blocking rules tell them to block, which meant Turner would be free. Cashman also dropped right into the throwing lane, so this was just a nice design and call here by Flores, who completely understood the situation. Caleb evaded Turner, but outside linebacker Andrew Van Ginkle (#43), who was chipped by running back Kyle Monangai, ran around left tackle Theo Benedet with little resistance and corralled Williams for the sack. Turner was the reason this play failed, and he was free due to a nice design and call by Flores, so I need to give at least half of this to Caleb (as Turner was his responsibility), but Benedet was too passive in his set, letting Van Ginkle dictate the rush, so half for him as well. To address Caleb’s part in this. Yes, I gave him some blame, but given the situation (they needed a big chunk of yards at the end of the half), I’m okay with him holding it in hopes of making a play by evading the rusher, which he nearly did, but Turner got a piece of him. Sack 4: 3rd Quarter: 1-10-CHI 13: (6:30) C.Williams sacked at CHI 10 for -3 yards (D.Turner) Turner gets home this time, but it’s a cleanup sack after quick pressure forced Caleb to move up. The Bears ran a two-man route concept, after a play action to show a run to the right, with tight end Cole Kmet leaking into the flat after the dive to cut Turner on the left side. Kmet’s “block” was just for show, because they also brought Colston Loveland over from the left side to block the edge. The Vikings show five threats with the three defensive linemen and two outside linebackers, and all five defenders come. The play action with the entire o-line going right freezes the Minnesota linebackers, but it didn’t freeze Van Ginkle, who was lined up far outside Darnell Wright. That meant Wright had a long way to go to get there while also trying to slow up Vikings defensive tackle Jalen Redmond (#61). That’s a long way for right guard Jonah Jackson to get to Redmond, and when he stayed on Domonique Orange (#97) for a split second to help center Garrett Bradbury get to Orange, Jackson couldn’t cut off the Big Citrus. Wright pushed Van Ginkle past the pocket, and Bradbury pushed Orange down the line, but Jackson was beat around the edge, and that missed block started the chain of events that led to Turner’s sack, so this one is on Jackson. Sack 5: 4th Quarter: 1-6-MIN 6 (7:42) C.Williams sacked at MIN 6 for 0 yards (B.Cashman) This is the play Williams slid down after pulling his hamstring, and as we now know, it’s a week-to-week injury. Cashman got credit for the 0-yard sack because he touched Caleb down. The hamstring pull is why this sack happened, and if it didn’t, this is probably 6, because Loveland was out in front, and Williams had the corner of the end zone in his sights. Sack 6: 4th Quarter: 4-2-MIN 12 (:01) (Shotgun) T.Bagent sacked at MIN 21 for -9 yards (D.Turner) The Bears received a gift when the refs put 1 second on the clock, giving them one final chance to tie the game with a touchdown. Just throw the ball to the end zone to give your receiver a chance. Or hit a player in the flat and let him make a play. Something, anything other than taking a sack. But as we now know, Bagent is in concussion protocol and may not have been able to focus entirely on this play, which could be why he didn’t feel the quick pressure from Turner, who beat Loveland off the left side. This was a seven-man protection by Chicago; the Vikings only rushed five, but here’s another play where Flores’ pre-snap look left Jonah Jackson with no one to block. I’ll give Loveland the sack allowed here, even though I think had Bagent been more aware, he would have chucked it toward the end zone. CHGO’s Marc Carmen, who is close with Bagent, said this 3rd-and-goal play, 2 snaps after Williams was injured, was the play Bagent was concussed on. This play was more egregious pic.twitter.com/A3LaNsGni2 — MattC (@MattCarl91) September 22, 2026 Here’s the individual Sackwatch tally after two weeks: Sacks happen – 2 Garrett Bradbury – 1 Jonah Jackson – 1 Colston Loveland – 1 Theo Benedet – .5 Caleb Williams – .5 Here are the total Bears’ sacks allowed through Week 2 going back to the Mike Martz era: 2010 Sacks – 5 (Martz) 2011 Sacks – 11 (Martz) 2012 Sacks – 9 (Tice) 2013 Sacks – 1 (Trestman) 2014 Sacks – 3 (Trestman) 2015 Sacks – 4 (Gase) 2016 Sacks – 8 (Loggains) 2017 Sacks – 5 (Loggains) 2018 Sacks – 6 (Nagy) 2019 Sacks – 5 (Nagy) 2020 Sacks – 5 (Nagy) 2021 Sacks – 6 (Nagy) 2022 Sacks – 5 (Getsy) 2023 Sacks – 10 (Getsy) 2024 Sacks – 9 (Waldron) 2025 Sacks – 6 (Johnson) 2026 Sacks – 6 (Johnson)

title: Ben Johnson confident in Bears’ QB room amid uncertainty heading into Week 3
summary: After Sunday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings left both Caleb Williams and Tyson Bagent dealing with injuries, the Chicago Bears enter Week 3 with uncertainty over which quarterback will suit up for Monday night’s matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Bears have not ruled out either Williams or Bagent for Monday night’s game, leaving the […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Case Keenum #11 of the Chicago Bears looks on prior to the game against the Minnesota Vikings at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images After Sunday’s game against the Minnesota Vikings left both Caleb Williams and Tyson Bagent dealing with injuries, the Chicago Bears enter Week 3 with uncertainty over which quarterback will suit up for Monday night’s matchup against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Bears have not ruled out either Williams or Bagent for Monday night’s game, leaving the team with several possibilities to sort through as the week progresses. Ben Johnson expressed confidence in the Bears’ quarterback room when addressing the media on Wednesday. “We’re fortunate here, we got three guys that can play ball in this league, that have won games in this league,” Johnson said. “Ryan [Poles] has constructed the room in a way that we feel really good about whoever ends up playing for us. That showed in the preseason, it shows up in practice every single day. We’ll let this thing play out, and we’ll go from there.” Bagent’s status will depend on his progress through the NFL’s concussion protocol, while the Bears continue to monitor Williams’ hamstring injury ahead of Monday night. If neither quarterback is cleared to play, the Bears would turn to their veteran third option, Case Keenum. Keenum was the only quarterback who practiced Wednesday in preparation to start if both Williams and Bagent are ruled out. Johnson pointed to the veteran quarterback’s experience as one of his biggest strengths that can be an advantage to them on Monday night. “He’s at the point of his career where he’s like another coach in a lot of ways. He’s seen a ton, he knows what good football looks like … he’s a key part of what we do,” Johnson said. Despite being in the later stages of his career, Keenum has the ability to play at a high level and has a strong connection with his teammates. “He’s got a knack. His teammates gravitate to him … he’s up there in years a little, but that experience has paid off for him,” Johnson stated. “He might be a step slower than he was when he first entered the league, and yet his mind’s going so fast, it helps catch him on up. He’s playing as good of football as he probably has his whole career is what he’d tell you.” As for Williams, Johnson described the quarterback not practicing as “foreign,” but noted that he has remained involved in the team’s preparation despite being unable to practice. “Caleb’s out there in walk-through, he’s actively out involved as well … he’s still being a great supporter in the quarterback room, walk-through right now, making sure he’s contributing ideas for what we want to get done,” Johnson said. Regardless of who starts, the Bears’ preparation process remains the same. Johnson emphasized that the uncertainty at quarterback will not change how the team approaches its game plan or preparation throughout the week. “It’s the same thing. We’re going to look for plays that we feel like might have a chance to get guys open, create some space in the passing game, running lanes in the running game,” Johnson explained. “It’s not just on one player, it never is. We got ten other guys out there with our quarterback. They got to help champion the cause and carry their weight as well. As far as I’m concerned, not a whole lot changes from a coaching perspective. We’re going to go out there and come up with as good of a game plan as best we possibly can, teach it as well as we possibly can, and let’s have a great week of practice.” With Monday night approaching, the Bears will continue to monitor both Williams and Bagent throughout the week before making a final decision at quarterback. Until then, Keenum remains prepared to step in if needed, while the rest of the team continues on course with its preparation for the Eagles.

title: Can the Eagles’ Jordan Davis keep the Bears’ 2 running backs in check?
summary: The rain on Sunday has not stopped (figuratively) pouring down on the Chicago Bears, as entering Wednesday it would seem that their top two QBs, Caleb Williams and Tyson Bagent, could potentially be unavailable when they play host to the Eagles on Monday night. This means a few things — the Bears rushing attack is […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - NOVEMBER 28: Philadelphia Eagles defensive tackle Jordan Davis (90) is blocked by Chicago Bears guard Joe Thuney (62) during the game between the Chicago Bears and the Philadelphia Eagles on November 28, 2025 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, PA.(Photo by Andy Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The rain on Sunday has not stopped (figuratively) pouring down on the Chicago Bears, as entering Wednesday it would seem that their top two QBs, Caleb Williams and Tyson Bagent, could potentially be unavailable when they play host to the Eagles on Monday night. This means a few things — the Bears rushing attack is going to be as potent as ever…and the Eagles rushing defense is going to do everything in their power to stop it. Entering week 3, Ben Johnson’s rushing attack leads the NFL with 212.5 yards per game, nearly 30 yards more than the next best team. Meanwhile, Vic Fangio’s unit is not where it wants to be at 24th in the league while giving up 127 yards of rushing per game. While the season is still young, it paints a familiar picture of a Bears rushing attack that ranked 3rd in 2025, and an Eagles rushing defense that ranked 21st last season. You don’t even need to look at the entire 2025 season to see what the Bears game plan ought to be on Monday night. All you need to do is look back to the performance they put on in Philly last November. In that game, the Bears had a whopping 281 rushing yards, with both Swift and Monangai tallying more than 125 yards each. While Caleb’s legs always provided a threat, he had a relatively quiet day with 13 yards rushing. He also had a pretty quiet and inefficient day passing, throwing 17/36 for 154 yards and a 57 rating. This is the blueprint for the Bears to get back on track in week 3. Still, it won’t be easy to replicate a performance like that, especially with the talent Philly boasts up front. The Eagles DL remains one of the best in the league, boasting two bona fide studs in Jordan Davis and Jalen Carter. While Carter works from the end, Davis is going to be heavily relied upon to plug up the middle of the line and slow the Bears rushing attack. Here is a series of clips from last year’s matchup showing: Drew Dalman and Joe Thuney immediately pushing Davis off the point of attack leading to an 18 yard pickup for Monangai. A huge gain by Swift where Davis wasn’t on the field. A 3 yard touchdown run by Swift where Thuney stymies Davis at the line. Drew Dalman beats Davis one on one while Jackson and Wright open up a massive hole on the right side to break Swift out for an 18 yard gain. Davis is once again missing while swift breaks off another chunk play. Thuney stands Davis up at the line and keeps him from moving laterally to stop Monangai, leading to a 30+ yard gain. Dalman and Jackson get a strong push left against Davis to open up a gap for a 5 yard touchdown for Kyle Monangai. The Bears ran all over the Eagles in their last matchup. – 281 rushing yards – Monangai: 130 yards (5.9 avg), 1 TD – Swift: 125 yards (6.9 avg), 1 TD pic.twitter.com/xHNO1yeklf — Depressed Bears Fan (@ImBearsFan) September 23, 2026 While the Bears no longer have Dalman, and Garrett Bradbury has not yet proven to be a perfect replacement, the duo of Jackson and Thuney in the middle should go a long way to help open up holes in the middle of the line. In looking at Davis’ snap count last season, he found himself on about 66% of snaps in most games, including the Bears. So far this season he is hovering around 50%, so I would expect the Bears to test his conditioning in the middle early and often with a power running attack. If the Bears can wear down Davis in the middle, we could see another big day from the rushing attack. If Monangai and Swift are unable to break loose — it’s going to be a long day at the office for Keenum.

title: Chicago Bears open the practice window for 2 players on the PUP List
summary: The Chicago Bears have three players on the Physically Unable to Perform list (PUP): cornerback Kyler Gordon, linebacker Noah Sewell, and defensive lineman Shemar Turner. Today was the first day they could have their 21-day practice window open to ensure they could play in Week 5, which is the earliest a player starting the season […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 21: Shemar Turner #95 of the Chicago Bears walks off the field after an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at Solider Field on September 21, 2025 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears have three players on the Physically Unable to Perform list (PUP): cornerback Kyler Gordon, linebacker Noah Sewell, and defensive lineman Shemar Turner. Today was the first day they could have their 21-day practice window open to ensure they could play in Week 5, which is the earliest a player starting the season on the PUP list could be activated. Head coach Ben Johnson announced today that Sewell (Achilles) and Turner (knee) would both be back at practice today. The Bears will be able to evaluate them, and if they are ready, they can be activated to the 53-man roster at any point before the 21 days expire. If they can’t return, then they’ll be moved to season-ending injured reserve. Regarding Gordon (calf), Johnson said , “I’ve got nothing to add there.” Also today, Johnson announced that starting cornerback Tyrique Stavenson is week-to-week with a hamstring injury. He was also asked about Ozzy Trapilo returning to the field for gameday, saying , “I think he is still gaining confidence to put his entire weight on it. It won’t be too long before we can get him back out there.” He added Ozzy will practice in full again today. With Caleb Williams (hamstring) and Tyson Bagent (concussion) both possibly out, Johnson said they will not add another quarterback to the roster. So, if those two can’t go, it’ll be Case Keenum and Miller Moss elevated from the practice squad.
