title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL: Injuries suck
summary: 1. I’ve already said my piece on the toxic discussion about Caleb Williams’ emotional reaction to his hamstring injury, and I don’t feel like I have much more to add. That said, since I called out the idiotic former players and talking heads that talked trash about Williams being too “extra” about a hamstring strain, […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD,CALIFORNIA - SEPTEMBER 21: Jaxson Dart #6 of the New York Giants lays on the field after being injured during the first quarter of an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium on September 21, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images 1. I’ve already said my piece on the toxic discussion about Caleb Williams’ emotional reaction to his hamstring injury, and I don’t feel like I have much more to add. That said, since I called out the idiotic former players and talking heads that talked trash about Williams being too “extra” about a hamstring strain, let me shout out ex-Bear Kyle Long for being a real one. 2. The rash of injuries to young quarterbacks this past week was brutal. At this point, the world just has it out for Jayden Daniels, who dislocated his elbow on a freak play. It feels like RG3 all over again as far as the excitement of Daniels’ rookie year being completely ruined by bad luck and shaky health afterward. Then, Jaxson Dart goes down with a knee injury that, after initially seemed manageable, looks like it could be season-ending—after having put up a stunning Week 1 performance against the Dallas Cowboys. Plus, you’re taking Williams and Tyson Bagent from us this week? Hate it. 3. Has any football player of this past generation been more insufferable than Aaron Rodgers? Seriously, this might be my question of the week to answer in the comments below. Because how are you going to play like that and then take shots st the coaching staff? Especially when you turned the ball over twice? We’re not going to act like Mike McCarthy is some kind of savant at this point in his career. But his longtime quarterback’s lack of self-awareness and reflection will never cease to amaze me. I’d say, “Just retire already,” but I’m also kind of enjoying him realizing in real time that he’s bad while being unable to admit or acknowledge it. 4. Maybe it really was Eric Bieniemy all along. Okay, but really: the Kansas City Chiefs look like a rejuvenated offense even with Patrick Mahomes still finding his footing post-ACL injury. I wasn’t sure how much stock I should put in Kenneth Walker coming into this season, given how the Chiefs struggled last year even with Mahomes. But apparently I didn’t buy nearly enough. I guess all KC needed was to get Matt Nagy away from the offensive coordinator spot. 5. I’m sorry, you can’t make me take the Raiders seriously with this 2-0 start. It’s just not going to happen. (Though maybe they’ll be better than I expected in an AFC West that looks way less mighty than in years past with the Chargers back to Chargering.) But you have to admit, this is an absolute dream scenario for the Fernando Mendoza development plan Vegas hoped to implement. Plenty of teams love the idea of drafting a kid and sitting him all season only to see the plan implode within three games because the veteran starter is awful. So far, Kirk Cousins is giving Klint Kubiak and Co. exactly what they need to keep Mendoza on the bench (barring injury). I’ve started coming around to the idea that sometimes these kids just need time to chill out and watch a seasoned pro do things. Then again, you don’t normally get someone like Cousins as your vet. Someone’s usually trying to peddle us Jacoby Brissett (sorry, bro) or Gardner Minshew. That’s the magic of it for Vegas and Mendoza. 6. Don’t be surprised if the Sean Payton-Mike MacDonald becomes a hot topic when training camp comes around, especially when it comes to filming plays. Payton was reportedly upset that Macdonald and the Seattle Seahawks watched plays posted to X as part of their scouting for last year’s matchup in Week 1, even threatening to go full Spygate on them until Seattle got litigation ready. While media members are generally prohibited from taking video during team periods or any time formations were being walked through, teams have a harder time stopping fans from snagging video of plays and posting them online. Technically, there’s nothing illegal about what Seattle did since the plays are in a public forum. One could see that loophole being contested heading into next season. 7. I’ll probably always have a slight soft spot for Kellen Moore just because he’s the one football player my wife has heard of. (They both grew up in Prosser, Washington—aka the middle of nowhere.) So it’s pretty fun seeing the Saints coming out guns blazing in 2026. Taking down a Ravens team that should be a legit contender in Week 2 after putting up a valiant effort in a loss against Detroit in Week 1 is a great start for a young team hoping to compete in a wide-open NFC South. Also, Tyler Shough is on a mission to make sure we all know how to pronounce his name correctly with the way he’s playing so far. 8. Look, I’m all for a good Josh Allen glaze—the guy is really good. But can we chill on even the suggestion that he’s the best running quarterback ever? He has indeed scored a lot of touchdowns on the ground, more than anyone in NFL history (83). You know who’s third after Cam Newton’s 75 rushing scores? Jalen Hurts (63), in two fewer seasons, mind you. You gonna tell me that Jalen Hurts is the third-best rushing QB of all time? Are we really going to argue any one of these three names is better than Lamar Jackson or Michael Vick just because they didn’t punch it in as often? Let’s be for real now. They want Allen to get another MVP so bad… 9. I never bought into the weirdness about CJ Stroud “little-broing” Caleb Williams by giving him advice after their game two years ago. Like, oh no, a second-year player acted like he had more experience than a rookie? How insulting! What I will say is: good lord, Stroud is going through a generational aura loss after that Rookie of the Year campaign. It’s not just all the injuries, the offensive coordinator changes, or lack of running game, either. Then again, he’s not the only one: Justin Herbert has put himself on fraud watch this year—a sentence I’m sad to be writing. The NFL is a fickle place, man. 10. I’m never doubting Brian Flores again. My bad, dawg. Also, given that this man was definitely right about Tua not being very good, is he allowed to have a head-coaching job again? I know there’s almost no chance of that as long as his lawsuit against the NFL is active. I’m just saying that if the NFL were actually a meritocracy, he’d have the top job somewhere that wasn’t Minnesota and, therefore, wouldn’t be torturing the Bears twice a year.
author: Khari Thompson

title: Caleb Williams Week 2 QB Grade: Vikings @ Bears Film Breakdown
summary: Note: I know I said last week that play breakdowns would return, but as I sit here writing this at 3 A.M., my full-time job has demanded a little more of my free time than usual. Rather than rush through them to meet the deadline for this article, I’m going to put together a separate […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears reacts against the Minnesota Vikings during the second quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images Note: I know I said last week that play breakdowns would return, but as I sit here writing this at 3 A.M., my full-time job has demanded a little more of my free time than usual. Rather than rush through them to meet the deadline for this article, I’m going to put together a separate article next week breaking down some of the more interesting plays from the first two games. People, what a difference a week makes. Seven days after the Chicago Bears opened their season by scoring 59 points and piling up 552 yards against the Carolina Panthers, they returned home to Soldier Field and gave us just about the exact opposite. In a rainy, sloppy game that featured very little offense from either side, the Bears fell to the Minnesota Vikings 9-3, dropping to 1-1 on the season. The frustrating part is that Chicago had plenty of opportunities to win it. The Bears actually outgained Minnesota 297-246, held the ball for more than five additional minutes and picked up 17 first downs compared to just 11 for the Vikings. Unfortunately, they also turned the ball over twice, committed eight penalties for 58 yards and finished 0-for-3 in the red zone. All three of those red-zone trips came in the second half, with Chicago reaching the Minnesota 1, 5 and 12-yard lines without scoring a single point. That’s certainly one way to follow up a 59-point performance. For as rough as things looked offensively, the Bears defense deserves plenty of credit for keeping them in the game. After surrendering 37 points in Week 1, Dennis Allen’s group held Minnesota to just 246 total yards and didn’t allow a touchdown all afternoon. For Caleb Williams, it was a much different afternoon than the one we saw in Carolina. Williams completed 15 of 26 passes for 138 yards with no touchdowns and one interception, finishing with a 56.2 passer rating. He added another 42 yards on five carries, but Chicago struggled to consistently find answers against Brian Flores’ aggressive defense. The box score, however, doesn’t tell the entire story of Williams’ afternoon. Despite everything Minnesota threw at him, his accuracy remained remarkably consistent. Williams finished with an 82.6% On Target rate, and while the explosive plays weren’t there, he generally avoided making a difficult situation worse. Against a defense constantly changing the picture before and after the snap, Williams remained patient, took what was available and largely avoided forcing the football into danger. That showed up in my grading as well. Williams still managed to finish with a positive overall game grade, thanks largely to consistently accurate throws and smart decisions. Even with Minnesota applying pressure throughout the afternoon, he had just one throw graded worse than “Bad.” And applying pressure might be underselling what Flores was doing. The Vikings blitzed Williams on 27 of his 33 dropbacks, good for an 81.8% blitz rate. According to Next Gen Stats, that would rank as the third-highest single-game blitz rate by a defense since at least 2018. Around The NFL shared the Next Gen Stats breakdown here. So while the final numbers certainly weren’t pretty, there was more good underneath the surface than the 56.2 passer rating would have you believe. Unfortunately, the biggest story involving Williams came midway through the fourth quarter when he went down with a right hamstring injury while scrambling on first-and-goal from the Minnesota 6. Tyson Bagent took over and eventually gave Chicago one final chance, driving the Bears to the Minnesota 12 with 10 seconds remaining before Dallas Turner sacked him on the final play of the game. The good news is that Williams appears to have avoided a significant injury. Ben Johnson announced Monday that his quarterback is considered week-to-week with a hamstring pull. Ian Rapoport shared Johnson’s update Monday morning. Now that we’ve got that depressing little recap out of the way, let’s get into Caleb’s Week 2 performance. For more information including scoring key, game-by-game grading sheets, weekly grading scorecards, and an overall look at his 2026 season, you can view Caleb’s entire season workbook here . Benchmarks Stat Formatting Key: (Last Season totals are underlined , Week 1 totals in Italics , and this week’s stats appear in regular text.) C/A: 330/568 (58.1%) | 19.4/33.4 (58.1%) | 15/26 57.7% Yards: 3942 | 231.9 | 138 Touchdowns: 31 | 1.8 | 0 Turnovers: 8 | 0.5 | 1 QB at Fault Sacks: 1 3 | 0.8 | 0 aDOT: 8.9 | 4.0 Passer Rating: 90.1 | 56.3 True Passer Rating : 125. 8 | 53.2 Time to Throw: 3.19s | 3.49s Time to Pressure: 2.56s | 2.56s Pressure Rate: 41.46% | 41.67% On-Target Rate: 84.0% | 82.6% Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 4.7% PPR / 11.6% BRP | 5.4% PPR / 2.7% BRP EPA per dropback: +0.54 | +0.05 ANY/A : 9.7 | 2.5 Game Scorecard The full grading sheet for each play can be found here. Game Notes Note: Last year, I included PFF grades in these breakdowns. With PFF continuing to expand its use of AI across its platform, and with my confidence in how accurately its grades reflect quarterback performance declining, I’ve decided to move away from them this season. In their place, I’ll be using PFN’s Impact Score , which will be notated as PFN on grading sheets moving forward. NFL Passer Rating / True Passer Rating / PFN Impact Score: 56.2 / 53.2 / 69.9 The NFL’s average passer rating through Week 2 sits at 96.4 , putting Williams’ 56.2 comfortably below the league average. His 5.3 YPA, zero touchdowns and one interception all worked against him in a metric heavily influenced by traditional box-score production. A 53.2 TPR represents a poor game in my model, where 100 serves as the baseline for “Average.” That’s a complete reversal from Week 1. The 53.2 would be Williams’ lowest TPR of any 2025 start by more than 25 points, with his previous low coming against Philadelphia in week 13. One major factor was an ADoT of roughly 4.0 yards, a massive drop from his 10.4-yard mark in Week 1. On the PFN scale, where 75 represents an average qualifying starter and 90 is elite territory, Williams finished Week 2 with a 69.9 Impact Score , ranking 25th of 30 qualifying quarterbacks. Despite the rough Week 2 showing, Williams still ranks 10th overall among quarterbacks this season with an 80.5 Impact Score. On-Target Throws: 2026 Average: 84.0% | Week 2: 82.6% Reminder: Completion percentage ≠ On-Target Percentage. I only chart aimed passes, meaning throwaways, spikes and passes deflected at the line are excluded. Drops can still be credited as on-target. Short-Level Passing (Behind LOS–9 yards): 15/17 | 88.2% On-Target Deep-Level Passing (10–20+ yards): 4/6 | 66.7% On-Target The accuracy has remained remarkably consistent through two games. Williams has now posted an On-Target rate above 80% in both starts, already surpassing the one such performance he had all of 2025. The short-range accuracy has been particularly encouraging at 90.9% on the season so far. This was an area where he struggled throughout 2025 . Poor Play Rate / Big Play Rate: 5.4% PPR / 2.7% BPR The interception and one poorly aimed pass late in the second half were the primary blemishes on an otherwise relatively mistake-free afternoon. As always, turnovers are double-graded in my system. Williams received the automatic -1.00 turnover grade, along with a separate contextual grade of “Below Average” on the throw itself. On tape, it appears Williams expected Luther Burden III to settle into the zone while Burden continued working with the quarterback. The pass was high, but still catchable with effort in Burden ended up settling. Williams’ lone “Great” or better play came on his scramble and sack avoidance before finding Kalif Raymond for eight yards,…

title: Bears-Vikings Upon Further Review: A Closer Look at the Referees
summary: Hello Chicago Bears Fans!  Well, this is a much sadder second installment in our series than I initially thought it would be after the game on Sunday. So welcome back to my in-season series on the striped ones, the zebras, the arbiters-of-the-yellow-flag: the referees.  Let’s briefly review the project:  Upon Further Review exists to answer […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - SEPTEMBER 20: Dallas Turner #15 of the Minnesota Vikings sacks Tyson Bagent #17 of the Chicago Bears during the fourth quarter of the game at Soldier Field on September 20, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello Chicago Bears Fans! Well, this is a much sadder second installment in our series than I initially thought it would be after the game on Sunday. So welcome back to my in-season series on the striped ones, the zebras, the arbiters-of-the-yellow-flag: the referees. Let’s briefly review the project: Upon Further Review exists to answer the questions about the calls on the field with film, the rulebook, and a consistent grading scale: Each week I isolate the flags and no-calls that went against Chicago and against the opponent, grade every one as Correct, Arguable, Incorrect, or Horrible, then roll those grades into four numbers: a Calls-Against-Bears rating, a Calls-Against-Opponent rating, an overall referee performance score, and a differential that shows which sideline got the better of the crew. I also pull the most controversial calls from around the league so we can see what call this week has NFL fans screaming, “wait, what?” and NFL rules analysts assuring us, “always has been.” Week 1 was a 59-point win and a pile of flags that mostly evened out. Week 2 is the first loss of the series, and it was a 9–3 slop-fest in the rain that Chicago donated on offense — then didn’t get back from Land Clark’s crew when it mattered. This week the accepted tape is mostly self-inflicted: Bradbury, Roush, grounding, a drive that started at the Minnesota 30 and ended in a punt. The Bears Tax, however, reared its ugly head in this game, and I have all of the gory details. Three no-calls in the fourth quarter, including forcible head/neck contact and a lift-and-slam on Tyson Bagent on the last two snaps from the 12, with the backup now in concussion protocol. The Vikings earned their 9–3 victory with some stellar plays in the downpour that killed near-certain Bears scoring opportunities. But that doesn’t mean the stripped ones didn’t play their own role in the Bears’ defeat. Below is every accepted flag, in order, with the player when named, the yardage, the game clock, and the score when the penalty was enforced. First Quarter MIN 3, CHI 0 Garrett Bradbury (CHI), offensive holding / Levi Rodriguez (MIN), roughing the passer — offsetting — 7:42. Chicago has reached 1st-and-10 at the MIN 35 after converting 3rd-and-1. Williams throws incomplete short right; Rodriguez is in on the play. Both flags come out. Down is replayed. Not in the official 8–58 / 3–25. Braxton Jones (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 7:00. 2nd-and-7 at the MIN 32. Monangai runs left tackle for 8 yards to the 24. Jones is flagged on the edge. Play comes off the board: 2nd-and-17 at the MIN 42. Williams dumps to Monangai for 4, then scrambles 6 on 3rd-and-13 to the 32. Santos still makes the 50-yarder at 5:03. MIN 3, CHI 3 Garrett Bradbury (CHI), false start, 5 yards — 2:57. After Wentz’s aborted snap turns 3rd-and-2 into 4th-and-24 and Thorson punts, Raymond fair-catches at the CHI 42. First play of the drive: Bradbury flinches. 1st-and-15 at the 37. Anthony Van Ginkel (MIN), defensive offside, 5 yards — 1:53. 3rd-and-12 at the CHI 40. Williams goes deep left to Odunze, incomplete, but Van Ginkel is in the neutral zone. Replay the down: 3rd-and-7 at the CHI 45. Chicago (team), delay of game, 5 yards — 1:47. Six seconds after the offside gift, the play clock expires in shotgun. 3rd-and-12 at the 40 again. Williams throws deep middle for Burden. Byron Murphy intercepts at the MIN 36. Second Quarter MIN 3, CHI 3 Jaylon Johnson (CHI), illegal use of hands — declined — 13:15. 3rd-and-4 at the MIN 42. Wentz hits Jefferson over the middle for 16 yards to the CHI 42. Johnson’s flag is picked up. Catch and first down stand. Minnesota will kick Reichard’s 49-yarder at 8:18. MIN 6, CHI 3 Dallas Turner (MIN), roughing the passer, 15 yards — 6:18. Chicago is answering. 2nd-and-10 at the CHI 40. Williams completes short right to Raymond for 5, to the 45. Turner hits Williams after the throw. Automatic first: 1st-and-10 at the MIN 40. Swift loses 2. Chicago later converts 4th-and-3 to the MIN 30 — then the next four flags live on this same drive. Sam Roush (CHI), illegal shift, 5 yards — 3:02. 1st-and-10 at the MIN 30, already in field-goal range. Williams hits Loveland for 14 yards to the 16. Roush is flagged for an illegal shift. Replay first down: 1st-and-15 at the MIN 35. Loveland’s catch does not count. Garrett Bradbury (CHI), offensive holding, 10 yards — 2:35. 1st-and-15 at the MIN 35. Swift right guard for 3, to the 32. Bradbury holds. Enforced from the tackle: 1st-and-22 at the MIN 42. Caleb Williams (CHI), intentional grounding, 13 yards — 2:13. Shotgun, 1st-and-22 at the MIN 42. Wilson’s pressure. Williams throws it into the dirt short right with no eligible in the area. Loss of down: 2nd-and-35 at the CHI 45. Two-minute warning next. Garrett Bradbury (CHI), false start, 5 yards — 2:00. After an 11-yard screen to Swift makes it 3rd-and-24 at the MIN 44, Bradbury false-starts in shotgun. 3rd-and-29 at the MIN 49. Incompletion to Kmet. Taylor punts 37 yards. Four accepted flags, 33 yards, MIN 30 to a punt from midfield. Third Quarter MIN 6, CHI 3 No accepted flags. Christian Darrisaw (MIN), illegal formation — declined — 6:49. 3rd-and-2 at the MIN 32. Wentz is sacked. Formation flag is picked up. Minnesota punts. Chicago (team), illegal formation — declined — 4:20. 3rd-and-10 at the CHI 27. Raymond catch for 7. Flag is declined. Chicago punts. Fourth Quarter MIN 6, CHI 3 Josh Oliver (MIN), false start, 5 yards — 14:43. Minnesota 2nd-and-10 at its own 12. Oliver jumps. 2nd-and-15 at the MIN 7. They still get enough to punt from the 21. Raymond starts Chicago at the 33 — the drive that will reach the 1 (Swift fumble) and the 5 (Rodgers block). Tyrique Stevenson (CHI), defensive holding, 5 yards — 4:05. 1st-and-10 at the MIN 32. Wentz throws deep right for Jefferson, incomplete. Stevenson is holding. Automatic first: 1st-and-10 at the MIN 37. Hockenson then picks up 19 to the CHI 44. Chicago burns timeouts. Reichard’s 39-yarder at 1:09 makes it 9–3. MIN 9, CHI 3 No accepted flags on the final Bears drive. The two RTP no-calls on Bagent (3rd-and-2 head/neck; 4th-and-2 Turner lift-and-slam) belong in the no-call column, which we will get to forthwith. Upon Further Review — Week 2: Bears 3, Vikings 9 Crew: Land Clark . Official totals: Chicago 8 penalties, 58 yards . Minnesota 3 penalties, 25 yards . The scale. Every accepted flag — and every no-call we put on the ledger — gets one of four grades: Correct — the rule and the tape agree. Arguable — judgment call; you can see both sides. Incorrect — the tape says the crew got it wrong. Horrible — bright-line foul (or non-foul) a wing official should not miss. The weight. Impact, 1 to 4, stacked on the grade: 1 — housekeeping (false start that doesn’t kill a scoring chance). 2 — drive disruption (down-and-distance flip, stalled series). 3 — scoring situation / red-zone / automatic first that feeds points. 4 — wiped score or takeaway, dead drive flipped into points, or a last-snap foul that would have been 1st-and-goal. Snapshot: Flags For and Against Welp, here we are, analyzing the flags that, at least arguably, cost us the game. Calls against Chicago play quarter clock score player penalty yards result grade weight situation 1 1 7:00 MIN 3-CHI 0 Braxton Jones Offensive holding 10 accepted Arguable 2 2nd-and-7 MIN 32; wiped Monangai 8-yard run 2 1 2:57 MIN 3-CHI 3 Garrett Bradbury False start 5 accepted Correct 1 1st-and-10 CHI 42 after punt 3 1 1:47 MIN 3-CHI 3 Team Delay of game 5 accepted Correct 2 3rd-and-7 CHI 45 after Van Ginkel offside; next snap INT 4 2 3:02 MIN 6-CHI 3 Sam Roush Illegal shift 5 accepted Correct 3 1st-and-10 MIN 30; wiped Loveland 14-yard catch 5 2 2:35 MIN…

title: Chicago Bears Midweek Musings: Whiplash
summary: Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: So I may have gotten a little bit ahead of myself tracking the Bears to eclipse the single season scoring record set by the Denver Broncos at […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson looks on in the rain before a game against the Minnesota Vikings at Soldier Field. Mandatory Credit: Matt Marton-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: So I may have gotten a little bit ahead of myself tracking the Bears to eclipse the single season scoring record set by the Denver Broncos at 606 points. Ben Johnson’s stated goal and the 59 point showing in Week 1 got me dreaming big. Now, with the Caleb Williams injury and the terrible Week 2 showing, I’m feeling whiplash. A lot has been said about the Caleb Williams injury and I’ll just say, I was thinking we were dealing with an Achilles tear and how the rest of the season was essentially over. Incredible news that Caleb is looking at a condensed rehab and will hopefully be back on the field by the Green Bay game in Week 5. Garrett Bradbury might have had the worst day of anyone on Sunday. I know Ben Johnson wants that veteran presence at center, but Logan Jones has the hairline of someone who has refinanced his mortgage – I think he can step in and do the job. To give Bradbury some benefit of the doubt here, the wet conditions seemed to really mess with his game – extra concentration to complete the snap combined with bad footing put him in conflict all day. The autumnal equinox has come and gone, and we are officially in the fall season. I have failed to complete my summer checklist for the umpteenth year in a row, but this year was particularly bad with the heat and humidity. Good riddance. I’ve been impressed with the rookie defensive backs thus far. Dillon Thieneman and Malik Muhammad have both played well in their first NFL action. Maybe not a surprise for Thieneman, the first rounder, but Muhammad stepping in early has been a pleasant surprise. This secondary will be tested with this schedule so it’s nice to see early returns on the rookies. Speaking of rookies, the second Ben Johnson draft class has had mixed results with Sam Roush’s poor Week 2 performance and Zavion Thomas’s lack of snaps. But that’s what September football is all about – figuring out what you have and what you don’t. Remember, Luther Burden was brought along slowly last year before catching fire late in the season. Give these guys a chance. I drafted Colston Loveland in the third round of the redraft fantasy football league I’ve been in forever. Let’s just say that the early returns aren’t great on that investment. It sure felt like the Bears paid some additional penalty tax in that game against the Vikings, particularly that late hit out of bounds on the punt return that didn’t draw a flag. I’ve never seen anything more obvious that didn’t draw a flag in my life. And then the guy flopped and it looked like he might’ve drawn a flag against the Bears before the refs picked it up. That would have been an insane double taxation moment had they marched off 15 against the Bears on a clear Vikings penalty, so I guess we should be thankful for that… After rewatching the game, I came away with the thought that I’d seen that game before, but in reverse, many times. How many times have the Bears played on a sloppy field that reduced the game to a messy field position game, getting the defensive plays when needed, and pulling out an ugly victory? Seems like a million. Bears fans got a taste of their own medicine as the Bears did have two drives that looked like TDs that came away with zero points. The first ended with a Swift fumble at the goal line. The second was disrupted with the injury to Williams where he had the angle for a score before eventually getting a 23-yard field goal blocked. Ridiculous odds of those two things happening in the same game. Bad luck, hopefully that’s the end of that. As the Bears shape their new identity under Ben Johnson, does it challenge anyone to think that maybe they would be better off playing in a dome where weather won’t slow down their high-flying offense? Detroit put up those great offenses under Johnson in part because they were never slowed by a bad weather game. Just a thought. It doesn’t matter because the Bears are never going to actually build a new stadium. They’re just going to keep torturing fans with new updates every few weeks that lead to more annoying questions from everyone you run into on the streets and over the the holidays with family. I thought Tyrique Stevenson and Jaylon Johnson bounced back after their rough Week 1 performances. I also think both defenses benefitted from the wet conditions. It’ll be a real test on Monday to see if these two can be a viable tandem this year. Pete Crow Armstrong is going to win the NL MVP this year with an incredible season for the Cubs. The last time the Cubs had an MVP was Kris Bryant in 2016. The Bears haven’t had an MVP since Walter Payton in 1977. In fact, they’ve only had 3 players in their 100+ year history to win the award – Harlon Hill in 1955 won one of the league MVP awards, and Sid Luckman took the honors in 1943. The Cubs have had 5 since Payton won his (Ryne Sandberg, Andre Dawson, Sammy Sosa, Bryant, PCA), and we’re not exactly talking about the most successful baseball team here. I need to see a Bears MVP season in my lifetime. I dug into the history of the Chicago Bears scoring 50 or more points in the regular season and was shocked (well, it’s the Bears so not that shocked) that they’ve only done it 14 times in their history. And they’ve never done it more than once in a single season. I have a feeling that we’ll soon be talking about number of times Ben Johnson’s Bears have scored 50 versus the rest of Bears history. My money is on Ben to eventually win that one.

title: 3 keys to a Cincinnati Bengals victory vs. the Pittsburgh Steelers
summary: One of the NFL’s fiercest rivalries renews this week when the Cincinnati Bengals head to the Steel City to face the Pittsburgh Steelers. If the Bengals are to win and start the year 3-0, here are three keys to getting it done in Pittsburgh. Establish the running game The Steelers still have a ton of […]
full_text: One of the NFL’s fiercest rivalries renews this week when the Cincinnati Bengals head to the Steel City to face the Pittsburgh Steelers . If the Bengals are to win and start the year 3-0, here are three keys to getting it done in Pittsburgh. Establish the running game The Steelers still have a ton of talent on the defensive side of the ball, specifically with their ability to rush the passer with their defensive line. One way to limit the impact of that defensive line is to establish the running game early. A quality rushing attack from Cincinnati will keep players like TJ Watt, Alex Highsmith, Nick Herbig, Cameron Heyward, Derrick Harmon, and others from teeing off on Joe Burrow and the Bengals’ passing attack. It will also open up play action for the big plays down the field to the Cincinnati playmakers. Chase Brown ran the ball 20 times for 80 rushing yards. A lot of those carries came late in the game with the Bengals having a two-possession lead. He also had an explosive run called back earlier in the game, on a very questionable holding call. If that run was factored in, that would have put Brown over 100 yards during the game. Continue generating pressure at a high rate The Bengals had an astounding 41 total pressures versus Houston in week two. The revamped defense is getting contributions from so many different players. Led by the sheer gravitational pull of Dexter Lawrence in the middle, this Bengals defense is looking legitimate. Meanwhile, the Steelers have allowed 28 pressures through two games. Will the Steelers offensive line be able to keep Aaron Rodgers upright on Sunday? Or will this Bengals defense continue being a matchup nightmare for opposing offenses? If the Bengals generate pressure at a high rate on Aaron Rodgers, they will have opportunities to create turnovers. That pressure could end up determining the outcome of this one. Feed Ja’Marr Chase It was Joe Flacco instead of Joe Burrow, but Ja’Marr Chase went off for 16 receptions and 161 yards during week 7 last season against Pittsburgh. After having just 2 catches for 12 yards in week 1, the Bengals made more of an effort to get Chase involved during week 2. He finished the game with 7 receptions, 75 yards, and 2 receiving touchdowns. That was with the Bengals playing conservatively on offense to finish the game with a two-possession lead during the second half. With the Steelers potentially without Joey Porter Jr. again this week, Chase could be in line for another monster performance this week. Establishing the run early will help the entire offense, but there will be times when the Bengals need to let Ja’Marr Chase just be Ja’Marr Chase. Good things happen when the ball goes his direction. I think the Bengals will find ways to get him involved early and often. Ja’Marr Chase is him pic.twitter.com/H7xpxwXkIy — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 24, 2026

title: Joe Burrow defends Orlando Brown Jr. amid early-season struggles
summary: Cincinnati Bengals franchise quarterback Joe Burrow entered Week 2’s victory over the Houston Texans with back soreness. While he was questionable to play, he ultimately finished the game without much issue, despite taking a good amount of hits from Houston’s talented defensive front. Many of those hits appeared to come from the left side of the offensive […]
full_text: Sep 20, 2026; Houston, Texas, USA; Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) celebrates with offensive tackle Amarius Mims (71) and offensive tackle Orlando Brown Jr. (75) after a touchdown during the third quarter against the Houston Texans at Reliant Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Cincinnati Bengals franchise quarterback Joe Burrow entered Week 2’s victory over the Houston Texans with back soreness. While he was questionable to play, he ultimately finished the game without much issue, despite taking a good amount of hits from Houston’s talented defensive front. Many of those hits appeared to come from the left side of the offensive line, leading to criticism of left tackle Orlando Brown Jr. Brown spent a lot of time in one-on-one matchups with Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter, who got in the backfield quite a bit. Brown did better in Week 1, though he still allowed two QB hits on Burrow. The 30-year-old Brown now leads the Bengals in allowed sacks (three), QB hits (three), and total pressures (six). Despite fan and media criticism, Burrow spoke to the media Wednesday and stood up for Brown, stating that all of the hits weren’t his fault. “I think Orlando was pretty good. There were a couple sacks that weren’t in his control at the end of the day. There’s a lot of different things that go into pass protection that’s not just on the offensive line, and that’s what you don’t see in the media,” Burrow said. Burrow is correct. On TV, we just see a player hit the quarterback, see who lined up in front of him, and then blame that player, but there truly is a lot more that goes into a sack or quarterback pressure than the naked eye sees on game day. “There’s very intricate details of past protection, and guys expecting help here. Guys expecting help from a different spot,” Burrow said. “A lot of different things that go into it that we would never explain to you guys, and then it’s left up to interpretation, and that’s that’s how football works, and that’s the o-ine position at the end of the day. “That is a thankless job from the exterior, so you try to pump those guys up as much as you can in the building. But I really think they were pretty good on Sunday.” While it may not have been his best day, Burrow doesn’t sound like he holds any ill will toward his left tackle. Instead, Burrow is publicly backing Brown ahead of a road divisional matchup with the Pittsburgh Steelers , who also have a dangerous pass rush. title: Bengals Film Room: Amarius Mims shines while Orlando Brown Jr. falters vs. Texans
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals were able to escape Houston with their first road win of the season, defeating the Texans 20-6. While it wasn’t the best day for the offense, there were still some quality performances on that side of the ball. However, there were also some causes for concern going forward. Orlando Brown Jr. One […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals were able to escape Houston with their first road win of the season, defeating the Texans 20-6. While it wasn’t the best day for the offense, there were still some quality performances on that side of the ball. However, there were also some causes for concern going forward. Orlando Brown Jr. One of those things to be concerned about is Orlando Brown Jr. I have written about his mediocre performance during last season, but I thought he played pretty well during the Bengals’ Week 1 victory. I cannot say the same about his performance this week against the Texans. Brown was credited with allowing four pressures, with three of those turning into sacks on quarterback Joe Burrow. He was also whistled for two penalties during the game. He graded out with a 35.6 PFF pass blocking grade for the game, and I cannot really argue with that. Anytime that you are getting your quarterback hit four times, it just isn’t anywhere near good enough. Of course, there is credit to go to Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter. Those guys are arguably the best pass-rushing duo at defensive end in the entire league. But if the Bengals want to get back to the playoffs and beyond, they are going to need a better performance from their left tackle. Brown really struggles with speed rushers. He was never the most athletic player, but now he is on the wrong side of 30 years old. The Bengals coaching staff will need to recognize when Brown is facing a mismatch, and give more help in his direction with tight ends and running backs. There isn’t a solution on the roster if he continues to struggle, so the coaches will have to be cognizant of how to plan around his deficiencies going forward. Orlando Brown Jr. vs. Houston **Viewer discretion is advised pic.twitter.com/vY3tk7MS4k — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 21, 2026 Amarius Mims On the opposite side of Brown, Amarius Mims continued looking like a player that is destined for a potential All-Pro at the end of the year. His athleticism, power, and size were on display again as he faced off against two talented pass rushers for Houston. Mims was credited with allowing one pressure during the game against the Texans. This comes a week after allowing 0 pressures against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The only offensive tackle who has played 50% or more of his team’s snaps and has fewer than one penalty is Garrett Bolles in Denver. After that, it is Mims, Lane Johnson, and DJ Glaze as the only three offensive tackles that have allowed just one pressure this season. His 57.3 pass-blocking grade from PFF is not nearly indicative of just how huge he was for the Bengals on Sunday. Facing off against two of the best pass rushers in the league, Mims was incredible. He is so quick out of his stance, has fantastic recovery athleticism, and will absolutely shut things down when he is able to get those giant hands on the defenders. Amarius Mims vs. Houston pic.twitter.com/keGmGqrWjD — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) September 21, 2026

summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are 2-0, atop (alone) the AFC North, and the team and its fans have every reason to be excited about what the 2026 Bengals are capable of and will do. However, not everyone sees it. Some look at the fact that the two teams the Bengals faced are both 0-2, the Bucs […]
full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals are 2-0, atop (alone) the AFC North, and the team and its fans have every reason to be excited about what the 2026 Bengals are capable of and will do. However, not everyone sees it. Some look at the fact that the two teams the Bengals faced are both 0-2, the Bucs losing at home to the lowly Browns in Week 2, and some seem to forget that the city of Cincinnati exists at all. PFF is a great example. They released their power rankings, which were derived from the quality of each team as defined by Point Spread Team Ratings (whatever that means), and to say that it’s ridiculous is a massive understatement. Not only do they have the 2-0 Bengals all the way down at No. 15 behind several teams not nearly as good, but they’re also three spots behind the 0-2 team they beat on Sunday. I’m not exactly sure what algorithm PFF used to come up with this garbage, but it should be scrapped for good. And then there’s the lack of respect from a vanquished foe. Texans wide receiver Kayshon Boutte recently told the media the Bengals didn’t do anything out of the ordinary to beat Houston; it was all Houston’s doing. You know, the whole, ‘they didn’t win, we lost’ thing. “We beat ourselves,” he said. “They wasn’t really doing nothing that we couldn’t handle. We just gotta be better in the red zone. We went there multiple times, came up with zero, bull—- offense.” This is the kind of thing players don’t pay much attention to, but fans tend to latch on. The Texans were outmatched on Sunday in almost every way, and especially when Boutte and his bullsh*t offense were on the field. It’s hard for CJ Stroud to find one of his receivers downfield when he’s running for his life. The Bengals didn’t allow him to get comfortable often, and it’s very clear it was something the Texans’ offense “couldn’t handle.” Al Golden may not be putting this stuff on the bulletin board in the locker room, but fans remember. We don’t get no respect! No respect at all! title: Bengals News: Why a 3-0 start is so important for Cincinnati
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals are 2-0 after defeating the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at home in Week 1 and then the Houston Texans on the road in Week 2. Well, according to RotoWire, it’s a pretty good indicator of what’s to come. “We sorted every team from 2016 through 2025 by its record through three games and tracked where each season finished,” wrote RotoWire’s Thomas Leary . “The table splits cleanly in two worlds: the 3-0 and 2-1 teams, who make the playoffs more often than not, and the 1-2 and 0-3 teams, who mostly don’t.” Hopefully the Bengals will fit into the first category and remain unbeaten. title: Stars of the Game: Ja’Marr Chase and the Bengals defense shine in Houston
summary: Joe Burrow, Zac Taylor, and Dan Pitcher made it clear throughout the week after the Bengals’ Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Week 2 game at the Houston Texans: they needed to do a better job getting the ball to Ja’Marr Chase. After just two receptions for 12 yards, one of which […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 20: Ja'marr Chase #1 of the Cincinnati Bengals catches a touchdown pass against the Houston Texans during the second quarter of the game at NRG Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images Joe Burrow, Zac Taylor, and Dan Pitcher made it clear throughout the week after the Bengals’ Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and Week 2 game at the Houston Texans: they needed to do a better job getting the ball to Ja’Marr Chase. After just two receptions for 12 yards, one of which went for -4 yards, the tone was set heading into Houston; Chase would get the ball early and often. The best part of the week between Weeks 1 and 2 is that Chase said all the right things. He kept his head down and just went about his business. Chase let his actions speak louder than his words, and whoa, did his actions speak volumes on Saturday. Here is a look at our stars of the game from the Bengals’ 20-6 win over the Houston Texans. 1. Ja’Marr Chase: 7 rec., 75 yds, 2 TD Chase had three receptions in the first quarter on Sunday, making his presence felt. The Bengals established him early, setting him up for big plays later in the game and a catch that will forever be on his highlight reel and in his future Pro Football Hall of Fame enshrinement video. Chase’s 32-yard touchdown reception was a kill shot. Joe Burrow had just hit Tee Higgins for a 23-yard reception on 3rd&4 to get to the Texans’ 32-yard line. Now, it was 1st&10. The Texans had just flubbed a 34-yard field goal attempt and gotten stopped on 4th&Inches. They were on their heels. Burrow sensed that, and he went for the home run play. Good lord, Chase’s catch is incredible. It’s so many things woven into one: body control, concentration, and footwork. Not to mention, it came against Derek Stingley Jr., one of the best cornerbacks in the NFL. But Chase wasn’t done there. On his second touchdown, it’s classic Burrow and Chase. Ja’Marr Chase knows what Joe Burrow will do when he’s out of the pocket. As soon as Burrow waved his thumb in the direction he wanted Chase to go, Chase sprinted to the right side of the end zone and hauled in a back-breaking 18-yard touchdown to put the Bengals up 17-3. It was very reminiscent of Burrow to Chase on a scramble drill against San Francisco in 2021 and against Philadelphia in 2024. This time, though, the play came in a Bengals win. There was no need to worry about Chase after Week 1. He was in a great headspace despite small numbers, and now he’s coming off a terrific performance going into an AFC North game at Pittsburgh. 2. Dexter Lawrence: 3 TKL, 1 TFL,1 QBH Dexter Lawrence single-handedly changed the game on Sunday in Houston. Lawrence only needed three tackles and one tackle for loss on the stat sheet because he does so many other things to impact the game. That said, Lawrence’s fourth-down stop on David Montgomery in the second quarter is why the Bengals traded for him. It’s that kind of play, stuffing a run on fourth and TWO INCHES to completely swing the momentum of the game. The Bengals needed a stud and beast in the middle of their defense to make plays like that to swing games when they are on their heels. That’s who Lawrence is. He’s the undisputed leader of the Bengals’ defense, the guy in the center up front who sets the tone. Lawrence’s fourth-down stop is his first big, game-changing play as a Bengal. It won’t be the last time you see him make a play like that this season. 3. Joe Burrow: 20/31, 207 yds, 2 TD, 105.2 Passer Rating Back tightness, Houston’s defense, clunky offense at times? None of it mattered for Joe Burrow on Sunday, who diced up the Texans and played a clean game despite taking five sacks. This is one of my favorite Joe Burrow games in his career. Given the week leading up to the game and the opponent, Burrow displayed a calm and toughness that made him one of the NFL’s best quarterbacks in 2021 and 2022. There’s no question Burrow is still one of the NFL’s best quarterbacks. Yes, he hasn’t posted prolific numbers yet this season. However, he’s still been productive through two games. Burrow only needed to throw for 207 yards on Sunday for the Bengals to have success against Houston, or, as he said, he only needed to be “incredibly average.” Here is one way to interpret that quote: this is Burrow’s floor, and that’s been good enough for the Bengals to win their first two games of the season. Just wait till Burrow starts putting up elite numbers on offense. 4. Demetrius Knight Jr.: 12 TKL, 1 QBH Knight led the Bengals in tackles on Sunday, and it was one of the first times in his young career I thought he looked like he belonged on an NFL field as a linebacker. He finally looks like a guy who can rally to the ball, take the right angle for a tackle, and knows where the ball is going. If Knight is leading the Bengals in tackles in a game, that’s really good for this revived Bengals’ defense. He was awesome on Sunday, and this is a performance he can build on.

title: Browns Week 15: Another Jaxson Dart injury update on Wednesday impacts Cleveland
summary: The cliché that the NFL stands for “Not For Long” has never been truer than at the start of the 2026 NFL season. Not only have we seen huge injuries, but teams who looked one way in Week 1 turned a different leaf in Week 2, including the Cleveland Browns. While fans are mostly standing […]
full_text: The cliché that the NFL stands for “Not For Long” has never been truer than at the start of the 2026 NFL season. Not only have we seen huge injuries, but teams who looked one way in Week 1 turned a different leaf in Week 2 , including the Cleveland Browns . While fans are mostly standing pat with their Browns expectations, the team is hoping to build on Week 2 successes while improving in areas that continue to be a struggle, like their run game . A lot of the outcomes in the NFL come down to quarterback play, a quality head coach, and injury luck. For Cleveland’s Week 15 opponent, the New York Giants, the roller coaster of the season has already hit a big high (Week 1’s victory), a low (Week 2’s loss), and now an off-the-rails experience with QB Jaxson Dart’s injury being worse than expected: #Giants QB Jaxson Dart suffered a knee injury last night that was worse than anticipated, sources told me and @MikeGarafolo after the MRI. He’s out an extended period of time, possibly the season. pic.twitter.com/QEA6zGvXqp — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 22, 2026 Shortly after Monday Night Football concluded, the expectation was that Dart would only miss a few weeks. Many were surprised given the violence of this hit’s impact on his left knee: Jaxson Dart went down on the Giants first drive of the game with an apparent injury and was holding his knee. He was able to walk off the field under his own power. pic.twitter.com/84e6GwqeRG — Yahoo Sports (@YahooSports) September 22, 2026 Tuesday’s news pushes former Browns starter Jameis Winston into the driver’s seat for the Giants. Winston struggled in relief of Dart, completing just 11 of 27 passes for 111 yards with one interception. On Wednesday, Ian Rapoport reported that Dart will have surgery that will actually end his season: #Giants QB Jaxson Dart is expected to have knee surgery that will lead to a full recovery but end his 2026 season, sources told me and @MikeGarafolo . Dart has been soliciting opinions on the injury. And the ACL is intact. But surgery is coming. pic.twitter.com/JD37w7m48f — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) September 23, 2026 Winston is the only quarterback left on the Giants active roster. Jake Haener is on New York’s practice squad, with 11 passing attempts in his career.

full_text: On Wednesday, the Cleveland Browns announced that they signed CB D’Angelo Ross to their practice squad. In a corresponding move, they released CB Myles Bryant from the practice squad. Ross was signed by the Browns last November and played in some regular season games. He competed for a roster spot this camp, but began the season on the practice squad. He was a practice squad elevation in Week 1, before being released September 15. With CB Tyson Campbell banged up heading into Week 3, if he has any injury issues this week, it’s possible the team will look to elevate Ross again. Ross previously played for the New England Patriots in 2021, and the Houston Texans in 2023, 2024 and part of the 2025 season before joining Cleveland. For his career, Ross has played in 37 games, with three starts while compiling 33 tackles and four passes defended. Ross has played 508 snaps on special teams compared to just 292 on defense. With Bryant’s departure, the only other cornerback on the practice squad is rookie Michael Coats Jr .

title: Quinshon Judkins could go crazy against Panthers, if this is any indication
summary: After two games, the Cleveland Browns have the 31st ranked rushing offense in the NFL, averaging 65.5 yards and 2.91 yards per carry. It’s not been a case of Cleveland abandoning the run game either. On top of that, much of those rushing yards have actually come from QB Deshaun Watson. He leads the team […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 11: Quinshon Judkins #10 of the Cleveland Browns runs a drill during the Cleveland Browns Mandatory Minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 11, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images After two games, the Cleveland Browns have the 31st ranked rushing offense in the NFL, averaging 65.5 yards and 2.91 yards per carry. It’s not been a case of Cleveland abandoning the run game either. On top of that, much of those rushing yards have actually come from QB Deshaun Watson . He leads the team with 60 yards rushing, while RB Quinshon Judkins has 54 yards rushing. A boost in production could be on the way, though, starting with this Sunday’s home opener against the Carolina Panthers. ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler was asked about fantasy football advice this week , and he immediately talked up Judkins: Don’t be surprised if Quinshon Judkins bounces back as early as this week. Judkins has been disappointing thus far, held to 54 yards on 24 carries and zero scores. But this week the Browns get Carolina, which has allowed a league-worst 448 rushing yards through two weeks. Judkins has too much ability to be bottled up for long. The Panthers’ run defense ranks dead last in the NFL through two games, allowing an astounding 224 yards rushing per game, and an average of 6.31 yards per carry. 291 of those yards came in the Panthers’ Week 1 loss to the Chicago Bears, in which they yielded 59 points. QB Caleb Williams ran for 65 yards, while RB DeAndre Swift ran for 124 yards and RB Kyle Monangai ran for 100 yards. Combined, they had 6 rushing touchdowns. Even in the Panthers’ 34-3 win over the Falcons last week, they allowed 157 rushing yards, with a long run allowed of 11 yards. So they were giving up a high clip still; it wasn’t one big run that skewed the numbers. Between the Panthers’ poor run defense and the Browns’ poor rushing offense, something has to give on Sunday.

summary: The Dallas Cowboys have the luxury of having CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens at wide receiver, but more importantly, they are rooting for each other to succeed. In Week 2, the Cowboys looked better in some ways against the Commanders. However, the Ravens will be a much stronger challenge in Brazil this Sunday. Getting the […]
full_text: Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys have the luxury of having CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens at wide receiver, but more importantly, they are rooting for each other to succeed. In Week 2, the Cowboys looked better in some ways against the Commanders. However, the Ravens will be a much stronger challenge in Brazil this Sunday. Getting the defensive unit clicking on all cylinders will take some time, but several rookies have stepped up to take the reins. Dalla was able to even their record at 1-1 last week, but things like the lack of a consistent running game still need to be addressed. Cowboys’ CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens playing with ‘no egos’ – Todd Archer, ESPN Lamb and Pickens already had a relationship before the latter made it to Dallas. That has helped them form a selfless bond with one another. “I don’t think you can get any much closer than we’ve been,” Lamb said. “I feel like at the end of the day, we want what’s best for each other and that’s to be with one another and to grind. “I feel like we both have that alpha mentality, that alpha dog component to us so just rubbing off on one another and just keeping this thing going. We gotta keep being who we are and at the end of the day prove it to each other every day.” Cowboys’ evolving defense faces tough questions, difficult challenge in Ravens’ offense – Calvin Watkins, Dallas Morning News Dallas is on Year 1 under Christian Parker as defensive coordinator, and they’re currently working the kinks out. On Sunday, the Ravens will present their biggest test yet. What the Ravens possess — an elusive quarterback in Lamar Jackson, an elite running back Derrick Henry along with a strong offensive line — seem like dangerous items for the Cowboys defense to handle. On the season, the Ravens have rushed for 310 yards (fourth-most in the league) with a 5.3 average (third-best in the league). Henry, despite limited work in the second half of the loss to the Saints in Week 2, averages 5.3 yards per carry. The Cowboys’ defense allows 5 yards per carry. Cowboys riding the wave of 3 rookies on defense: ‘They don’t repeat mistakes’ – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram Defense was a major issue for the Cowboys coming into this season. In the first two games, three rookies on that side of the ball are leading the way. In fact, there are more encouraging signs that the Cowboys defense is simply a work-in-progress rather than a lost hope. Among those, three rookies have found key roles on defensive coordinator Christian Parker’s unit: defensive back Caleb Downs, outside linebacker Malachi Lawrence and inside linebacker Jaishawn Barham. While Downs was the only one among those three to start both games for the Cowboys, Lawrence has played 38-percent of snaps in key pass rush situations and Barham has filled in as the starting green-dot linebacker in the absence of DeMarvion Overshown (hamstring strain). Download the SB Nation app today! Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . 3 pressing questions following Cowboys’ season-saving win over Commanders – Jess Haynie, The Landry Hat It wasn’t pretty, but Dallas was able to beat Washington last Sunday. However, several questions still need answers. What’s wrong with the run game? Dallas has yet to crack 4.0 yards-per-carry in either game this year . For an offense that averaged 4.6 in 2025 and brought back every starter and coach, this early-season stagnation is surprising and, after two weeks, increasingly concerning. The easy answer is LG Tyler Smith’s absence, which will extend through at least Week 4. Going from Smith to T.J. Bass is certainly a detriment to the rushing attack, but would Brian Schottenheimer and Klayton Adams be smart to lay this entirely at Bass’ feet? Jaishawn Barham looked the part for the Cowboys, but he’s got an urgent problem to fix to reach full potential – Mauricio Rodriguez, AtoZ Sports Barham had a great bounce-back performance in Week 2 after struggling in his NFL debut. With that said, one thing is holding him back from being even better. Barham briefly had to exit the game to be checked out by trainers. Later in the game, he was seen puking before a play, missing most of the game after that. With Barham being one of the best defenders from Week 2, the Cowboys need him to play as much as possible. Head coach Brian Schottenheimer was asked about his conditioning on Wednesday. “Young player, he has been working actually pretty hard on it,” Schottenheimer said of the rookie’s conditioning. “The best way to get in shape is to play, so he’s working through that.” Labeled a Cowboys’ Bust, Tyler Guyton is Growing Before our Eyes in 2026 – Cody Warren, Inside The Star Guyton has been looking for the consistency in his game since he was drafted in the first round in 2024. He’s gradually doing just that this season. We watched a rookie year marred with penalties and inconsistency, but the penalties were the biggest headache as he committed 18 of them that year. It seemed like every time the offense did something right, we would see a yellow flag lying on the ground near the offensive line and we knew it was Guyton. 18 penalties is a brutal number for any offensive lineman, especially your starting left tackle. You can survive a bad rep now and then, you can survive pressure, but one thing a young offensive lineman can’t keep doing is wiping out good plays.

title: Numbers reveal how the Cowboys ignited a highly efficient offense
summary: It takes a rare mix of confidence and strategy to abandon the identify of your offense, but that is exactly how the Dallas Cowboys managed to outsmart the Washington Commanders defense on Sunday. Looking closely at the game, we found some interesting numbers that explain their approach, and it could help prepare us for what’s […]
full_text: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images | Getty Images It takes a rare mix of confidence and strategy to abandon the identify of your offense, but that is exactly how the Dallas Cowboys managed to outsmart the Washington Commanders defense on Sunday. Looking closely at the game, we found some interesting numbers that explain their approach, and it could help prepare us for what’s coming this season. Let’s dive in. Passing on first down The Cowboys struggled to run the ball. All efforts were thwarted by the Commanders aggressive play near the line of scrimmage. The offense missed blocks and couldn’t get any push to open any running lanes for running back Javonte Williams. But the offense wasn’t impacted. The Cowboys recognized the Commanders’ intentions and simply deviated from the run, proving that flexibility beats stubbornness every single time. The most impressive thing about the offense is how many times the team tried to pass the ball on first down. They had 23 first down plays in the game and they dropped back to pass on 14 of them (61%). That’s a large number considering the team was playing with the lead almost the entire game. More impressive than that quantity of dropbacks was the quality of plays in those situations. The Cowboys had successful plays on 11 of those 14 plays, a 79% success rate, compared to just 4 of 9 (44%) on designed runs. Whether it was bootlegs, play-action, or even productive scrambles after not finding an open receiver, the offense repeatedly had success on first down when dropping back. They averaged 8.6 yards per play at those moments, compared to 3.0 ypp on running plays. It was a testament to the offensive coaching staff to recognize what the defense was doing and repeatedly counter. The Cowboys maximized their strength and kept attacking and Washington never had an answer for them. Touchdown machine The first down success led to the Cowboys scoring 37 points. The offense scored on seven of their eight possessions, and four of them were touchdowns. The impressive thing about that was that once again, the offense didn’t get a lot of opportunities. Eight possessions are still on the low side when a typical game usually provides double-digit chances. In each of the Cowboys’ first two games, they’ve lost the time of possession battle. The good news is they only had the ball three minutes less than the Commanders compared to 13 minutes less than the Giants in the opener. That’s because the defense did a little better, but they’re still having trouble getting off the field, much to the exhaustion of anyone watching. Over the first two weeks, the offense has only had 14 possessions, which isn’t many opportunities, but thankfully they have scored touchdowns on half of them. This level of efficiency isn’t sustainable, but they should improve the number of possessions as the defense continues to improve, assuming the defense does, in fact, improve. All hands on deck The offense is using everyone. If you look at the snap counts over the first two games, there are a couple of things that jump out. First, the team’s WR3, Ryan Flournoy, is seeing a lot of action, playing in over 70% of the snaps in each game. The team is very comfortable in a three wide receiver set and uses it often. The other thing is that they are using a good balance arrangement of Brevyn Spann-Ford, Luke Schoonmaker, Hunter Luepke, and Jonathan Mingo. All these guys are playing roughly 20% of the snaps in each game. These guys add extra blocking, or extra deception depending on what happens during the play. None of these guys will fill up a stat sheet, but they have a specific purpose in the offense, and it’s working well. This also allows players like CeeDee Lamb to get more of a breather as he’s had back-to-back games of less than 50 snaps. For reference, the last time that happened was three years ago. But less can be more. Lamb remains a huge focal point of the offense. He has scored three touchdowns so far, already matching his touchdown total from last year. He looks like a new man (better health will do that) as a more preserved Lamb is a good Lamb. Ultimately, this efficiency highlights a coaching staff willing to adapt rather than slam forward with a pre-determined mantra of “being a physical offense.” By sharing the load and picking their moments perfectly, the numbers prove that this success is no fluke, especially when they have a good decision maker at quarterback. If the defense can eventually hold up their end of the bargain, this team is going to be hard to slow down.

title: Cowboys report card: Grading Week 2 vs. the Commanders
summary: The Dallas Cowboys season finally got back on track with a win against their division rival, the Washington Commanders. Falling 0-2 is bad enough, but falling 0-2 in the division would have felt even worse. Dak Prescott’s performance steadied the ship while the defense was still working through some things. The win against Washington wasn’t […]
full_text: Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys season finally got back on track with a win against their division rival, the Washington Commanders. Falling 0-2 is bad enough, but falling 0-2 in the division would have felt even worse. Dak Prescott’s performance steadied the ship while the defense was still working through some things. The win against Washington wasn’t always pretty, and you wonder what the outcome would have looked like if Jayden Daniels hadn’t gotten hurt, but a win is a win in the NFL. Never apologize for that. The report card looks a lot better than it did last week. A grades: Dak Prescott (A+): Whenever something historic happens in a game, it has to be recognized and given high marks. On Sunday, Dak Prescott became the franchise leader in touchdown passes. Two touchdowns to Jake Ferguson and CeeDee Lamb got him past Tony Romo with 249 career touchdowns. Prescott not only broke records, but he also played exceptionally against a poor Commanders secondary. Coming into the game, the Cowboys have never gone 0-2 to start a season under his command, and they’ll have to wait until next year to see if that streak continues because he’s a big reason why the team is 1-1. CeeDee Lamb (A+): From the opening drive, CeeDee Lamb looked poised for a big day. He finished with eight receptions for 153 yards and two touchdowns. After missing most of last season due to injury, it was easy to forget how good a player Lamb can be at his best, even with George Pickens still in the mix. The Cowboys will have to rely on their passing attack while Klayton Adams and Brian Schottenheimer work through the kinks of the run game. Thankfully, Dallas has a playmaker in Lamb who isn’t afraid to carry the load until then. Brandon Aubrey (A+): Brandon Aubrey went three for three on his field goal attempts, with the longest one being 60 yards. He also went four for four in his PATs. The offense isn’t always going to light up the scoreboard, so seeing Aubrey get back to his consistent self at home checks that box for optimism for the rest of the season. Jake Ferguson (A): While George Pickens is taking a little bit more time to get going in the offense this year, Jake Ferguson stepped up in Week 2. Ferguson caught all four of his targets for 43 yards and two touchdowns. What can elevate Ferguson to an A-plus level this year is dominating as a run blocker. The Cowboys have struggled to run the ball through two weeks, so they need all hands on deck to dominate the line of scrimmage, and that includes Ferguson. Tyler Guyton (A): Tyler Guyton came out of Week 1 as the highest-graded player in this exercise, and now he jumps into the A category for what he showed two weeks in a row. The Cowboys’ left tackle allowed just two pressures and earned a 73.9 grade on offense from Pro Football Focus . The Commanders don’t have the same caliber of pass rushers as the New York Giants, but Guyton kept things in check on his side all game. Through Week 2, Guyton ranks as the 14th-best offensive tackle (playing at least 50 percent of snaps) with a 74.0 PFF grade. Coming into a season with make-or-break expectations, Guyton has certainly exceeded them so far. B grades: Caleb Downs (B+): The Cowboys rookie has been one of Dallas’s most consistent defenders so far. It could be his football intelligence or the mindmeld with Christian Parker. Whatever it is, it’s put him ahead of the rookie curve. The only knock against him and why he isn’t an A for this week was the missed assignment from the first Stefon Diggs touchdown, and the coverage bust pointed out by Tom Brady on the broadcast that he missed. It might be nitpicking for a player who’s been PFF’s second-highest-graded player on defense, but it was still a solid start for Dallas’ young star. Jaishawn Barham (B+): With DeMarvion Overshown out of the lineup, Jaishawn Barham is tasked with filling in for him with green-dot responsibilities. In his first opportunity, Barham fared pretty well. His forced fumble on Commanders wide receiver Dyami Brown helped seal the game for the Cowboys. Two plays later, they went up 27-13. Barham looked like a rookie trying to find his way in Week 1, but he bounced back in a way that should give fans hope he can fill the void left by Overshown until he returns. However, if he keeps making plays in the backfield and forcing turnovers, Barham could keep the gig. Dee Winters (B): Just like his linebacking counterpart, Dee Winters had a very active game as well. Winters tied for the team lead with nine tackles, plus a fumble recovery and a tackle for loss. The entire defense played with a little more hair on fire than in the game vs. the Giants, and Winters consistently set the tone. KaVontae Turpin (B-): The Cowboys’ return game looked as good as it ever has with KaVontae Turpin. Dallas’ average starting field position in Week 2 was their own 40.1-yard line. That is the best starting field position for the Cowboys since Week 15, 2020. Over the last few years, fans have wanted Turpin to show off the speed that landed him with the Cowboys in the first place. If he can consistently keep the Cowboys in a favorable position where the offense can start at their own 40-yard line, they only need 30 more yards to get in Aubrey’s range to score. That’s the player Dallas is hoping for each and every week. C grades: Donovan Ezeiruaku (C+): Last week, Donovan Ezeiruaku got a B grade, with the hope that it would turn into bigger and better things the following week. While he and everyone else on the defensive front pressured Jayden Daniels, Ezeiruaku couldn’t bring him down. The Cowboys defense will face its biggest test of the season against a mobile quarterback in Lamar Jackson. If Ezeiruaku has the opportunity to take him down, he has to capitalize. Kenny Clark & Quinnen Williams (C): The truth is, through two weeks, the Cowboys’ star defensive tackles have been average. They aren’t liabilities on the field, but they certainly haven’t flashed the way they did at times last season. Williams not being the same player as last year would be a bit more alarming, considering the Cowboys handed him a hefty contract extension in the offseason. He’s supposed to be a core piece of the defense for years to come. Parker and Williams aren’t set to go anywhere anytime soon, so the defensive coordinator needs to find a way to maximize the best defensive tackle duo the Cowboys have had in a very long time. Obvious caveats given the small sample of only 2 games this season, BUT I'm starting to wonder whether this scheme is the BEST fit (doesn't mean it's a bad fit) for Quinnen Williams. In Eberflus' scheme, Big Q was able to shoot gaps and play upfield, which made it easy to… https://t.co/lO5KCxC2T8 — John Owning (@JohnOwning) September 22, 2026 D grades: The Cowboys pass rush (D): Another game, another week with the Cowboys’ defensive line earning a D grade. Along with Donovan Ezeiruaku, Kenny Clark, and Quinnen Williams, the entire defensive front and rotation of players aren’t getting the sacks they need. The Cowboys have just two sacks through two games, tied with the Los Angeles Rams, who are without Myles Garrett, and just above the New York Giants (1) and Miami Dolphins (0). One of the offseason’s unsung hires was Dallas going after pass-rush specialist BT Jordan, who helped the Denver Broncos set records for quarterback sacks. Dallas has a long flight to Rio this weekend, so it may give them extra time to plan how to exploit the Ravens’ offensive line. It’s not a five-alarm fire, but it’s becoming a concern.

title: Cowboys injuries: Both teams “hamstrung” to start the week
