title: 49ers News: Welcome to the Bay, Brandin Cooks!
summary: Someone on Warriors twitter posed an interesting comparison: Brock Purdy and Steph Curry. Curry runs Steve Kerr’s system to a T, with discipline, setting off-ball screens with the same fight as a G-League guy. When things fall apart and the moment calls for it, Curry is capable of going off-script and boldly improvising. 40-foot pull-ups, […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Someone on Warriors twitter posed an interesting comparison: Brock Purdy and Steph Curry. Curry runs Steve Kerr’s system to a T, with discipline, setting off-ball screens with the same fight as a G-League guy. When things fall apart and the moment calls for it, Curry is capable of going off-script and boldly improvising. 40-foot pull-ups, behind-the-back crossovers, floaters at the rim. Brock Purdy has shown that against a weaker or jet-lagged defense, he can do both extremely well: play within Kyle Shanahan’s system masterfully while also extending plays and doing the “Mahomes stuff”. He finds the right answer when there is one and creates it when there isn’t. It’s early but it feels like shades of watching Steph Curry’s 2015/2016 seasons. The next three weeks will tells us a lot. Faithful, take 49ers game day wherever you go! Stay connected to the action and share every reaction with fellow 49ers fans on the SB Nation app. Join the live game-day chat Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Brandin Cooks will be a nice addition. I wonder how much juice he has left but his veteran experience will be necessary to get him up-to-speed in the offense. 49ers add veteran Brandin Cooks to reinforce ailing wide receiver corps (paywall) “Cooks last played for the New Orleans Saints and Buffalo Bills in 2025. In 15 combined games, he caught 24 passes for 279 yards. The Stockton native is well past his prime, having last racked up 1,000-plus receiving yards with the Houston Texans in 2021. Nonetheless, Cooks was one of the most accomplished receivers on the market, ranking sixth among active players in career receiving yards (9,811), receptions (734) and receiving touchdowns (60). Cooks and Brandon Marshall are only two players in NFL history with 1,000-yard receiving seasons with four teams.” 49ers practice and media schedule ahead of Week 3 matchup vs. Cardinals “Wednesday, September 23: 12:35 p.m. – Kyle Shanahan press conference 1:30 p.m. – Practice Thursday, September 24: 12:45 p.m. – Practice After practice (approx. 2:35 p.m.) – Raheem Morris press conference Following Morris – Klay Kubiak press conference Following Kubiak – Brock Purdy press conference Friday, September 25: 12:35 p.m. – Practice After practice (approx. 1:35 p.m.) – Kyle Shanahan press conference” 49ers overreactions: Is run defense a concern for team’s 2026 NFL playoff hopes? “The 49ers did not do a good job against the run early in the game against the Dolphins, who controlled the clock and stayed on the field for nearly two-thirds of the first half. But the final stat sheets looked OK for the 49ers’ run defense, just as it did in Week 1 against the Los Angeles Rams. The 49ers faced 58 rushing attempts in two games and gave up just 3.9 yards per rushing attempt.” 49ers game review: Kyle Shanahan still stressed about one area after blowout win (paywall) “[CJ] West’s run-defense grade (26.4) ranks last among the 135 defensive interior linemen who have played at least 15 snaps against the run, according to Pro Football Focus’ grading system. On Sunday, early in the second quarter, West received the rag doll treatment on back-to-back plays. First, on a replay of Jaylen Wright’s 8-yard run over right guard on 2nd-and-10 from the 49ers’ 17, Johnston used his telestrator to alert fans about what happened to West: Center Aaron Brewer got leverage on West, turned him to the side and planted him on his back deep in the backfield. The next play, Wright’s 3-yard, up-the-middle run on 3rd-and-2: Brewer and left guard Kaden Proctor had a combo block on West before Proctor peeled off and Brewer drove West 5 yards downfield, a play that, again, ended with West looking up at the sky.” 49ers report card: The offense is exceeding expectations because of Brock Purdy “Luke Farrell didn’t get enough credit for how well he blocked in Week 1. Farrell and George Kittle played the same number of snaps in Week 2. Only one of these players was targeted. It was good to see Kittle still has enough burst to run away from safeties. He stiff-armed the poor rookie safety. Kittle benefited from a couple of coverage busts, but this group blocked well again….Trent Williams is amazing and seems to be inventing new techniques. As always, he brings up the grade. It’s rare to see somebody get the best of Williams, but that happened in pass protection. It was somewhat mesmerizing to see Williams off balance on a play. The pressures were low, but Miami won enough times to make Purdy move or at least stand tall in the face of pressure. Overall, the offensive line was good. But probably not good enough for an opponent like the Broncos or Seahawks…..Romello Height’s sack should have an asterisk next to it since Bosa was the one who made Malik Willis run for his life. Bosa pressured Willis on 27.8% of his dropbacks. Bosa continues to impress as a run defender, though he missed a couple of tackles. Keion White keeps finding ways to be disruptive. The roughing-the-passer call on White was comically bad. He was penalized on third down for tackling. White’s getting the opportunity to play inside, and he’s flashing a couple of times a game. That’s what the 49ers need. CJ West has been this close to making plays two weeks in a row. For whatever reason, he’s missing the tackle at the point of attack. It’s hard to explain. West wins. He’s there. Then the running back slips out of his grasp. Don’t be surprised to see West start finishing those plays. But you can’t ignore the plays where West and James Thompson Jr. get blown off the ball. That’s been consistent two weeks in a row now. It’s why this group didn’t get an A. Osa Odighizuwa competes, but he also gets moved. Odighizuwa makes up for it by pressuring the quarterback, something Thompson and West have not done. The star of this group was Gracen Halton…”

title: JC Latham is actually playing really well
summary: JC Latham has one really tough play on Sunday. It came at a terrible time, as the Tennessee Titans were set up with 1st and goal from the 8-yard line in a 17-17 game with 2:33 left to play. Latham got beat and allowed Cam Ward to get sacked. Former Titans scout Blake Beddingfield wrote […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 13: JC Latham #55 of the Tennessee Titans runs out prior to an NFL football game against the New York Jets at Nissan Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images JC Latham has one really tough play on Sunday. It came at a terrible time, as the Tennessee Titans were set up with 1st and goal from the 8-yard line in a 17-17 game with 2:33 left to play. Latham got beat and allowed Cam Ward to get sacked. Former Titans scout Blake Beddingfield wrote at PaulKuharsky.com that the play design was poor there, giving Latham “no options on his block.” On the whole, Latham has been much improved this season. Check out this graphic from Pro Football Focus: JC Latham's ranks this season among OT Island Rate: Highest Island Pass Block Win Rate: 5th Highest pic.twitter.com/AJu8rIXMPI — PFF (@PFF) September 23, 2026 Latham is consistently winning in pass blocking without the Titans having to give him help. Look, those are the numbers you expect from a guy when you draft him with the 7th overall pick. It took Latham longer to get here than we had hoped, but it finally seems like the Titans have a right tackle they can count on (left tackle is another story). This gives the Titans two really good young players on the offensive line with Latham and Peter Skoronski. They are going to have to address left tackle sooner rather than later, but in case you didn’t know, it’s a whole lot easier to find one tackle than two. #math Rookie left guard Fernando Carmona improved from Week 1 to Week 2. If he can develop into a solid player, the Titans might not be as far away from having a good offensive line as we feared at the beginning of the year.

title: Jeffery Simmons is still dominant for the Titans
summary: There was chatter going around about Tennessee Titans DT Jeffery Simmons after Week 1. The Titans endured a lifeless performance versus the New York Jets, and Simmons didn’t pop enough. Well, it’s clear after Week 2 that he’s still a dominant defender. Simmons leads the entire NFL in pass-rush wins through two weeks, according to […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 20: Jeffery Simmons #98 of the Tennessee Titans warms up prior to the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Nissan Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images There was chatter going around about Tennessee Titans DT Jeffery Simmons after Week 1. The Titans endured a lifeless performance versus the New York Jets, and Simmons didn’t pop enough. Well, it’s clear after Week 2 that he’s still a dominant defender . Simmons leads the entire NFL in pass-rush wins through two weeks, according to ESPN Stats & Info. The Pro Bowl defender has been credited with 19 wins as a pass rusher. No contender has more than 15, with Minnesota Vikings EDGE Dallas Turner currently ranking second. Top 10 players by pass rush wins this season. -Jeffery Simmons, dear god -Dallas Turner has arrived -Boye Mafe being what Bengals need, keeping up PRWR with expanded playing time! -I thought Bradley Chubb was washed and was critical of that signing. Looking like a bad take! pic.twitter.com/jnCnlYJTlm — Seth Walder (@SethWalder) September 22, 2026 Simmons’ pass-rush-win-rate stands at 37%. Only New England Patriots DT Christian Barmore has a slightly higher win rate at 38%, because Simmons has played more reps. Not a single edge rusher in the NFL currently matches Simmons’ 37% win rate. Pro Football Focus’ metrics largely agree. They have Simmons tied for first among defensive tackles in pressures with nine. His PFF win% of 17.7 percent ranks fifth among DTs, but none of the four interior defenders ahead of him have played as many reps as he has (Aaron Donald is in first after making his Week 2 debut with just 19 pass-rushing snaps. Simmons has 66). Simmons dominated an Eagles offensive line in Week 2 that had Cam Jurgens and Drew Kendall starting in prominent roles. Kendall replaced the injured Landon Dickerson. He had absolutely no answer for Simmons. There was some concern that Simmons would take time to adjust to Robert Saleh’s new attack-style defense. Those whispers grew after Week 1 when fans believed Simmons’ impact was muted versus the Jets. This clearly isn’t the case at all. Simmons is as dominant as ever. Every advanced metric (across different outlets) proves it. The Titans still have a superstar defensive tackle in Jeffery Simmons. Hopefully the rest of the defense catches up soon.

title: Washington Commanders vs. Seahawks in Week 3: Inside the Matchup
summary: Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates […]
full_text: Back in June and early July, HH veteran writer Bill-in-Bangkok, offered a week-by-week preview via the 5 O’Clock Club of the Washington Commanders regular season schedule for 2026. As we roll into the actual games during the regular season, Hogs Haven will revisit each of these previews with John Portis adding additional thoughts and updates as we go inside the matchup to get you ready for every opponent the Commanders face in 2026. From John Portis: Bill-in-Bangkok was certainly right back in June, when he originally evaluated this Commanders-Seahawks matchup. A lot has changed since the initial preview. His write-up hits close to home, as Washington enters Week 3 with quarterback Jayden Daniels sidelined by yet another elbow dislocation and Marcus Mariota once again behind center. The Seahawks are expected to start their own backup quarterback, Drew Lock, though it should be noted that Sam Darnold practiced in a limited capacity on Wednesday. It’s at least possible that Darnold could be available. Lock has performed well in Darnold’s absence, completing 35-of-48 passes for 422 passing yards, four touchdowns, and no interceptions in two games. Three of those touchdowns went to receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba last week versus the Cardinals, and the prospect of facing him with a Commanders’ secondary that will be already be missing Nick Cross should keep coordinator Daronte Jones up at night. If the Commanders’ defense can somehow contain JSN, they will be left with Cooper Kupp and Rashid Shaheed in the passing game. Jaxon Smith-Njigba, Week 2 🔥 11 targets 9 catches 155 yards 3 TD 42.3% target share Two weeks: 22 targets, 17 catches, 277 yards, 4 TD. pic.twitter.com/kZVTmD3nwP — Outside Zone (@OutsideZoneIO) September 21, 2026 Rookie running back Jadarian Price is recovering from a shoulder injury and may miss the game — time will tell on that front — but free agent-signing Emanuel Wilson, who spent 3 seasons with the Packers, has been a solid addition to the Seahawks backfield and will work alongside last year’s undrafted free agent signing George Holani, who is dealing with a knee issue. Seahawks offensive coordinator Brian Fleury, who utilizes an outside zone rushing scheme, has leaned on the run with Darnold out, running the ball over half the time with 55.4% running plays to 44.6% passing . Washington has been surprisingly good in run defense, stuffing 29% for no gain, which ranks 3rd overall , with defensive lineman Javon Kinlaw ranking 3rd in the NFL in individual rankings of run stop rate. The real strength of the Seahawks is head coach Mike Macdonald’s defense. They have continued their outstanding play from 2025 as outlined by Bill in his preview, and the Seahawks are the first team since 2006 not to allow a play of 20-plus yards through two weeks. Second-round safety Bud Clark broke his ankle in preseason, and Coby Bryant left in free agency. First-round safety Nick Emmanwori returned on a limited basis last week, playing eight defensive snaps, and was a full participant on Wednesday. He seems in line to play on Sunday, but we will see. Meanwhile, free safety Julian Love has been making a case to be considered an elite player. Washington offensive coordinator David Blough will have his hands full, and so will Washington’s embattled interior offensive line, which is likely to be without starting right guard Sam Cosmi, who is in the concussion protocol. Defensive tackle Leonard Williams continues to play at a high level, along with the rest of the defensive line. These wackos. They don't move. pic.twitter.com/c2oV0Dpgni — Ben Fennell (@BenFennell_NFL) September 21, 2026 The perspective hope for a Commanders win lies in quarterback Marcus Mariota’s ability to read defenses and get the ball out quickly to short and intermediate parts of the field. The other is Drew Lock’s past history of inconsistent play. He’s a gunslinger prototype at the quarterback position, and has a career completion rate of 60.2% with over 28 career interceptions in 29 starts. Through two games, the Commanders’ defense has forced zero turnovers, which is a statistic that will need to change if Washington wants a chance to win their first game at Northwest Stadium this season. Betting Lines Oddsmakers have established the visitors as the favorites for this matchup. Point Spread : Seattle -7 Game Total (Over/Under) : 40.5 points Bill-in-Bangkok’s original preview published June 28: Week 3 Preview: Seattle Seahawks at Washington Commanders Date: September 28, 2026, 1 p.m. ET Location: Northwest Stadium in Landover Maryland After road games in Weeks 1 & 2 against a pair of hated division rivals, the Commanders will return home in Week 3 to face the Super Bowl Champion Seattle Seahawks in Week 3. No easy games to open the 2026 season! A lot could change by the time these two teams meet, but it’s no surprise that the early betting lines favor the Seahawks on the road against the Commanders. The All-Time Series Numbers While these two teams wouldn’t seem to be natural rivals, they have played one another 24 times since Seattle joined the league as an expansion team in the mid-1970s. Washington leads the overall series 13-11-0, and the burgundy & gold has won 8 of 15 games played in this millennium. The Seahawks have prevailed in the postseason, however. The two teams met in the playoffs three times between the 2005 and 2012 seasons, with Seattle sweeping the Redskins by winning all 3 games — none by less than 10 points. Interestingly, Washington has been more successful as the road team in recent years, losing 4 out of the last 5 games played in Landover while winning 3 of the last 5 games played in Seattle. Commanders quarterback play and health has been an issue at times I’m sure everyone will remember the gruesome-looking play in which Jayden Daniels suffered a dislocated left elbow in the fourth quarter of the Week 9 game against the Seattle Seahawks at Northwest Stadium. A similarly gruesome-looking knee injury ended the rookie season of Robert Griffin III against the Seahawks in the playoff game at Landover in January 2013. In the three Seattle-Washington games played between those two injuries, Washington’s offense was led by Dwayne Haskins (2020), Taylor Heinicke (2021) and Sam Howell (2023), which may help explain the .250 win percentage under Ron Rivera and Dan Quinn. Hopefully, Jayden Daniels can put an end to this streak of quarterback infamy and injury with a complete and winning effort in Week 3. Seahawks quarterback stability Seattle’s starting quarterback is Sam Darnold. Not so long ago, that would have been a reason for many NFL fans to scoff, but Darnold has just finished back-to-back Pro Bowl seasons with the Vikings and Seahawks, and he has a shiny new championship ring. Like last year, Darnold is backed up by Drew Lock and Jalen Milroe. #Seahawks HC Mike Macdonald says the team isn’t talking about defending its Super Bowl or “running it back.” Instead, the phrase internally is: “We want to run it forward,” with the “it” referring to their process and identity as a team. pic.twitter.com/055rmwwEw5 — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) May 27, 2026 Seahawks 2026 Coaching Changes * New to staff this season: Offensive Coordinator – Brian Fleury Offensive Line – John Benton Running Backs – Thomas Hammock Inside Linebackers – Zach Orr Quarterbacks – Tyson Prince The Seahawks coaching staff changes could be significant. Sam Darnold will have both a new offensive coordinator and a new quarterback coach. Fleury comes from 7 seasons with the 49ers; Prince is a 4th year coach who has moved up quickly in Seattle after one year in the college ranks. Add in John Benton’s promotion to senior offensive assistant & offensive line coach, and we could see a very different Seahawks offense in 2026. Fleury’s offensive scheme will be a highly structured, modern variant of the Shanahan-style West Coast offense, built on wide-zone running, heavy pre-snap motion, and calculated deep shots…

title: Commanders analysis: Can Washington rebound after rough start in 2026?
summary: After an uneventful opening drive, Washington put the game squarely in quarterback Jayden Daniels’ hands. He immediately tied Sunday’s game against the Dallas Cowboys up with a masterclass in efficient passing and authoritative scrambling. He looked even better than his rookie self – decisive, sharp and smart enough to get down before taking big hits. […]
full_text: After an uneventful opening drive, Washington put the game squarely in quarterback Jayden Daniels’ hands. He immediately tied Sunday’s game against the Dallas Cowboys up with a masterclass in efficient passing and authoritative scrambling. He looked even better than his rookie self – decisive, sharp and smart enough to get down before taking big hits. This was the franchise savior Washington had been praying for over the last 10 years. Then, seconds before halftime, everything crashed. Following an uncharacteristic drop by Terry McLaurin on first-and-goal and then a second-down throwaway, Dan Quinn had a choice with three seconds on the clock. With Washington set to receive the second half kickoff, he chose to pass up the field goal attempt and go for it. They paid for it dearly. Daniels took the snap under center, guard Chris Paul stepped on his foot and the play collapsed into a painful nightmare reminiscent of last season. I turned the TV off right then and there. I couldn’t stomach watching an otherwise brilliant performance by JD end like that. There are definitive moments where a season’s trajectory flashes before your eyes. Right then, I knew my high expectations were entirely divorced from reality. I intentionally avoided making a record prediction in my season preview. The truth is, this team was always a wild-card capable of swinging in either direction. Between an uneven preseason and a devastating wave of training camp injuries, the Commanders had zero identity on either side of the ball. Losing Laremy Tunsil was a massive, foundational blow. Yet, part of me hoped the roster could rally together, survive his absence and come out stronger on the other side. Sunday’s game completely shattered that optimism. The warning signs were there in Week 1 against Philly, but Week 2 in Dallas officially confirmed it: Washington’s defense still has massive issues. Following a promising yet imperfect debut against Philadelphia, Washington’s defense laid bare its massive, lingering issues. Traveling to Dallas in Week 2 was always going to be a monumental task. Dak Prescott is virtually flawless at home, piloting a lethal offense that ruthlessly capitalizes on any opportunity. Historically, Washington has struggled with giving up big chunk plays against him, a fatal flaw that ultimately ruined a relatively solid opening week from coordinator Daronte Jones and company. Dallas watched the tape, identified the blood in the water, and ripped them to shreds. Washington couldn’t stop a cold out there. Out of eight total drives, Dallas only punted once – the rest resulted in scoring drives. CeeDee Lamb saw absolute BBQ chicken looking across the line at Washington’s 5’9” cornerback crew, though Amik Robertson managed to hold his own relatively well. The pass rush disappeared for long stretches, the linebackers were consistently out of position to stop the bleeding, and the seams were left wide open all afternoon. Exposing these kinds of gaping holes by Week 2 is a massive red flag, echoing the defensive nightmares we all witnessed last season. At its core, this is a deep personnel issue. Mike Sainristil has become the butt of every joke online, looking completely outmatched on the field and clearly losing favor with this coaching staff. It has reached a point where opposing offenses are actively hunting him down. Even if he flashes with an occasional turnover, it doesn’t balance out the damage of watching the kid get beat like a drum week in and week out. Defensive back is a position entirely dependent on confidence, and right now, his looks completely shot. Sainristil isn’t an isolated incident either; the 2024 draft class as a whole is looking like a monumental flop for Washington right now, though that deserves its own multi-part article. What once looked like a promising young secondary core has turned into an easy target checklist. Players like Jartavius “Quan” Martin and Jeremy Reaves have become unplayable outside of special teams’ units. Martin’s performance completely sours the idea of drafting a high-round nickel/safety hybrid ever again, while Reaves, despite giving maximum effort, simply lacks the raw skill set required to take starting safety snaps. This entire defensive back room needs a top-to-bottom overhaul. You cannot ask your front seven to consistently generate instant pressure just to mask structural deficiencies in the secondary without at least getting respectable coverage. That said, the front seven needs to be put on notice as well. Daron Payne’s lack of effort is painfully visible on tape. He is being paid like an elite, upper-tier defensive tackle, yet he has failed to progress to that level on the field. As the last man standing from the highly drafted 2020s defensive line core, Payne has yet to find his true ceiling, and this should absolutely be his final year in Washington. Meanwhile, off-season additions Leo Chenal and Sonny Styles are still visibly trying to find their groove in this system. Linebackers play a massive role in this scheme, and both of them—alongside Frankie Luvu—need to get back on track immediately. But it’s only a two-game sample size, and early personnel shifts or rapid player development could still rewrite the script. But if teams keep picking up massive chunks of yardage at will, the story of this season is already written. While the defense struggles, the offense tells another story entirely – one defined by systemic growing pains and a staggering lack of depth. My biggest concern with offensive coordinator David Blough is the sheer amount of patience this team will have to exercise as he irons out his play design and sequencing. While the unit looked marginally better against Dallas than it did in the opener against Philly, the tape still reveals glaring spacing issues and offensive linemen literally tripping over themselves. These are typical growing pains for a first-year play-caller, and these systems usually get progressively better as the season grinds on. But for an organization in a pivotal, high-stakes year, do they really have the luxury of time? This gamble at offensive coordinator will remain a central talking point for weeks if the unit doesn’t fully click soon. Compounding Blough’s learning curve is a devastating rash of injuries. Losing your two best offensive linemen – Laremy Tunsil and Sam Cosmi (who is hopefully only out for a week with a concussion) – is a recipe for disaster. To make matters worse, frankly, it was irresponsible of general manager Adam Peters to rely so heavily on Coleman given his well-documented injury history. Failing to bring in a dependable veteran left tackle to sit behind Tunsil or rotate into that slot is a front office oversight that is costing them right now. Without the starters, the drop-off in talent and scheme fit is painful. Chris Paul simply does not possess the athleticism required for this blocking scheme. If this were a gap-based, power-running system, he has the frame to thrive. But in a wide-zone scheme, he is too much of a “phone booth” blocker, lacking the lateral mobility to let plays connect. His limitations play a part in an uneven rushing attack. Nick Allegretti looked slightly better on Sunday, but severe reservations remain about his long-term viability in this lineup. The silver lining is that the quarterbacks are processing quickly and getting the ball out faster than usual. However, the ground game must find traction to unlock this offense’s true potential. Striking that balance will make a world of difference, but so will getting dynamic playmaking from the wide receiver room. We need to have a brutally honest conversation about Terry McLaurin. He is currently sitting on a dreadful 30% catch-on-target rate and has already dropped three heavily tracking touchdowns he absolutely should have secured. While it is too early to completely give up on a franchise staple, he looks much closer to the age cliff than anyone anticipated.…

title: Commanders mailbag: Discussing Marcus Mariota, Daronte Jones and more
summary: The Washington Commanders are not in a great spot. They’re 0-2. Their quarterback is hurt. Their coach is taking some serious flak.   What comes next? How will they respond?  That’s the unwelcome situation that we’ve got, and Washington must find a way to respond. All that sounds so ominous, doesn’t it? There’s so much […]
full_text: The Washington Commanders are not in a great spot. They’re 0-2. Their quarterback is hurt. Their coach is taking some serious flak. What comes next? How will they respond? That’s the unwelcome situation that we’ve got, and Washington must find a way to respond. All that sounds so ominous, doesn’t it? There’s so much within the details here, though, that we’ll parse through and try to prep fans for what comes next in this Commanders mailbag. We don’t need a long intro to your questions, do we? Let’s get to them right here, right now: What’s our backup QB situation looking like? We know Hartman hasn’t, nor should he be considered an option. I’m fine with AK being the next man up, but is the team? QB3? Vet or youngster? — jdawgaz Athan Kaliakmanis is the guy right now. He earned the No. 3 job and should be the now second in command. We’re not going back to Sam Hartman in a panic. I also don’t think it’s prudent to go out and sign a veteran off the street who doesn’t know the system. That smells of panic, too. Kaliakmanis would be the best possible backup at this point, thought we’re talking about real bummer scenarios if he ends up making it into a game. So… was Joe Whitt really the problem??? — Redskinrex I wasn’t around at that time, but I still answer the question. Yes. The Commanders needed a new defensive direction and they got it with Daronte Jones. I don’t think the scheme is issue. I’m not even sure it’s the general execution. It’s the explosives that are the problem. The Washington secondary was always going to be suspect and the longer the front doesn’t get pressure, the more the Commanders feel vulnerable in the backfield. I think Dan Quinn did the right thing in letting his ego (and his system) go in an effort to try something new. That was a positive impulse that he had. Jones’ scheme is going to be fine. This isn’t a time to panic. It’s s time to be resolute about the scheme and the decision to choose a bold play caller. What O linemen are available that could possibly help? Especially a LT that would allow Coleman to move back to LG. Same with center, but at least if Coleman could move back to LG it might help Allegretti assuming Comi can bounce back. — WillThomas Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said that Sam Cosmi is still in the concussion protocol, and that Matt Gulbin might be the guy at guard. I think we’ve got the offensive linemen that we’re going to have at this point. Brandon Coleman is going to be okay. The line depth was always an issue and that’s being exposed a bit with Laremy Tunsil and possibly Cosmi out will expose that.

title: Commanders film session: Washington run defense improved, pass problems remain
summary: Washington’s defense has been one of the biggest storylines through the first two weeks of the season, but not necessarily for the reasons the team wanted. The pass defense continues to give up too many explosive plays, and the defense has yet to create a turnover under new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. One area that […]
full_text: Washington’s defense has been one of the biggest storylines through the first two weeks of the season, but not necessarily for the reasons the team wanted. The pass defense continues to give up too many explosive plays, and the defense has yet to create a turnover under new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. One area that deserves more attention, however, is the dramatic improvement against the run. Improving the run defense was a major priority for general manager Adam Peters this offseason, and Washington has already shown signs of progress. The defense has consistently created second- and third-and-long situations by producing tackles for loss and no-gain runs. The front is playing faster, winning at the point of attack and allowing linebackers and defensive backs to attack downhill. Let’s take a look at a few plays that explain why Washington’s defense has been successful against the run. Daron Payne’s impact against the run Daron Payne hasn’t been an impactful pass rusher yet this year, but his presence in the run game has certainly been felt. Payne, aligned over the top of the right tackle (4-tech), makes the tackle as a backside defender. Payne wins this rep with good pad level at the point of contact, then shows the functional strength to stack and sheds the lineman to free himself for the tackle. Payne’s ability to stay clean and his vision to locate the ball carrier keep the run from getting anywhere. Javon Kinlaw also deserves credit for stalemating his blocker and preventing the running lane from developing toward the backside. Javon Kinlaw is winning at the point of attack Javon Kinlaw has also made his mark in the run game. Javon Kinlaw (3-tech) is aligned in between the right guard and tackle, and Dallas is attempting a power run to his side, making him a playside defender. The Cowboys’ right tackle tries to down-block him, aiming to send him toward the center, but Kinlaw doesn’t allow it. This is a great example of his play strength and hand usage. Kinlaw uses his outside hand to knock the tackle off balance and create a direct path to the ball carrier. Instead of allowing the offensive line to dictate his movement, Kinlaw controls the block and puts himself in position to make the play. Nick Cross is playing fast Nick Cross has lived at the line of scrimmage in Jones’ system and in the opponents’ backfield. After recording two tackles for loss against Philadelphia, Cross added another against Dallas. His mental processing and closing speed let him attack the line of scrimmage before blockers can get into position. On this play, Cross blitzes as Dallas runs away from him. The Cowboys’ receiver is supposed to account for Cross, but Cross gets downhill so quickly that the receiver never gets a clean shot at him, and he is a free runner in the backfield. Tim Settle is giving Washington interior stability Tim Settle has been one of the more important additions to Washington’s defensive line early this season. Aligned as a shade (2i) inside the right guard, Settle stalemates the combo block and prevents offensive linemen from moving him off the ball. His functional strength gives Washington a different type of presence in the middle of the defense. But Settle’s strength isn’t the only thing that stands out. His hand usage and ability to disengage from blocks—particularly with his long-arm technique—make it difficult for runners to get through the line and reach the second level. The Commanders have stuffed 29% of runs for no gain, 3rd best in the NFL. They've done a really good job against Saquon Barkley and Javonte Williams so far. I was worried about how well they'd stop the run but it's a defensive strength so far. — Grant Paulsen (@GrantPaulsen) September 22, 2026 The run defense has improved; pass defense still has work to do What hurt Washington’s rush defense was Jalen Hurts mostly in week one, but beyond that, it has been the most improved area of the defense as a byproduct of this offseason’s retooling. Washington is playing with more speed and overall play strength, and the defense is getting downhill much faster. The Eagles and Cowboys have both struggled at times to create consistent movement at the line of scrimmage. But the improvement against the run also highlights the biggest problem facing this defense. Washington is playing well enough in one area to put offenses in unfavorable situations, yet the defense continues to give those offenses opportunities to create explosive plays through the air. The problems against Dallas went well beyond Mike Sainristil and Jartavius Martin, who have both struggled to start the season. Receivers came open at multiple levels of the defense, and several of those plays resulted from communication breakdowns, defenders losing track of receivers in their zones, and overall poor positioning. Dak Prescott deserves credit for making plays with his arm, but Washington made his job easier by not being in a good position to defend against him. In this Trap or Dive film session below, we dissect the struggles in the pass game. Specifically, we’ll discuss a handful of plays that highlight critical communication and coverage breakdowns that continue to hurt the defense in the passing game. Comment and let us know your thoughts on the state of the Commanders defense. Don’t forget to also subscribe to the Trap or Dive Podcast.

summary: Dan Quinn spoke to reporters before the Washingt0n Commanders returned to the practice fields in Ashburn, VA today. full_text: Dan Quinn spoke to reporters before the Washingt0n Commanders returned to the practice fields in Ashburn, VA today. The team is preparing for their first home game, and they’re dealing with a lot of injuries as they get ready to host the Seattle Seahawks. The big name is Jayden Daniels who dislocated his left elbow on the final play of the first half on Sunday. He is seeing a specialist today so Quinn didn’t provide a medical update. Quinn was asked about video of players walking past him on the way to the locker room before halftime that has been getting some play online. He said the referees weren’t delaying halftime and players needed to get to the locker room, but they did return to the field to check on him. Daniels won’t play on Sunday, and Quinn also ruled out S Nick Cross, who suffered an internal injury against the Cowboys. He didn’t return with the team, but is back home now. Several other players left the game on Sunday, and the team has other injuries they’ve been dealing with. Sam Cosmi is in the concussion protocol after a friendly-fire hit from rookie RB Kaytron Allen. Quinn said he would need to be cleared by Friday to possibly play this week. Brandon Coleman left the game with a finger injury and was replaced by Andrew Wylie. Thankfully Coleman should be fine and resuming his LT duties against the Seahawks. Quinn mentioned several players who are rehabbing this week including Javon Kinlaw (shoulder) who was injured late vs Dallas, Frankie Luvu (groin), and Chig Okonkwo (hamstring). full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - SEPTEMBER 13: Rachaad White #1 of the Washington Commanders runs for 9 yards before being tackled by Jihaad Campbell #11 of the Philadelphia Eagles during the second quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on September 13, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 23 September 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Commanders Film Room: Jayden Daniels vs Cowboys [ The play described in the excerpt below is the one in the video clip in the embedded tweet from Mark Bullock ] Jayden Daniels looked at his absolute best during the first half against the Cowboys. As a passer, he was processing reads quickly and moving well within the pocket to avoid rushers while still finding receivers down the field. But he also was more prepared to take off scrambling when there was an opportunity for him to do so. He showed signs of that combination which made him lethal at the end of the 2024 season in the fourth quarter against the Eagles last week, and it continued in the first half against Dallas. Daniels looked sharp early as a passer, processing through reads quickly to get the ball out efficiently. On third downs, Daniels stepped it up a gear and delivered some nice passes down the field. One of his best throws of the day came from a third and 18 situation. Prior to getting injured, Jayden Daniels was having a strong outing against the Cowboys. I broke down his performance: https://t.co/W5tyfhWerb pic.twitter.com/6VxjWItUtK — Mark Bullock (@MarkBullockNFL) September 22, 2026 On third and 18, the Commanders call a dagger concept to the left and have Terry McLaurin running a deep curl route to the right. At the snap, a defensive tackle stunts inside right guard Sam Cosmi. Cosmi adjusts to shove the defender down the line, but he still penetrates and generates pressure. Like on the previous play, Daniels does a good job climbing the pocket but remaining a passer as he does it. He can see McLaurin spotting up on his curl route, with the underneath coverage defenders nowhere near him and the deep safety getting far too much depth. So as he climbs the pocket, Daniels pulls the trigger and throws a strike over the middle to McLaurin, who picks up a first down and more after the catch. Daniels continued to pick up third down conversions as the game went on. Fox Sports The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly From The Commanders Loss To The Dallas Cowboys The major event is the injury to Jayden Daniels, which will be discussed a length, however the even scarier injury to S Nick Cross. The Commanders hardly have time to reset as the defending super bowl champion Seattle Seahawks come to Landover. Here is what I saw from the game. Rachaad White- Running Back Rachaad White looked a but off in week one however against the Cowboys we saw the back he was planned to be. White was good running the ball, catching the ball out of the backfield, and in pass protection. Washington needed some dynamic players and White played his part. Pass Defense- For all the good stuff up front, the back end was bad. Routinely the secondary was confused, not effectively communicating, and getting beat. Add LB Leo Chenal to that equation and the Cowboys receivers had a field day. A serious decision needs to be made about CB Mikey Sainrisil because he is now the target of every offensive passing attack. Even when Sainrisil was in position Cowboys receivers still caught the ball. He needs a hard reset and needs to come off the field. It would help all parties for him to take a step back and really work his technique and understanding of Daronte Jones’ defense. Drew Stevens- With so many other issues on the team, K Drew Stevens missed another field goal on Sunday. This one would not have mattered but it shook the belief of the team that they could come back. Stevens has a monster leg but the accuracy needs to be better. If this happens a few more times then he maybe looking over his shoulder. Leo Chenal- A lot of attention has gone to the secondary and their struggles but LB Leo Chenal has looked outright confused out there. Commanders Roundtable Jayden Daniels injury puts Commanders season at a crossroads Despite how doom-and-gloom things feel right now, head coach Dan Quinn needs to make adjustments quickly. Otherwise, another losing season could put his future in Washington in serious jeopardy. The Commanders have been riddled with injuries throughout training camp and the regular season. Washington lost star left tackle Laremy Tunsil to a torn triceps injury that will keep him out for most of the season, cornerback Trey Amos is on IR through Week 4, and now Jayden Daniels could be out for the foreseeable future. Head coach Dan Quinn needs every phase of the team to step up in Daniels’ absence. When Washington trailed 17-3 in the second quarter, Daniels ran the ball effectively and connected with wide receiver Stefon Diggs for a touchdown to cut the deficit to 17-10. He then led the offense into the red zone to close out the half before disaster struck and he suffered the injury. Quarterback Marcus Mariota finished with a serviceable performance, completing 11-of-16 passes for 111 yards and one touchdown. He’ll need to build on that performance if the Commanders want to have any chance against upcoming tough defenses like Seattle, Indianapolis, and New York. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Athlon Sports Terry McLaurin: 14 targets; 4 catches; 64 yards; not good enough Terry McLaurin was held in check for most of Week 1 with 14 receiving yards . After McLaurin was thrown the ball only four times in Week 1, his nine targets during Week 2 are supposed to seem like an improvement. However, McLaurin was only able to haul in two of the nine balls thrown his way for 50 yards. With a cap hit of $18 million, four receptions over two weeks is an unacceptable stat line for someone that is supposed to be the team’s No. 1 wide receiver. When Stefon Diggs was brought in late in training camp, he was supposed to be a complement to McLaurin, not take over the entire show. Having McLaurin on the outside and Diggs on the inside, Jayden Daniels was expecting a dynamic duo in the wide receiver room as Antonio Williams develops and learns. Now that Marcus Mariota is expected to fill in for an injured Daniels , first-year offensive coordinator David Blough will need to adjust how the offense will operate . Mariota plays a similar dual-threat style to Daniels but lacks some speed and arm strength. Both Mariota and Daniels tried to take shots down the field on deep go routes but mostly came up unsuccessful. title: NFL Week 3 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips
summary: What now for the Giants with Jaxson Dart out? What's the buzz on Patrick Mahomes through two games? Are running back depth charts firming up in Tampa and Carolina?
full_text:
We're onto Week 3 of the  2026 NFL season , and insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

 There was optimism around the Giants coming into Week 2, but things went south quickly Monday night. They lost their quarterback on the first drive and lost the game in a 28-6 blowout . How are the vibes in their building and where do they go with Jaxson Dart out ? On the other end of the spectrum, the Chiefs moved to 2-0 with  Patrick Mahomes  back from last season's torn ACL . What are people saying about his play?

 Around the league, we have a sample size to draw some conclusions. What looks different through two weeks from our preseason expectations? And which previously uncertain running back hierarchies are getting clarity? It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 3.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Next steps for the Giants 
 Early thoughts on Mahomes 
 Preseason take do-overs 
 Updates on RB depth charts 
 Fantasy football advice 
 More notes and intel 

 
 

 What are you hearing out of the Giants' building? 
 Graziano: They're disappointed, obviously. They had designed a game plan for their Monday night game against the Rams around Jaxson Dart, believing his mobility would help mitigate the interior pressure they knew they were going to face from Aaron Donald and the L.A. defensive front, and they suddenly had to play a far less mobile Jameis Winston . The run game was limited once the Rams didn't have to worry about the quarterback run threat. They thought they could get more pressure on Matthew Stafford than they did. Very disappointing night all around.

 They do believe Winston will be better with a full week of practice as the starter and with a game plan built around his strengths. We are waiting to find out whether they will have Malik Nabers , Andrew Thomas or Brian Burns , all of whom also left Monday night's game due to injuries. That becomes much more important because the Dart injury has turned out to be more serious than they believed Monday night.

 

 Fowler: Your point about the game plan is an important one -- the Giants entered Monday's game with a plan tailored around Dart's skill set. But now the Giants' offense is in the hands of Winston, who signed a two-year, $13 million extension on Sept. 6. Winston is comfortable operating out of the shotgun, which offensive coordinator Matt Nagy -- with his ties to Kansas City and Andy Reid -- can accommodate.

 But man, the Giants offense looked so good in Week 1 with Dart under center, operating at a high level and making quick decisions (Dallas' defense contributed to that, to be sure). And then it looked so sloppy without him, especially in that end-of-half sequence in the red zone Monday night. This is where Nabers enters the fray. He has been slow to launch through two games, which is understandable given his recovery from a  torn ACL . But elite receivers can make backup QBs look like starters. The Giants will need Nabers to have that effect. And Winston did provide a spark last season, so perhaps he finds that groove again.

 Graziano: The problem with Winston -- or any backup, really -- is that while he can probably get you through two or three games, his deficiencies are likely to show up the longer he plays. The Giants will need to bring in someone else, even if it's just for depth. Jake Haener is on their practice squad, so he's obviously a candidate to be elevated. But there's no magic solution here.

 Jimmy Garoppolo is a free agent. Maybe they could talk the Steelers out of Mason Rudolph for a draft pick. At some point this season, maybe guys such as Jacoby Brissett (Arizona) or Kirk Cousins (Las Vegas) get replaced by younger QBs and become available in trade. But it's way too early for that now, and it looks like the Giants will have to go with Winston and work to help him play better than he did in relief Monday night.

 Fowler: Yeah, the quarterback options are scarce. Garoppolo appears to be in that half retirement phase. It might be worth a call to Minnesota, where J.J. McCarthy toils on the bench. General manager Joe Schoen did a lot of homework on the 2024 draft class of quarterbacks, so he knows the pros and cons of McCarthy's game. Rival teams believe McCarthy can be acquired at a value since Minnesota doesn't appear to have him in the long-term plans .

 Luckily for the Giants, the Thomas and Burns injuries are not believed to be serious. The Giants' strength is in the offensive and defensive lines, and the defense has enough players to maintain respectability. The Giants must find a way to run the ball effectively and keep Winston on time from the pocket. He can still throw to all levels of the field when he's decisive. Scramble plays are probably something New York wants to avoid due to the turnover threat that plagues Winston in those situations.

 

 

 
 What's the leaguewide buzz about Patrick Mahomes ' first two games back from his knee injury? 
 Fowler: That Mahomes might not be all the way back ... but he's not far off. He looked more fluid and confident in Week 2 vs. Indianapolis . "His ability to drive throws -- I thought he was ripping the ball," one NFL personnel evaluator said of Mahomes' performance against the Colts. The confidence he showed throwing the ball was something which he can build upon. It was an improvement from Week 1 vs. Denver , where Mahomes was a modest 15-of-27 for 184 yards and looked choppy as a runner. That's to be expected early as he strengthens his knee flexion.

 But overall, throwing five touchdown passes, taking four sacks and winning back-to-back games is a roaring start for Mahomes coming off reconstructive knee surgery . The Chiefs were pleased with how Mahomes looked all camp and that has spilled over. And his supporting cast looks more equipped to perform for him over 17 games.

 Graziano: And he will look even better equipped to perform once the Chiefs get left tackle Josh Simmons back from his injury. They've been leaning on the run at least in part because they've been starting undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson at left tackle. But they're earning praise around the league for the extent to which they've been willing to run it with  Kenneth Walker III . He was their big free agent signing , and they talked throughout camp about using him as their primary rusher and in the passing game. But to see Reid actually commit to it has been surprising to many.

 I believe the Chiefs will involve the downfield passing game more as the season goes along and they get more whole, but people around the league are noticing that they have embraced the run game as a means of creating explosive plays. Their offense has lacked big plays in recent years and needed to find a way to get them back. Mahomes is a marvel, and while it's objectively amazing that he looks this good so soon after that injury, I don't know if anyone is surprised by anything he does anymore.

 Fowler: You're right, Mahomes' success this season feels directly tied to Walker, who has been a revelation. Eventually, the Chiefs will want to spell him. He has 56 touches through two games (47 rushing attempts), equating to 476 over a full season. Reid game plans based on what it takes to win, and leaning on the running game early has helped Mahomes reacclimate. But that could vary depending on the week.

 The good news is rookie Emmett Johnson looks capable of being the RB2 and can aid the offense in stretches. He's not only gifted in the open field but also eager to take on tough yards. When Simmons returns, perhaps Reid can do more offensively. But Benson, to his credit, has acquitted himself well at left tackle.

 

 Graziano: He has! Benson is quite a story. He was so good in the spring that they opened camp in late July with him competing a bit with veteran Jaylon Moore for the starting…

title: Evaluating surprise early-season trends for 32 NFL teams
summary: T.J. Watt is dominant again? The Packers can't run the ball? Drew Lock is fourth in QBR? Let's figure out which early stats and trends have staying power and which are a mirage.
full_text:
We're two weeks into the 2026 NFL season , which means we know everything about all 32 teams.

 Just kidding.

 But narratives are beginning to take hold. Which early trends will stick and which will dissipate as the season goes on? The eight remaining 2-0 teams probably won't all be playoff-bound, and the eight 0-2 teams are not all doomed. And some players have had shocking performances so far -- good and bad -- and they won't all continue.

 So, what's real and what's a mirage? We tasked our 32 team reporters with identifying a trend or a stat that sticks out for every team through two weeks and sizing up whether it is likely to continue over the rest of the season.

 
 Jump to: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 

 Buffalo Bills 
 The early surprise:  Greg Rousseau is emerging as a top-tier pass rusher.

 

 The verdict:  Real. Rousseau has 4.0 sacks and nine pressures. Since 2018, the only other edge rushers to start a season with that many sacks and pressures through two games have been Aidan Hutchinson (2024), T.J. Watt (2023) and Chandler Jones (2021). That's All-Pro company, and Rousseau is doing it without fluke sacks; only one of his takedowns registers among the 20 quickest sacks from snap to tackle. His sacks appear to be products of good all-around play, not one-off big moments. -- Nick Suss 

 
 

 Miami Dolphins 
 The early surprise:  The Dolphins have allowed points on 10 of their 17 defensive possessions.

 

 The verdict:  Real. Miami has yet to register a defensive stop in the first half through its first two games, and it allowed the 49ers to score touchdowns on their first five possessions in Week 2. Teams likely won't keep scoring against the Dolphins at that rate. But until first-year coach and defensive playcaller Jeff Hafley can figure out a way to manufacture a pass rush, a young Dolphins secondary will likely keep getting attacked by opposing quarterbacks. -- Marcel Louis-Jacques 

 
 

 New England Patriots 
 The early surprise:  Drake Maye has four interceptions on throws of 15-plus yards.

 

 The verdict:  Mirage. This matches Maye's total from all of 2025 on such throws and is the second-highest total through the first two games of a season since ESPN began tracking in 2006. Part of that is facing the Seahawks and the Steelers, two of the NFL's best defenses. Being without top wide receiver  A.J. Brown ( ankle ) is a factor too. Maye's accuracy and decision-making, which are his calling cards, should improve with more time on task after not playing in the preseason. -- Mike Reiss 

 

 
 

 New York Jets 
 The early surprise:  The defense is No. 1 in yards allowed (197 per game).

 The verdict:  Mirage. No doubt, the defense has improved from last season (25th), but No. 1 in the league? Let's tap the brakes. The Jets have yet to face a top-shelf offense. Ordinarily, the Packers could be in that category, but they were compromised without running back  Josh Jacobs ( commissioner exempt list ) and with a patchwork offensive line. Despite an overtime loss, the Jets held Green Bay to 199 yards. We'll know a lot more about New York's defense on Sunday against the Lions. -- Rich Cimini 

 

 

 AFC NORTH 
 

 Baltimore Ravens 
 The early surprise:   Lamar Jackson leads the NFL with 10 yards per passing attempt.

 

 The verdict:  Real. One of the buzzwords for new Ravens offensive coordinator Declan Doyle is explosiveness. So, it's not a surprise that Jackson tops the league with an average of 10 yards per attempt. He has completed four passes of 40 yards or longer, connecting with Zay Flowers (twice), Chris Moore and Devontez Walker . The QB is far ahead of last season's pace, when he totaled six passes of 40 yards or longer in 10 games. -- Jamison Hensley 

 
 

 

 Cincinnati Bengals 
 The early surprise:  The Bengals' defense is putting pressure on QBs.

 

 The verdict:  Real. Cincinnati wanted its defensive line to be a true strength of the team. And all the offseason moves have made the intended impact. According to ESPN Research, the Bengals rank fifth in team pressure rate (40.2%) and are fourth in QB hit rate (20.5%). And it's not just Dexter Lawrence II creating chaos. Free agent signee Boye Mafe is tied for fourth in the NFL in pressures (nine), while Cashius Howell is tied for the most pressures by any rookie (seven). -- Ben Baby 

 
 

 Cleveland Browns 
 The early surprise:  Jared Verse has recorded zero pressures.

 

 The verdict:  Mirage. It's not the start Verse had hoped for with his new team, but opportunities have been lacking for the two-time Pro Bowler. Verse's snaps have been limited through two games; he has had only 43 pass-rush snaps. Much of his team debut in Week 1 was spent facing a large deficit, but his average get-off time through two games -- 0.77 seconds, according to NFL Next Gen Stats -- would be a career-best mark. If Cleveland can play more close games, such as its Week 2 upset over the Buccaneers, Verse should get more chances, and those pass-rush numbers should rise. -- Daniel Oyefusi 

 
 

 Pittsburgh Steelers 
 The early surprise:  T.J. Watt is back to his dominant ways.

 The verdict:  Real. Watt has been quick to remind the NFL that even after two down seasons, he's still otherworldly. Reinvigorated by defensive coordinator Patrick Graham's scheme, the 31-year-old Watt is playing fewer snaps (thanks to Graham's carefully monitored rotation) and varying his rush locations. A better rested and more unpredictable Watt? That's a nightmare for O-coordinators. Through two weeks, his 3.5 sacks is second only to Buffalo's Rousseau. Watt also has as many touchdowns (one) as the Steelers' offense through two weeks. -- Brooke Pryor 

 

 

 AFC SOUTH 
 

 Houston Texans 
 The early surprise:  The Texans' run game is struggling again . 

 

 The verdict:  Real. Houston's running back duo is having issues generating an efficient offense. David Montgomery is averaging 2.7 yards per carry, and Woody Marks has a 2.9 average through two weeks. That's not all on them, though. The O-line hasn't consistently provided lanes for them; that's why it feels real. Sometimes, Montgomery and Marks have to fight for every yard while getting hit in the backfield. Against the Bengals, quarterback  C.J. Stroud  led Houston in rushing yards (29); that's never a recipe for success. -- DJ Bien-Aime 

 
 

 Indianapolis Colts 
 The early surprise:  The Colts have one of the NFL's worst defenses.

 

 The verdict:  Real. Indianapolis was hardly expected to dominate on defense, but its hopes for improvement were largely built on getting dominant play from the secondary. That hasn't transpired, and it's hard to see a path toward significant improvement without it. The Colts rank last in the NFL in yards per play (7.2), yards per game (514.5) and points allowed per game (37.0) as well as 31st in defensive expected points added (minus-28.3). -- Stephen Holder 

 

 
 

 Jacksonville Jaguars 
 The early surprise:  Bhayshul Tuten is RB1.

 

 The verdict:  Real. The Jaguars signed RB Chris Rodriguez Jr.  in free agency, and the expectation was that he and Tuten would share the workload. Through the first two games, however, Tuten (28 carries) has more than doubled Rodriguez's workload (12 carries). Tuten is averaging 4.7 yards per carry and also has three catches for 19 yards, and he should be fully entrenched as the lead back. -- Michael DiRocco 

 
 

 Tennessee Titans 
 The early surprise:  The Titans have been dominated in time of possession.

 The verdict:  Real. The Titans' offense had the ball for only 21:14 against the Jets, followed by 23:35 versus the Eagles. Each game presented a different reason for the discrepancy. Tennessee coach Robert Saleh credited the Jets for running the ball well and staying ahead of the chains. The imbalance against the…

title: How to bet Falcons-Packers on TNF: Analysis, tips and top plays
summary: Odds, bets and analysis to help you bet Falcons-Packers on "Thursday Night Football."
full_text:
"Thursday Night Football" features the Atlanta Falcons visiting Lambeau Field to take on the Green Bay Packers . With Michael Penix Jr . healthy and slated to start, the Falcons get some stability at the quarterback position. Off to an 0-2 start, behind an offense that couldn't find any sense of rhythm with No. 3 QB Cooper Rush taking snaps, we finally get to see how coach Kevin Stefanski schemes for his two playmakers in the pass game -- Drake London and Kyle Pitts Sr . -- versus a Packers defense that is playing zone coverage on 70.5% of opponent dropbacks.

 

 Now, Stefanski's call sheet will be based off the volume for running back Bijan Robinson , who is averaging 18.5 carries per game. We should see a lot of outside zone schemes (which should mirror the play-action passing game) versus a Green Bay defense allowing only 2.9 YPC (second fewest in the league) through the first two weeks.

 For the Packers, quarterback Jordan Love has completed only 52.1% of his passes to start the season, but he has hit on eight explosive-play throws (20 or more yards), which ranks fifth in the league. Christian Watson is a big-play target who has scored three touchdowns through two weeks, while Matthew Golden is emerging as a go-to option. It's a committee approach in the backfield, one that lacks difference-making ability.

 

 

 

 Betting outlook 
 

 Looking at a line that has dropped to Green Bay -4.5, I'm going to take the Packers to cover the spread (and a moneyline bet), plus I'm hitting the over at 42.5. I like Love and the Green Bay pass game against a Falcons defense that struggled in Week 2 versus the Panthers and quarterback Bryce Young (287 yards, three touchdowns). Expect more rhythm throws to the middle of the field, plus the isolation shots to Watson. And I think Green Bay can get enough out of this makeshift backfield ( Kaleb Johnson  flashed on tape last week) to sustain and control tempo. Plus, I'm betting on that Packers defense to win enough early-down situations to keep the Falcons' offense off schedule based on the game plan. We know Robinson will get his touches, and there will be schemed throws for Penix to hit based on Stefanski's history as a playcaller. But I don't think it's enough to cover or knock off the Packers at the home opener at Lambeau Field.

 Total points UNDER 42.5 (-108) 

 Ben Solak: The Falcons finally get functional quarterback play with Penix healthy and stepping in, but he was not even an average starter when we last saw him and now takes snaps in a new offense and having seen no preseason action. I'm expecting plenty of rust against a solid Packers defense. On the other side of the ball, DC Jeff Ulbrich remains a quality designer of pressure packages -- something with which the Packers' young and injury-riddled O-line is likely to struggle. I see sacks, punts and field goals in this one.

 

 Notable player props, bets 
 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change. 

 

 

 Drake London receiving yards OVER 66.5 (-112) 

 I think you can bet London in this one, especially if Green Bay leans on its two-deep zone shells. This is where London can find the voids on deep-in breakers. Plus, he can win perimeter matchups when the Packers roll to man coverage.

 Tucker Kraft anytime TD (+185) 

 If you want an anytime TD scorer? I'd take a shot on Kraft. The Packers tight end has run at least 22 routes in both games played, and he can press the seams in scoring position or see the ball off play-action in the low red zone.

 Kyle Pitts Sr. receiving yards OVER 34.5 (-113) 

 Eric Moody: Pitts has just four targets so far this season, but with Penix under center, he should see more opportunities. He cleared this line in seven of the nine games Penix started last season while averaging 5.9 targets per game.

 Matthew Golden receiving yards OVER 52.5 (-114) 

 Moody: Golden has seen 18 targets through two games while maintaining a high route participation rate. Green Bay's offensive line is a mess right now, and the team has struggled to run the football. That could force the Packers to lean more heavily on Love and the passing game against a Falcons defense allowing the 10th-most passing yards per game.

title: Ranking eight winless NFL teams: Texans, Bucs, others at 0-2
summary: Can the Texans turn it around (again)? Do the Buccaneers, Colts or Chargers have a chance to get right? Is the season already over for the Falcons and Dolphins?
full_text:
This time every year, I tell you that the NFL playoffs secretly start in Week 3 . For the league's 0-2 teams, Week 3 might as well be an eliminator game.

 In an era with 17 games and 14 playoff teams, it's possible to dig out of an 0-2 hole and make it to the postseason, something three teams managed to do in 2025. Two of them -- the Bears and Panthers -- even managed to win their divisions at the end of the year.

 But since 2002, 102 teams have started their seasons by losing three consecutive games. Even if we expand our scope and treat the seventh seed from 2002 to 2019 as a would-be playoff team, just four of those 102 teams overcame their 0-3 start and finished in the playoff picture, for an advancement rate of 3.9%. Two of them were Mike Tomlin-led Steelers teams that finished seventh in the AFC in 2013 and 2019, missing the postseason because the league hadn't yet gone to the 14-team field.

 The other two teams were both editions of the Texans -- and they actually did advance to the playoffs. One came in 2018. The other was last season's Houston squad. The Texans started 0-3, losing to the Rams, Buccaneers and Jaguars by a combined 13 points. From that point forward, they went 12-2, with their only losses coming to the eventual top seeds in the AFC (Broncos) and NFC (Seahawks).

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 Here we are one year later, and the Texans are back again, joining seven other winless teams through two weeks of the 2026 season. They'll be in the only matchup of 0-2 teams in Week 3 as they travel to Indianapolis to play the Colts . Can they get back on track and avoid needing to defy history yet again ? Are there any other teams that have a shot at making it back from 0-2 to advance into the playoffs?

 Today, I'll take stock of the eight 0-2 teams around the NFL, break down why each has gotten off to a slow start and rank their chances of still sneaking into the postseason. I also included chances to make the playoffs via ESPN's Football Power Index .

 For teams such as the Dolphins, a playoff berth in 2026 wasn't really in the cards to begin with. For many of the teams ahead of Miami, though, there's going to be a sense of urgency to fix things quickly. Nobody wants to give up on their playoff dreams and start thinking about 2027 after three weeks. The Falcons have the first chance to get into the win column with a Thursday night matchup against Green Bay , but they aren't No. 1 on this list as the most likely 0-2 team to turn it around.

 

 
 Jump to an 0-2 team: 
 ATL | HOU | IND | LAC 
 MIA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 

 1. Houston Texans 
 Chances of advancing to the postseason, via ESPN's FPI : 41.8% (16th highest)

 Well, as we just discussed, the Texans have been here before, starting 0-3 and living to tell the tale in January -- even after losing  quarterback  C.J. Stroud for a month. That 2025 team went 12-2 after its 0-3 start, driven by the league's best defense. From Week 4 onward, the Texans led the NFL in points allowed per drive (1.5) and were second in EPA per play (minus-0.1). There aren't many 0-3 teams that can count on being the best at anything in football over a three-month span moving forward, which might be why the Texans are one of the rare exceptions to the rule I form this column around each year.

 This season's defense, though, hasn't been quite up to the usual standard. Starting with games against  Josh Allen and Joe Burrow might do that to a team, but the Texans are 19th in points allowed per drive and 23rd in EPA per play through two weeks. This same defense had also famously flummoxed Allen in regular-season victories during the 2024 and 2025 seasons, but Allen threw for 334 yards and was responsible for four touchdowns in Buffalo's Week 1 victory .

 

 I'm not sure it's time to get alarmed about the Texans' defense.  Derek Stingley Jr . has been Mossed for spectacular catches in back-to-back weeks by Dalton Kincaid and  Ja'Marr Chase , something that isn't going to happen on a weekly basis. Houston has yet to generate a turnover despite forcing two fumbles and a wild throw from Allen with the game on the line in Week 1, which Kamari Lassiter dropped (Allen threw the winning touchdown pass on the next snap). The 2025 Texans had just two games without a takeaway across their 19 regular-season and postseason contests. The 2026 Texans have two in two.

 Instead, I'd just point out that it's really difficult to be one of the very best defenses in football for any sort of multiyear stretch of time. The Texans aren't going to be a below-average unit for very long, and they're going to look a lot better when they're facing the likes of Daniel Jones and Cam Ward in the weeks to come. It would be stunning if they really struggled for months on end.

 Consider, though, that the Texans finished second in scoring defense last year. If we take the second-best scoring defense for each season since 2002 and see where they ranked the following year, their average rank fell to 12th. I would be surprised if the Texans were outside the top 10 by the time we looked at the end of the season, but it would hardly be a surprise or unreasonable to expect something closer to the bottom half of the top 10 than a return to the top two.

 And that would be an issue, because while Stroud has righted the ship after last season's disastrous playoff run, the problems that have plagued the Texans' offense around Stroud during his time in the pros haven't improved. After adding running back  David Montgomery , re-signing guard  Ed Ingram and offensive tackle  Trent Brown  and adding offensive linemen  Keylan Rutledge , Evan Brown , Wyatt Teller  and Braden Smith , the hope was that general manager Nick Caserio had finally found a running game for his quarterback.

 Through two weeks, that run game hasn't been present. The Texans are 28th in success rate, 29th in EPA per snap and 30th in yards per carry on designed runs. Montgomery scored three touchdowns in the opener, but he has found space hard to come by, averaging 2.7 yards per attempt on the ground. Part of the problem has been availability. Ingram missed the loss to the Bengals , and Smith is on injured reserve because a foot injury .

 The run issues materially impacted the Texans against the Bengals. Despite Caserio expressing his confidence  that coach DeMeco Ryans had confidence in the run game after Week 1, Ryans quickly pivoted in the other direction one week later.

 After the Texans were stuffed on a fourth-and-1 in the first half and failed to pick up a yard on second-and-1 and third-and-1 on a drive in the second half, the Texans decided to attempt a 58-yard field goal in lieu of trying to convert on fourth-and-short, only for Ka'imi Fairbairn 's attempt to fall short. This isn't a situation where teams try to kick anymore; over the past three years, when teams have trailed by four points or more and faced a fourth-and-1 between 35 and 45 yards away from the opposing end zone, they've gone for it 180 out of 190 times.

 NFL Next Gen Stats saw the decision to attempt a field goal (let alone miss it) as one that cost the Texans 7.4 points of win probability. You can understand why Ryans thought the situation was hopeless, but the Texans can't afford to make those sort of decisions and survive against good football teams. It didn't really matter in the big picture given that the Texans lost by 14 points, but the Texans need to be able to run the ball effectively enough for their coach to at least retain a tiny bit of hope.

 

 A win against the Colts on Sunday in what amounts to a de-facto playoff game would calm concerns in Houston. And after what happened in 2025, there isn't the same sort of panic after an 0-2 start that there would typically be for a team with championship aspirations. Given those expectations, though, starting the season by losing to a pair of teams that the Texans would expect to see again in the postseason picture is a…
