title: 'Ugh,' a lefty QB: How the Falcons are defying NFL history
summary: With Michael Penix Jr. starting Thursday and Tua Tagovailoa on the roster, the Falcons enter a rare NFL realm.
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- Atlanta Falcons offensive coordinator Tommy Rees had never coached a left-handed quarterback before this season, and suddenly he had two in Michael Penix Jr . and Tua Tagovailoa .

 He also had a problem.

 "Do we flip the drawings [of plays] so they don't look right-handed all the time, and leave them as lefty?" Rees asked. "Poor Mike Bearden, our [coaching fellow], he starts flipping all these things [to be] left-handed-friendly."

 But the Falcons had a bigger problem. They couldn't leave the diagrams lefty-friendly because neither Penix nor Tagovailoa was healthy heading into the regular season. Righty Cooper Rush started the first two games, both losses.

 The Falcons finally get one of their lefties back this week, and the stakes are high. Penix will start in primetime Thursday on the road against the Green Bay Packers (8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video).

 Only 33 left-handed quarterbacks have made an NFL appearance, and just two -- Steve Young and Ken Stabler -- are in the Pro Football Hall of Fame. What makes the left-handed QB unique isn't just which side he passes from, but how the ball spins and curves. Teams have to draw plays differently and make sure the right tackle -- as opposed to the left for righties -- is ready to protect the blind side.

 "If you think about the number of lefties in NFL history, abnormally few," Young told ESPN recently. "Just from a data perspective, it doesn't make sense how few quarterbacks are lefty.

 

 "And one of the main reasons I can say why is because of the coaches. I think they're very right-handed and they don't encourage it. They see a lefty and they're like, 'ugh.' As if it's going to be more work."

 Having two left-handed quarterbacks on the roster is rare, and it has demanded extra measures.

 The Falcons have done everything they could to make things easier for their top quarterbacks, including QB coach Alex Van Pelt flipping how he teaches footwork and changing receiver routes.

 Since 1991, when Elias began tracking such things, only two teams have started more than one left-handed quarterback in a season, per ESPN Research. The Jacksonville Jaguars had Mark Brunell and Steve Matthews in 1997, and the Cincinnati Bengals played Boomer Esiason and Erik Wilhelm in 1991.

 Will the Falcons be the third?

 "I love that Michael and Tua are together," Young said. "But I think all of us [lefties] feel like there's nothing about me that's different. Throwing the football, dropping back, it doesn't matter.

 "It's a thing because coaches, they don't affirm it. If coaches would just say, 'Sweet, I got a lefty,' boom, you get all the benefit and none of the negative."

 

 YOUNG WAS A  freshman at BYU in 1980. Doug Scovil was the offensive coordinator and quarterbacks coach and as Young tells it, he had an aversion to left-handed QBs.

 "[Scovil] told me midseason that he hated coaching lefties and that he wasn't going to coach me," Young said. "So, they literally moved me to defense because I was lefty."

 Despite the position change, Young continued to throw with the quarterbacks whenever he could. The following season, Scovil left for San Diego State and Ted Tollner became BYU's quarterbacks coach. Tollner saw Young throwing one day and wondered why his position on the roster was different.

 "[He] stopped me and said, 'I thought you played quarterback,'" Young said. "And I go, 'I do, but they said I'm lefty, they won't let me play quarterback.' And he's like, 'That's ridiculous.'"

 Young said it wasn't until he got to the San Francisco 49ers under head coach Bill Walsh when he felt truly welcomed as a left-handed QB. Walsh, Young said, didn't just tolerate that he was a lefty; Walsh told Young it was an advantage.

 Former Falcons great Michael Vick had similar experiences to Young coming up as a left-handed QB, but not to the same extreme.

 

 "Most offensive coordinators are right-handed, so you naturally gear everything up to go right or from a right formation," Vick told ESPN recently. "For a lefty, [some coaches] feel like they got to change everything around and go left.

 "But at the end of the day, it really don't matter. I was a left-handed quarterback who liked rolling right and throwing across my body, but you got to express that to your coach."

 What Kellen Moore expressed to his quarterbacks coach was almost an apology for being left-handed. Joe Lombardi was used to calling plays for right-handed Drew Brees in New Orleans, so when Lombardi came to Detroit and coached Moore -- a third-team undrafted lefty -- things got awkward.

 "For Joe it's just like, 'I've never called it this way.' I said, 'Just call it as you're a righty and I'll flip it. It's my job, it's my fault,'" said Moore, who is in his second year as the Saints' head coach.

 Moore had a similar experience when he was playing for the Dallas Cowboys .

 "They never ran a play-action -- it's called naked where you keep the ball away from the outside zone," Moore said. "It was always naked right. They've never even called naked left before.

 "And so, while I was battling for the QB position, it was still naked right no matter what. They said 'until you win the job, we're never going naked left.'"

 There are more significant differences for left-handed quarterbacks than footwork and receiver routes. The spin on a left-hander's pass is different, and it does take some getting used to for receivers.

 

 "Maybe you don't think about it right away, but you just have to think all the time, when it comes from a left-handed quarterback it's going to kind of spin away from you," said Denver Broncos wide receiver Jaylen Waddle , who played with Tagovailoa on the Miami Dolphins . "And then when you [have] a righty, you're going to have that feeling like it's spinning toward you."

 When Young played with HOF wideout Jerry Rice, the spin was such a change that Rice had to do something completely outside the box. San Francisco had an equipment manager, Ted Walsh, who was a lefty. Rice would have Walsh (no relation to Bill) throw to him countless times per day. Every practice, every defensive drill. Rice told Young that Walsh must have thrown him 10,000 balls over his first few years with the Niners.

 "Ted Walsh said he wore his arm out," Young said. "His arm just collapsed."

 

 JAHAN DOTSON PLAYED with a left-handed quarterback in high school and did not think there would be anything different when he got to the Falcons. But the former Washington Commanders and Philadelphia Eagles wide receiver had a rude awakening during OTAs.

 "One day Tua, he threw me a ball, and it was midair, I was like, what the ... ?" Dotson said. "It felt like slow motion. It was just turning the complete opposite way. But yeah, it's something you just got to adjust to."

 Now, there are Jugs machines that can be switched to throw balls with the opposite spin, simulating left-handers. Dotson and his Falcons teammates have spent a fair amount of time after practice working with the machine in addition to catching passes from Tagovailoa and Penix.

 "It's just reps," Dotson said. "Reps on top of reps on top of reps catching from those guys."

 

 This is Penix's third season with the Falcons, so many of his teammates are used to the spin. Plus, Atlanta star wide receiver Drake London is left-handed, as is All-Pro running back Bijan Robinson . That makes things easier. But for newcomers such as Dotson, Olamide Zaccheaus and Zachariah Branch , it has been an adjustment.

 Chicago Bears receiver Rome Odunze played college ball at Washington with Penix, and he said: "It's a little bit different. I like it, honestly because the way the lefty hand spins, the torque of the ball is spinning into my right, dominant hand."

 Young encountered another issue as a left-handed quarterback. Either he had to adjust his hands taking snaps from a right-handed center or the center would adjust and snap the ball with the laces down. The latter was an issue…

title: Baltimore Ravens feel prepared for Rio 'business trip'
summary: This is the Ravens' first game in Brazil, but coach Jesse Minter was there last season.
full_text:
OWINGS MILLS, Md. -- A few days before playing the Dallas Cowboys , Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson was reminded that he is facing a franchise historically known as "America's Team." 
 
 "Yes, but this is America," Jackson said with a smile. "That is Brazil." 
 
 Jackson and the Ravens were in good spirits on Wednesday heading into one of their most challenging road trips in team history. Baltimore (1-1) will take a 10-hour flight to play the Dallas Cowboys (1-1) on Sunday in the NFL's first game in Rio de Janeiro (4:25 p.m. ET, CBS). 
 
 While there's been a lot of talk about the field condition at Maracanã Stadium, the Ravens believe there is a bigger factor for success in Brazil. 
 
 "I feel like the rhetoric around the game after it is done is who handled the travel and everything better," Ravens safety Kyle Hamilton said. "I think that just goes hand in hand on who is being more of a pro or not. That is something that I think we can thrive at." 
 
 
 
 This is the Ravens' first game in Brazil, but coach Jesse Minter was there last season. He was the defensive coordinator for the Los Angeles Chargers , who beat the Kansas City Chiefs , 27-21, in Sao Paulo. 
 
 Minter feels the biggest challenge is figuring out when to fly. The Ravens decided to stick to their normal practice on Wednesday and Thursday in Baltimore before leaving for Rio on a red-eye flight Thursday night. 
 
 The team will arrive in Brazil on Friday morning and will hold one full practice in the afternoon in Botafogo, which is about a half hour outside of Rio. The Ravens will get their first chance to see Maracanã Stadium on Saturday, when they will have a walkthrough there. 
 
 Minter chose not to leave earlier because it's only a one-hour time difference. 
 
 "I do not think there is a perfect answer for any of that stuff," Minter said. "It is all about how the team plays when the ball is kicked off." 
 
 Minter is already resigned to not sleeping much on the flight. But he acknowledged he doesn't sleep much on Thursday nights during the season anyway. 
 
 For the players, many will pass time by watching their favorite TV series. 
 
 "I just started watching Peaky Blinders, so [I'll] probably do a good bit of that, [and] sleep," Hamilton said of the British gangster show. 
 
 Wide receiver Rashod Bateman just started watching The Sopranos. 
 
 "They have a lot of episodes," Bateman said. "So I will try to catch up on that." 
 
 Jackson is thinking he will split up the time on the plane. 
 
 "I am just going to try to sleep as much as possible and just relax -- that is all I can do," Jackson said. "Keep my legs [moving and] try to walk around as much as possible, but at the same time sleep as much as possible. Five [hours awake] and five [hours sleeping] -- try to balance it out." 
 
 This marks the Ravens' third international game. In 2017, Baltimore played one of the worst games in team history, losing to the Jacksonville Jaguars , 44-7, in London. In 2023, the Ravens returned to London where they beat the Tennessee Titans , 24-16. 
 
 For this trip, once the Ravens arrive in Brazil, Minter said the team schedule will occupy much of the players' time. He added there may be a chance for players to see a few places but everyone understands the mission. 
 
 "It is a business trip for us," Jackson said. "It is not to go have fun, to sightsee or anything like that. We are just going out there to play football."

title: Panthers' Bryce Young to Darren Waller has been money in red zone
summary: The veteran tight end's height, catch radius and history of red zone success make him a tough cover in big moments.
full_text:
The connection between quarterback Bryce Young and tight end Darren Waller has been automatic for the Carolina Panthers in the red zone during the first two games of the 2026 regular season. And as the Panthers continue to put up points (they've scored 71!), Waller is at the heart of their red zone plans.

 The veteran (6-foot-6 and 238 pounds) has towered over opposing defensive backs, particularly in the end zone. While he had a Week 1 touchdown catch called back for a questionable offensive pass interference penalty against the Chicago Bears , Waller snagged both of his Week 2 red zone targets from Young for two touchdowns against the Atlanta Falcons .

 "Big people win," former Panthers QB Jake Delhomme, who now serves as a color commentator for the team's radio broadcasts, told ESPN. "Big people -- there's not many walking around this earth, right? Like [defensive end] Derrick Brown , there's not many walking around the earth like that. And when you have them, they help. ... The same thing with Waller, and [Falcons cornerback] C.J. Henderson [listed as 6-1] is not a small guy, and he made him look like he was like 5-9 on the touchdown in the corner right before half."

 

 Waller, who signed a one-year deal with the Panthers in August, skipped the bulk of training camp and the entirety of the preseason as he got up to speed with Carolina's playbook. But since hitting the field for his Week 1 debut, the 34-year-old has hauled in all five of his targets for 61 yards and the two TDs. He has provided the Panthers with scoring opportunities they might not have had otherwise, and that has made him an intriguing option both in reality and in fantasy football.

 Since coming out of retirement to play in nine games for the Miami Dolphins last season, Waller has run 37 routes in the red zone for Miami and Carolina in 11 total games. He has caught eight of his nine targets in the red zone for 62 yards and eight touchdowns. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, Waller has 3.8 receptions over expected in the red zone (a stat that measures the difficulty against the completion probability for each catch), which is second only to  San Francisco 49ers tight end George Kittle (5.3) from the start of the 2025 season through the first two games of 2026.

 "I feel like, last year with Miami, getting there kind of late -- I got there earlier than I got here -- but just kind of dealing with trying to learn things quickly and try get in the mix, I feel like kind of gave me a little bit of a trial run of how to approach things and be as efficient as possible as far as learning and getting on the same page with the quarterback and things like that," Waller said in an interview with ESPN's "Unsportsmanlike" on Wednesday.

 "So, I'm not really that surprised [by the early success in Carolina]. I feel like if I get some opportunities, I'm just going to try to make a play and keep it simple like that."

 Following Sunday's 34-3 win against the Falcons, Panthers coach Dave Canales acknowledged Waller's impact on the passing game, particularly with how he helps everyone else around him. On the Panthers' first touchdown against Atlanta, Waller drew two defenders, which created a delay in coverage that got running back Chuba Hubbard wide open for a touchdown in the flat.

 Canales said finding those mismatches was part of the reason the Panthers signed the towering tight end.

 

 "Just the ability to take advantage of matchups with safeties, with linebackers," Canales said. "That's exactly the type of impact that he can have on this offense. Then it opens other things up, and we got all these other beautiful players sitting on the other side of the field as well to be able to distribute it and create a little bit more balance in our pass game."

 Young, who has thrown for 648 yards, six touchdowns and one interception to start the season, has confidence in the experienced pass catcher. The QB's chemistry with the tight end is based in communication and trust in Waller's experience.

 "Yeah, Waller's played so much ball," Young said Sunday. "So, obviously, he's a pro. It's been great coming in -- us getting on the same page quickly has been just a lot of conversation. A lot of him asking questions. A lot of him telling me the stuff that he likes and vice versa. Being able to have a guy that's played so much ball that I trust, it's great."

 On Sunday, the Panthers (1-1) will play at the Cleveland Browns (1-1), who have allowed eight catches for 70 yards and a touchdown to tight ends over the past two weeks. While that production isn't particularly notable, Waller is a very different player compared to the likes of Cleveland's previous tight end matchups in Jacksonville's Brenton Strange and Tampa Bay's Cade Otton .

 Waller is quicker than both players, and his background comes with a bit more route-running prowess as well.

 

 "I've never made my career off of: 'I need a certain amount of targets or opportunities,'" Waller said Sunday. "It's more so like, 'What's the impact I'm making with those [targets], and then can I also have an impact when the ball is not coming to me to just keep myself engaged?' But you never know when opportunities are going to come. So, just to be able to make those plays, I think, is important."

 Young has thrown six touchdown passes to three different players over the past two weeks. Wide receiver Jalen Coker has two TD catches; Hubbard and Waller also have two apiece.

 In 2025, Young threw eight touchdown passes to tight ends and running backs over 16 games. In his first two games this season, he has already tossed four to those positions, which is a trend the Panthers should be able to take advantage of in the red zone.

 Waller ranks 10th among tight ends in ESPN PPR fantasy points through the first two weeks of the season. As of late Wednesday afternoon, Waller is rostered in 7.6% of ESPN leagues, a jump from the 2.9% of rosters he was on entering this week. And according to ESPN Fantasy, tight ends  Dalton Schultz , Dalton Kincaid and Oronde Gadsden have been added to rosters more than Waller at the midway point of Week 3.

 Regardless of what Waller's production will look like in Week 3, the tight end's chemistry with Young is a trend fantasy football users should keep a close eye on in the coming weeks.

title: NFL survivor power rankings: Why you should use 49ers, Chiefs in Week 3
summary: ESPN NFL survivor pool strategy, predictions and picks for Week 3 including the 49ers and Chiefs.
full_text:
Welcome to 2026 ESPN NFL Survivor ! The rules are simple: Pick one NFL team each week to win its game. If that team wins (or ties), you advance to the next week. If that team loses, you are out. Survive all 18 weeks and you can take home a share of the $25,000 grand prize. The catch is that each team can be chosen only once.

 While the rules are simple, the game theory is not. Depending on the size of your group or what platform you play on, the optimal selections could change drastically. Smaller groups will likely end well before Week 18, so optimizing win probability each week is paramount. However, the larger the group, the more you need to focus on saving strong teams for later. ESPN's game requires just one team each week, so that will be the strategic focus of this column, though we will touch on the big contests at Circa and Splash Sports.

 

 For the second straight week, the most-selected team in ESPN Survivor lost as an 8.5-point favorite. In Week 1, the Chargers knocked out 21% of entries, falling to the Cardinals. In Week 2, it was the Buccaneers' turn, blowing a 10-point lead at home against the Cleveland Browns to eliminate 27% of the field. That wasn't the only Week 2 upset, as the Chargers lost again as 6.5-point favorites, while the Baltimore Ravens were stunned by the New Orleans Saints as 8.5-point favorites.

 As a result, 68% of the original entries are already out just two weeks into the season. The Chargers are responsible for 33% of those eliminations, while the Buccaneers are responsible for another 23%.

 This week, the major decision concerns the Kansas City Chiefs , who are going to be the most-selected team so far (currently 35%). Even though they are on the road, they are the largest betting favorites as they face the Miami Dolphins . Plus, they are widely available, having been used by only 9% of entries.

 The second-biggest favorites are the San Francisco 49ers , who are available to only 59% of the ESPN Survivor field after hammering Miami last week. They are the only other team besides the Chiefs laying more than a touchdown, but with three of their next five games coming against the  Washington Commanders , Atlanta Falcons  and Ravens, they will be a staple of this column.

 

 I was planning on making the New York Giants my top choice on Monday morning, but after injuries to Jaxson Dart and others on Monday night, they are a much more difficult click. The Green Bay Packers also were going to be one of my top picks before Sunday's games, but they looked sluggish in an overtime win against the New York Jets and picked up more injuries. The Philadelphia Eagles are a consideration if Case Keenum starts for the Chicago Bears , but they have less win equity than other teams while having strong future value, so I will pass. And as bad as the Pittsburgh Steelers offense has looked, I am not ready to fade them as a divisional home underdog against the Cincinnati Bengals .

 For contests that require multiple picks this week, the Carolina Panthers are a fun but risky pick. Despite last week's win, the Browns still grade out as the third-worst team in the NFL according to ESPN Analytics, and the Panthers aren't projected to be more than a 54% favorite again until Week 18 according to our two models.

 All that said, my top two picks for ESPN will be the two biggest favorites, the 49ers and the Chiefs. 

 Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Future value based on Mike Clay's cheat sheet .  

 The Road to 18-0 

 
 Week 1: Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. Browns) -- Win 
 Week 2: San Francisco 49ers (vs. Dolphins) -- Win 
 Week 3: Kansas City Chiefs (at Dolphins)  
 

 

 1. San Francisco 49ers (vs. Cardinals ) 

 If you still have the 49ers available, the best question is when to deploy them. Considering that both our models have this as the most-lopsided game this week and the easiest game remaining for the 49ers, and they will likely be less than 10% owned, this is as good a week as any. They are a stronger pick in ESPN and Circa than they are in the two main Splash contests.

 
 Chance to win: 89% (ESPN Analytics), 91% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: 49ers -8.5 (-485 moneyline) 
 Future value: Fourth 
 ESPN Selection: 7% 
 

 2. Kansas City Chiefs (at Dolphins ) 

 

 The Chiefs will be the heavy chalk, but deservingly so as they are the biggest betting favorites while also having less future value than any of the other big favorites. Plus, for those of you in contests that have double-pick weeks, most of the Chiefs' hardest matchups fall in those slots, making them even less valuable down the road. They will likely be my most-selected team on both major Splash contests.

 
 Chance to win: 84% (ESPN Analytics), 87% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Chiefs -11.5 (-850 moneyline) 
 Future value: Ninth 
 ESPN Selection: 35% 
 

 3. Detroit Lions (vs. Jets ) 

 Out of the three teams favored by around a touchdown, I lean towards the Lions, especially on ESPN. While the Lions have eight games after this week where our models have them as at least a 60% favorite right now, they don't have the high-end ceiling of the  Seattle Seahawks and Buffalo Bills  with no games higher than a 79% win probability. Detroit is a very valuable team to hold on Splash, since most of their easiest games fall in double-pick weeks, but if you've burned the 49ers already and want to fade the Chiefs, the Lions are a fine pivot.

 
 Chance to win: 75% (ESPN Analytics), 75% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Lions -6.5 (-305 moneyline) 
 Future value: Eighth 
 ESPN Selection: 10% 
 

 4. New Orleans Saints (vs. Raiders ) 

 

 Finally, a riskier pick for those of you who truly like to hoard the elite teams. The Saints are under 2% selected right now, and with so many other teams trending higher, they will likely remain low. New Orleans' remaining schedule is one of the easiest, but the Saints are ranked only 17th by ESPN Analytics, which is not the type of team you are obligated to save. Both of our models are higher on the Saints than the betting market, so they are a fine contrarian pick with risk.

 
 Chance to win: 65% (ESPN Analytics), 71% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Saints -3 (-185 moneyline) 
 Future value: 15th 
 ESPN Selection: 2% 
 

 5. Green Bay Packers (vs. Falcons ) 

 

 It's a tough spot for the Packers, coming off an overtime game on Sunday with a game on Thursday. Teams in that spot are 13-37 all-time. Combine that with injuries to Zach Bako-Bewele and Jayden Reed , while the Falcons get back Michael Penix Jr ., and it makes sense Atlanta is taking money. But our models like the Packers more than the betting market does. And out of all the teams favored by four-plus points, no team has a harder schedule than the Packers, despite a Week 15 home games against Miami. Ultimately, their ownership keeps them this low on the list. While I expect them to come in lower than 14%, there are too many other options to take on the risk.

 
 Chance to win: 74% (ESPN Analytics), 79% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Packers -5.5 (-265 moneyline) 
 Future value: 14th 
 ESPN Selection: 14% 
 

 6. Carolina Panthers (at Browns ) 
 

 The Panthers have too little of a win probability for me to trust them on ESPN, which is why they are ranked this low, but in contests with double-pick weeks this early, they are firmly in play. To survive the season undefeated in the Big Splash, you will use 26 teams, meaning that eventually you have to take some mediocre teams against bad teams. Despite last week's upset win, the Browns are still one of the three worst teams in the NFL. ESPN Analytics' model is high on the Panthers compared to the betting market, and with Carolina having little future value, this is a spot to gain leverage.

 
 Chance to win: 63% (ESPN Analytics), 54% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Panthers -2.5 (-148 moneyline) 
 Future value: 28th 
 ESPN Selection : 6%

title: Cowboys' CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens playing with 'no egos'
summary: Lamb and Pickens believe their off-field connection is helping their on-field production.
full_text:
FRISCO, Texas -- One day recently, CeeDee Lamb walked out of the locker room and into the Dallas Cowboys ' weight room with George Pickens a stride behind as they laughed about something.

 During training camp, most days the Cowboys' star receivers walked onto the field in Oxnard, California, together. On off days, they were often together.

 About the only time, it seems, they are apart is when one lines up to Dak Prescott 's right and the other is to the quarterback's left.

 "I don't think you can get any much closer than we've been," Lamb said. "I feel like at the end of the day, we want what's best for each other and that's to be with one another and to grind.

 "I feel like we both have that alpha mentality, that alpha dog component to us so just rubbing off on one another and just keeping this thing going. We gotta keep being who we are and at the end of the day prove it to each other every day."

 

 Lamb and Pickens believe their off-field connection helps their on-field production. Last year, they both had more than 1,000 yards receiving, even with Lamb missing three full games and three quarters of a fourth because of injury.

 Pickens set career highs in catches (93), yards (1,429) and touchdowns (nine) while Lamb joined Michael Irvin as the only receivers in Cowboys' history to post five straight 1,000-yard seasons.

 The start to 2026 has been different, however, as the Cowboys (1-1) head toward Sunday's game against the Baltimore Ravens  (1-1) in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil ( 4:25 p.m. ET, CBS ).

 Lamb has caught 13 passes for 197 yards and three touchdowns. With 153 yards and two touchdowns last week against the Washington Commanders , Lamb has six career games with at least 100 yards and multiple scores, tying him with Tony Hill and Irvin for the second most in team history (Bob Hayes, 13).

 Pickens has nine catches for 68 yards. He had two drops in Week 1 against the Giants, including one that could have been a 76-yard touchdown.

 "I, of course, want to get him and CeeDee the ball," coach Brian Schottenheimer said. "I think CeeDee's playing great. I think George is playing really well. I mean, some of the catches he made [against Washington] were really big-time plays in big-time situations for us. ... He just didn't have the highlight-type catches and the explosive catches and things like that. But he draws a lot of attention out there.

 "Believe me, we're looking for ways to continue to get those guys the ball. And if you look at George last year, he didn't really take off until a couple games in, and the rest is history."

 

 Wide receiver is a position in the NFL known for its individuality. Some have had their own touchdown celebrations, such as  Dez Bryant throwing up the X or Terrell Owens  extending his arms for a "TO."

 They can be moody, especially if they don't get the ball enough. Every move can be -- and has been -- scrutinized by camera angles catching poor body language, a comment or a shake of the head.

 

 "We go through the same stuff just being at the same position," Pickens said. "So I feel like that makes us super close."

 Schottenheimer has said numerous times he wants to "build the best culture in professional sports." He said he has been around teams where the jealousy among receivers was a detriment.

 "I think it can affect a game. I mean, it can affect a playcaller. It can affect the quarterback, but there's not really a great way to handle it," Schottenheimer said. "And so that's why we're so fortunate, because our guys, they both want the ball. They both want to score touchdowns. They both want to celebrate, but I love how excited they get when the other guy gets it -- or even Ryan Flournoy , [ Jake Ferguson ] -- their excitement because they love playing the game, and they love this locker room that we've built."

 

 Quarterbacks can get caught in the middle of wide receivers' desires to be the top option. Prescott said he doesn't care about that. He throws it to whoever is open based on his read of the playcalls.

 "They can get mad," Prescott said. "Only one of them can get the ball at one time, so they'll probably be getting it the next play. So don't get mad and miss your opportunity."

 With Lamb and Pickens -- or Pickens and Lamb, if you prefer -- Prescott said "there's no egos."

 "Both of those guys are selfless," he added. "They want to see each other succeed. They're probably each other's biggest cheerleaders to that extent."

 When Pickens came to the Cowboys last year in a trade from the Pittsburgh Steelers it was with a narrative that painted him as tempestuous and broody, but he was immediately accepted by the entire organization, starting mostly with Lamb.

 "I feel like for him, he wanted to do it for [himself] personally just [welcoming] a new guy in," Pickens said. "That's why I was saying last year, the guys on the team were more welcoming than I've ever experienced from any other team. When I came here, they were all open arms, trying to get me hooked up on the playbook fast. But definitely CeeDee, especially, I feel like he took pride in that."

 Said Lamb, "That's my boy. I don't think he questions anything about where my loyalty stands with him and vice versa."

 

 There might be an expiration date on the duo's time together with Pickens playing on the $27.3 million franchise tag. It will be difficult for the Cowboys to pay two top-of-the-market receivers, though not impossible, and there is always the chance the Cowboys could use the franchise tag again on Pickens in 2027.

 Lamb and Pickens are not letting contractual futures impact what they want to accomplish.

 Offensive coordinator Klayton Adams said Lamb and Pickens are "total opposites." Certainly in fashion with Lamb being more stylistically inclined than Pickens. Lamb wears diamonds and flashy bracelets, even on the field. Pickens is just as happy in a T-shirt and pair of shorts.

 "I think CeeDee, probably personality wise, is I guess a little bit more like what I would expect a receiver just in terms of the way that he operates day to day," Adams said. "George, you just don't always know exactly what you're going to get. A little bit more unpredictable, but both are awesome in their own ways."

 And together, they are one of the best receiver duos in the league. Well, maybe not just one of the best.

 "Yeah, we definitely think we're the best," Pickens said. "Now for everybody else's brains and mindsets, I don't know what they're going to say. But for us, yeah, we're the best."

title: Denver Broncos to face another MVP QB in Matthew Stafford
summary: Sunday marks the 10th time the Broncos have faced an MVP quarterback since Vance Joseph became defensive coordinator in 2023. Can Denver get the best of Stafford?
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- In weeks when the Denver Broncos are pitted against one of the NFL's best quarterbacks, defensive coordinator Vance Joseph often responds with a sigh when asked questions about how to stop them.

 "That's our league, you know?" Joseph said. "Every week, every season, every time I look up I kind of feel like there is a quarterback waiting who can just punish you. Every week, man."

 This is one of those weeks, as the Broncos will host the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday night at Empower Field at Mile High ( 8:20 p.m. ET, NBC ). Reigning MVP Matthew Stafford will stand across from Joseph's defense six days after his 69th career 300-yard passing game and his 22nd career game with at least four touchdown passes.

 He is also the last remaining active player who has been an NFL MVP that Joseph will face since being hired as Denver's defensive coordinator in 2023. The Broncos have played against Patrick Mahomes , Lamar Jackson , Aaron Rodgers and Josh Allen at least once since, and Sunday's match-up against Stafford and the Rams will complete the set.

 

 The five quarterbacks have won a combined 10 MVP awards, including the last eight. They've had 10 meetings (including playoffs) against the Broncos over the past three-plus seasons. Denver has already faced one former MVP this season, losing to Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs 31-10 in the season opener. The loss to Mahomes makes those former MVPs 5-5 against the Broncos since Joseph became defensive coordinator.

 The Broncos have allowed one 300-yard passing game in that stretch -- Mahomes threw for 306 yards in Week 6 of the 2023 season. They have thrown a combined 14 touchdown passes to nine interceptions and have been sacked 27 times (2.7 per game). Jackson had the best all-around day from that batch, completing 16 of 19 passes for 280 yards and three touchdowns in the Ravens' 41-10 win over the Broncos in Week 9 of the 2024 season. Allen had 283 passing yards and three touchdowns with two interceptions in the Broncos' overtime divisional round win this past January.

 "Every week is a tough week because everybody has players who can make plays," Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II said. "... But those quarterbacks at the top of their games, they force you to pay attention to all the details because the smallest things, the little details, that's all they need to put you in a bad spot. And once they find a bad spot, they're not going away from it until you take care of it."

 The Broncos' defense re-calibrated from their Week 1 loss to the Chiefs with a Week 2 win over Jacksonville. The Broncos improved from giving up 173 rushing yards to Kenneth Walker III and missing an alarming 19 tackles against Kansas City to allow only 115 net yards and three points to the Jaguars in the second half to spark a comeback win. The Jaguars had 64 combined yards in their final three possessions of the game, which included an interception by Broncos cornerback Riley Moss .

 "We got back to ... [winning] first down," Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton said. "... Win first down and then get to second down, third-and-long, get off the field."

 They'll have to continue that against the Rams and Stafford, who many defenders around the league consider the best pure thrower in the NFL. He had 327 passing yards and four touchdowns in Monday's 28-6 win over the New York Giants and is a player that Broncos fans aren't used to their team facing.

 In a quirk of his career arc and scheduling, the Broncos are the team that Stafford has competed against the least in his 17 previous seasons -- 12 with the Detroit Lions and five with the Rams. Stafford has played against the Broncos only twice and in Denver just once, a 45-10 Detroit win in 2011 when Tim Tebow was the Broncos' starting quarterback.

 

 His main target in his second trip to Denver could be veteran receiver Davante Adams , who had 195 receiving yards and two touchdowns in Week 2. The former All-Pro was forced into the premier pass-catching role when 2025 first-team All-Pro Puka Nacua was ruled out Monday with an injured groin . If Nacua misses a second consecutive game, the Broncos could choose to match Surtain on Adams.

 In addition to Stafford's performance, the Rams added 163 rushing yards as their two running backs -- Kyren Williams and Blake Corum -- each averaged at least 6.6 yards per carry. The Broncos know another tackling performance like they had against the Chiefs will likely result in the same outcome.

 "I've said [Week 1] wasn't our standard by any means," Broncos defensive tackle Zach Allen said. "[Week 2] was better, but you always have to look at it and decide 'are guys in the right spots for the most part and we're just not tackling or whatever or are we making mistakes, not being where we're supposed to be?'

 "I think we've been where we're supposed to be and when we finish, good things happen."

title: Meet Cam Achord: The Packers' secret special teams weapon
summary: Part old-school coach, part Gen Z analytics savant, Achord is "just a ball of energy" as he aims to fix Green Bay's special teams unit.
full_text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. -- He wears cleats to practice even though he won't take a snap. He runs stride for stride with the kick returners, yet he doesn't have a ball in his hands. He takes a knee to demonstrate how kickers want the ball angled, but he's not a holder. He'll even throw himself -- nose first -- into a player even though he's not in pads.

 He's Cam Achord, and he's here to change everything you ever thought about the Green Bay Packers ' special teams.

 The 39-year-old Mississippian is part your father's football coach with a hands-on, foul-mouthed approach, and part Gen Z analytics savant.

 "He's one of a kind, there's no doubt about that," former New England Patriots special teams star Matthew Slater , who played for Achord from 2018 to 2023, told ESPN. "When you said that he's still running around out there with cleats on, I couldn't help but laugh to myself."

 Not because Slater finds Achord funny. More a shake of the head because he still can't believe some of the things Achord does on the field.

 "He wanted to make sure that we were prepared, even if that meant putting his body on the line," said Slater, a five-time All-Pro selection as a special-teamer. "I've seen Cam break a nose. I've seen him on the ground several times, but it's all in the name of ensuring that his players are ready to go. As a player, as a pro, you really have to appreciate that."

 

 

 THE BROKEN NOSE story was largely unknown outside of the Patriots' inner circle before coach Matt LaFleur  hired Achord in late February to replace Rich Bisaccia unexpectedly resigned.

 It happened in 2019, when Achord was a Patriots assistant special teams coach. One day in practice, Achord was putting Justin Bethel , Slater and the other gunners through a drill designed to help them beat a double team, otherwise known as a vice.

 "I tell them, 'Quit pulling me like you're gonna pull a coach,'" Achord recalled earlier this year. "I was like, 'Pull me like you're gonna pull the freaking vice. Yank!'"

 And yank they did.

 "Ask Justin about the broken nose," Slater said. "See if he remembers that."

 Said Bethel: "Was it me?"

 According to both Achord and Slater, yes, it was.

 Bethel did exactly what Achord said, and the next thing anyone knew the coach was face down on the turf.

 "So after that, I started wearing cleats just for better grip," Achord said.

 

 Those cleats helped Achord in an August training camp practice, when he was nearly able to keep up with Bo Melton on a long kick return.

 "He told me right before that play. He said, 'I'm running with your ass,'" Melton said. "So I was like, 'Oh man!'

 "He brings it every day. Like whatever you do, he going to get on your ass when you do great. He's going to be happy as hell. He's going to be jumping around when you do good. And he going to rip your ass when you're not doing so well. So he's a through-and-through coach."

 

 ACHORD LOVES TO teach. Since his arrival in Green Bay, every one of his sessions with the media has been part press conference, part educational opportunity. Few coaches can match Achord's words-per-minute rate. Throw in the Mississippi native's thick southern accent, and it's sometimes hard to keep up.

 Responding to a media question earlier this year about how kickers want the holder to position the ball, Achord came off the podium, got down on one knee and gave a two-minute demonstration unlike anything a coach has done before in the Lambeau Field media auditorium.

 "You guys also got a coaching clinic I understand?" Packers coach Matt LaFleur said the next day. "That was the first one I've seen in a long time. He's juiced up about football and brings great energy for our guys."

 

 Two days after the Packers' 39-22 season-opening loss to the Vikings -- a game in which Skyy Moore made the seemingly risky decision to catch two punts off the bounce, returning them for 12 and 5 yards -- Achord was asked about the fine line between aggressiveness and unnecessary risk.

 "When the ball hits the ground on average in the NFL, it rolls around 14 yards," Achord said. "So we're saving potentially 14 yards if we're able to field the ball off the bounce."

 The natural follow-up, of course, was how in the heck does Achord know the average is 14 yards?

 "You just gotta take the time to watch the plays and study," Achord said, explaining how a couple of years ago he charted every punt that hit the ground for a several-year stretch.

 "I don't mind watching 3,000 punts," he said almost sheepishly. "Honestly, it probably took me two days to watch them all."

 This offseason, he wanted to know what a reasonable standard was for gunners on punt returns to beat double-teams. For that, he turned to Slater.

 "I went back and watched all of Matt Slater's vice reps for the last six years when I coached him," Achord said. "Just to see, how much did he win? And that way it gives it to our guys in percentages and stuff. It was pretty high. But obviously he's probably a Hall of Famer -- should be a Hall of Famer. 

 "But that's the standard we want, right? We want to have high standards. We want to live up to those standards. So to me you want to look at what the best of the best is and that's what you want to hold yourself to."

 By the way, Slater beat those double-teams 80.2% of the time, according to Achord's study.

 "He did everything that's humanly possible to make sure that his players are prepared," Bethel said of Achord. "But a lot of it goes to the type of players you have in the room. You can have all that information, but if you have guys who don't take advantage of it, it's kind of a waste.

 "It starts with the head coach, and Bill [Belichick] was always adamant about having good special teams, and he would keep players for that reason."

 Like Belichick, Achord isn't afraid to get on players. During training camp, Achord grew frustrated by repeated mistakes and went into a tirade where every other word out of his mouth was an F-bomb.

 "He's actually becoming one of my favorite coaches, just bringing that energy to the meeting room and to the field," Moore said just before the start of the season. "He's just a ball of energy and the players feed off of that, so I like it."

 

 THE PACKERS' SPECIAL teams have been so bad for so long, why should anyone get excited about another coach tasked to change the seemingly unchangeable? 

 Every special teams coordinator the Packers have employed from 1999 through last season -- nine in total -- has either been fired (six of them), forced into retirement (two) or left under circumstances not fully explained (Bisaccia  after last season ).

 Special teams blunders have cost the Packers at the worst possible times. To name a few:

 
 The 2014 NFC Championship Game loss against the Seahawks, who ran a fake field goal for a touchdown in the third quarter and recovered an onside kick in the final minutes ( bye-bye special teams coordinator Shawn Slocum ). 
 The 2021 wild-card loss to the 49ers, who became the first team in 33 years to block both a punt and field goal in the same playoff game (and  the end of Maurice Drayton's tenure as coordinator after one season). 
 The 2023 three-point loss to the 49ers in the divisional round, when Anders Carlson missed a 41-yard field goal attempt in the fourth quarter in his only season with the Packers. 
 Last season against the Bears, who recovered an onside kick and forced overtime in Week 16, then went on to win the game and the NFC North. 
 The wild-card loss to the Bears last season, when kicker Brandon McManus missed two field goals and an extra point in what turned out to be Bisaccia's last game. 
 
 During Achord's four seasons (2020-23) as the Patriots' special teams coordinator, his units ranked first, third, 26th and 31st in ESPN's FPI rankings. After New England, Achord spent two seasons as the Giants' assistant special teams coach. Now, two games into his Packers' tenure, he will make his Lambeau Field…

title: How Chiefs TE Travis Kelce turned wedding shape into football shape
summary: Kelce, who leads the NFL in YAC, has had an average route speed of 11.56 mph, the fastest he's been since 2022.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- At some point late Sunday, perhaps after he bearhugged kicker Harrison Butker , who made the game-winning field goal in the  Kansas City Chiefs ' overtime win against the Indianapolis Colts , star tight end Travis Kelce learned he earned yet another NFL record in his illustrious career.

 In the second quarter, Kelce caught a short pass from quarterback Patrick Mahomes , a reception he turned into an 11-yard gain. That moment was when Kelce broke the record for the most yards after the catch in NFL history, passing Hall of Fame running back Marshall Faulk.

 

 "I had no idea," Kelce said after the game of breaking the mark. "It's pretty freaking cool, man, to be in talks with guys like Marshall Faulk, Larry Fitzgerald, Terrell Owens. That's some pretty cool stuff, man. Those are the guys I grew up watching. Guys like that fueled my love for this game."

 Not only has Kelce, 36, recorded 6,287 yards after the catch in his 14-year career, but he also leads the league in the statistic this season (128), which represents the most such yardage in his first two games of a season, according to ESPN Research.

 Such impressive production has helped the Chiefs to a 2-0 start and provided evidence that Kelce's individual performance has been better than the past two seasons, when he showed dips in speed and athleticism.

 "Travis worked his tail off," coach Andy Reid said Monday. "He likes his surrounding cast, too, which sure helps as just an extra challenge there to make sure that you're up there and competing and doing your part.

 "I know everybody questioned the wedding and all that. Would he be out of shape and honeymooning the whole time? But he works his rear end off. [With] Taylor [Swift], you're putting on four-hour shows. You've got to work hard, too. I'm sure she kicks him in the butt a little bit there, too."

 

 Kelce entered training camp in late July three weeks after his wedding to Swift, the international pop superstar. His transition from wedding shape into football shape was smooth, too, since he didn't miss a practice and was still one of the Chiefs' best pass catchers, especially in one-on-one drills against linebackers and safeties.

 Kelce's average route speed this season, according to NFL Next Gen Stats, is 11.56 miles per hour, the fastest he's been since 2022.

 "It's not as much about the shape that I look like I'm in," Kelce said, smiling. "It's about the grit that I have and the heart that I have to get that ball north."

 One of the best examples against the Colts was Kelce's highlight inside the red zone. In the first quarter, Kelce showcased his speed and quickness to run away from nickel cornerback Justin Walley for a 13-yard touchdown.

 "I saw Cover 4 and that the flat defender was a little inside of me," said Kelce, who finished with a game-high 101 receiving yards. "I knew Pat was going to give me a chance, so just get the ball north and find a way to get into the end zone."

 

 Once again, Mahomes and Kelce were instrumental in the Chiefs' offense scoring 33 points, a strong indication that the unit can continue to be potent this season.

 Mahomes played with better rhythm and accuracy in his second game since recovering from the torn ACL and LCL in his left knee to finish with 382 passing yards and three touchdowns without a turnover. Sunday's game was the 23rd time in which Mahomes recorded at least 300 passing yards and Kelce finished with at least 100 receiving yards. The pair has produced the second-most such games of any quarterback and tight end duo in league history, just two games shy of tying Tom Brady and Rob Gronkowski .

 "He's still doing it and he knows how to get open," Mahomes said of Kelce after Sunday's game. "He can make guys miss. For him to make the plays he made in the big moments of the game, that's who he's always been.

 "Just as much as it's cleaned up the game for me, I think having [running back]  Kenneth [Walker III ] and the way he's running the ball gets [Kelce] into these matchups that he's going to win -- and he showed that."

 Walker's ability to break tackles -- which has helped him lead all skill position players in the league with 369 all-purpose yards -- has created more opportunities for Kelce to avoid double coverage. The Chiefs lead the NFL in yards per game (457.5) and are third in points (32).

 "Guys are playing their tails off for the guys next to them, and that's why I love this team right now," Kelce said Sunday. "We're in a zone right now where everybody is feeding off of each other. It's only making us better and making us play harder for each other."

 On opening night, the Denver Broncos blitzed Mahomes in the third quarter on a third-and-6 snap. Recognizing the Broncos' man-to-man coverage, Kelce ad-libbed into a whip route, which allowed him to get open against nickel cornerback Ja'Quan McMillian . Kelce gained 54 yards after the catch on his 59-yard reception -- and his top speed during the highlight was 16.88 mph, according to Next Gen Stats.

 

 Two of Kelce's teammates, receivers  Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton , executed blocks downfield for him. Against the Colts, receiver Xavier Worthy made a block near the goal line for Kelce to reach the end zone. Those moments of teamwork are one element he emphasized in Wednesday's episode of the "New Heights" podcast, hosted by Kelce and his brother, Jason.

 "This is by far the craziest and, honestly, one of the coolest accomplishments I've ever had," Travis Kelce said of the yards after the catch record. "I've had unbelievable playcalling, unbelievable players around me blocking downfield, and you don't get this kind of [record] without the guys around you to help you to get these yards.

 "But at the same time, man, it's a pretty cool stat to be a part of that when I've got the ball in my hands, I'm doing the most I can with it."

title: With Kyler Murray back, will Vikings open up passing attack?
summary: Coach Kevin O'Connell said he is "still a believer in explosives" despite a long stretch of tepid air production for Minnesota.
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- Inside the visitors locker room Sunday at Soldier Field, Minnesota Vikings players peeled off layers of rain-soaked uniforms and equipment. Coach Kevin O'Connell soon launched into a postgame speech that precisely depicted his mindset, excitement -- and maybe even a bit of distress after a 9-3 victory over the Chicago Bears .

 O'Connell praised players for "trying to figure out a way to find a way."

 Later, he roared: "The only thing that matters is winning!"

 That line represented the culmination of a very public reckoning O'Connell has put himself through while heading into his fifth season in Minnesota. The Vikings (2-0) have won seven consecutive games, dating back to last season, in ways that are almost unrecognizable from the pass-happy teams he first fielded upon arrival in 2022. But as quarterback Kyler Murray returns to the field, and with a hot but otherwise clear weather forecast Sunday at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers ( 4:05 p.m. ET, Fox ), O'Connell has far from given up on the passing game he craves. 

 "I'm still a believer in explosives," he said Monday. "I'm still a believer in taking some yards when they present themselves and doing it at a level where we pitch and catch at a level that I know our guys are capable of."

 

 From 2022 to 2024, the Vikings put up the NFL's third-most passing yards (12,886) with the league's fifth-lowest rate of designed running plays (35.3%). They built their offense around receiver Justin Jefferson , who averaged a league-best 100.4 receiving yards per game over that period. Since that point, however, the Vikings rank No. 31 in passing yards (3,093) and have the league's fifth-fewest number of offensive plays -- rushing or passing -- that have gone for 10 yards or more (197). They've had fewer than 200 passing yards in 16 of their past 21 games.

 Fortunately for them, that stretch has coincided with a defense and special teams that have been among the NFL's best, ranking No. 3 and 7 in expected points added (EPA), respectively. 

 During their unbeaten start this season, with Murray playing only 11 snaps because of a concussion and leading rusher Jordan Mason  going on injured reserve with a thumb injury after one week, the Vikings have managed a league-low 13 plays of 10 or more yards. O'Connell has protected the offense, particularly last week in Chicago, by leaning on the run game more than all but one other NFL playcaller. His rate of designed runs (50%) is higher than every team but the Seattle Seahawks , who also lost their starting quarterback ( Sam Darnold ) early in Week 1. Relatedly, the Vikings are tied with the Seahawks and Cincinnati Bengals for the NFL's fewest turnovers this season (one). 

 "You've got to learn some things on how you approach trying to win one game every Sunday," O'Connell said this summer. "And they're all different. Every weekend is a challenge schematically, personnel-wise, where your team's at from a health standpoint, where your team's at with certain positions. Ultimately, all we're tasked with doing is trying to win a game for 60 minutes every week.

 "It sounds like a cliché until you learn [that] it doesn't matter what the stat box looks like. It doesn't matter what an EPA looks like. ... Ultimately, you learn that none of those other things matter because winning is the only thing that matters. That's what we were able to learn as a team. But most importantly, probably [for] me last year, figuring out different ways to win, however we had to, each week. The principles don't change."

 

 On a nicer day in Chicago, even with backup Carson Wentz behind center, the Vikings likely would have tried to exploit a Bears defense that had given up 387 passing yards in its previous game to the Carolina Panthers . Instead, after two games, Jefferson now ranks No. 20 in the NFL in receiving yards per game (73.5). Fellow starter Jordan Addison has a total of two receptions on seven targets, and no other wide receiver has caught a pass. 

 "Of course I would love to have 150 [yards], three touchdowns and just the fantasy stat line," Jefferson said in Chicago. "I definitely would love that. But with these conditions, with this type of game, it wasn't that type of day, which is totally fine. As long as us coming off the ball, executing our plays and just being a factor in the win, that's all that matters.

 "So just coming in here, difficult environment with the weather conditions, a lot of adversity in our way. It doesn't matter. We're just not going to really think about it. Just come in there and just lean on each other to get the done."

 

 O'Connell referenced that quote Monday, noting Jefferson has "enough experience now to see the big picture." But he also made clear that he connects the Vikings' offensive numbers this season to the unique circumstances of losing Murray in Week 1 and the weather in Week 2, and not a more fundamental issue of poor play.

 He jokingly lamented losing some yards when officials flagged the Bears for a 5-yard defensive holding foul rather than defensive pass interference -- a spot foul -- on a play that Jefferson otherwise would have likely caught for a 68-yard touchdown. O'Connell also praised Addison for his blocking and said: "His time's coming as far as registering the things he's capable of in the stat column."

 The same is true, the Vikings clearly hope, for the entire group.

 "We know that offensively were going to continue to grow," offensive coordinator Wes Phillips said, "and we're going to make plays. And there's going to be some times when those other phases are going to have to lean on us. We're well aware of that and we're working hard every day to make sure that we're going to be the ones that step up when we're needed."

title: Why Patriots must be better at managing the clock before halftime
summary: After two straight games with questionable decisions before halftime, the Patriots admit they need to improve on possessions late in the second quarter.
full_text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. --  New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel and quarterback Drake Maye are working to regain their edge in an area they mastered last season but have fallen short in the first two games of the 2026 season.

 Can they reclaim their standing among the NFL's best in the possession directly before halftime?

 Back-to-back road games against 2025 AFC playoff teams in the Jacksonville Jaguars  (1-1) and Buffalo Bills  (2-0) provide a tough test to get back on track when points will be at a premium. The Jaguars have scored 43 points through two games and the Bills have scored 77. 

 "I felt like it was one of the best things that we did last year -- whether getting points or ending with the football," Maye said Wednesday after the team's first practice in preparation for Sunday's contest against the Jaguars ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ). "When the defense gives you the ball back, you try to end with the football in the first half, especially when we're coming out and having the ball in the second half. That's definitely a big emphasis for us."

 A combination of game-management hiccups by Vrabel and VP of game strategy and operations John Streicher and Maye's decision-making has contributed to a disappointing start in 2026.

 

 Maye and the offense had the ball on their own 20 with 1:48 on the clock in last Sunday's 20-3 win over the Steelers. They led 10-0 and still had all three of their timeouts. But the drive never got started, with Maye running into a sack on a three-man rush on first down.

 "That's definitely something you have to know the time and place, speaking for myself, of getting the ball forward, [even] an incomplete pass and it's second-and-10," Maye said. "When you're under two minutes and you let them get three [points] from it, that's one of our jobs on offense [to not let that happen]."

 The Patriots (1-1) punted back to the Steelers (1-1), who took over at their own 35-yard line with 40 seconds left. Vrabel gifted the Steelers an additional 5 yards with 12 seconds remaining when he called timeout and was penalized for delay of game. On the prior play, cornerback Marcus Jones was injured and the Patriots were assessed a timeout as a result, per league rules when there is less than two minutes on the clock, which meant they couldn't call timeout again before the next snap.

 "I blew it," Vrabel acknowledged, explaining that he had been talking with officials on why Steelers tight end Pat Freiermuth was ruled to be out of bounds when his shin appeared to come down in the field of play. "I was all caught up on the fact that they should've been winding [the clock on] that play, which again, I don't understand."

 The Steelers capitalized with a 56-yard field goal on the final play of the half.

 In the season opener against the Seahawks, Vrabel also made a debatable choice. The defense had stopped the Seahawks on third-and-6 from their own 22-yard line with 12 seconds remaining, and despite having a timeout left, Vrabel elected to let the clock run out instead of forcing a punt to either go all-out for a block or give elusive Jones a chance at a return.

 "It's probably something we could have done," Vrabel told sports radio WEEI. "The guy [punter Michael Dickson ] is really good and I didn't think he would give Marcus a chance to return -- like they had the entire night. We feel like our strength is our ability to get a catchable ball for Marcus and take care of the gunners. We probably could have rushed 11 guys."

 

 The Patriots' elite work late in the second quarter last season began in the game that turned around their season -- a Week 5 road win over the Bills. They took over at their own 30 with 2:22 left and drove to the Bills' 1-yard line before kicking a field goal on the final play of the half.

 That sparked a dominant run of pre-half execution, with one highlight coming against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers when Maye and the offense started at their own 22-yard line with 7:10 on the clock -- and ultimately converted on a 1-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs with two seconds left until halftime.

 "I'm not stressing it too much. I thought last year sometimes we scored almost too quick a couple times. [Other] times I thought we did a nice job of getting points and ending with the football," Maye said.

 "Play good football and try to double up, as they call it. That's something we try to be mindful of as the best way to finish a half."

title: With Jaxson Dart out, what's next for Giants, Jameis Winston?
summary: New York fans just don't seem to be allowed nice things these days. Our insiders get into the implications of Dart's injury and its effect on the Giants going forward.
full_text:
Just like that, Jaxson Dart 's sophomore season with the New York Giants is over.

 The quarterback injured his left MCL and meniscus on the opening drive of the Giants' Week 2 game, wiping away all the optimism from the arrival of coach John Harbaugh and a season-opening win against the Dallas Cowboys . He is expected to have season-ending knee surgery , sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo Wednesday.

 Giants fans just don't seem to be allowed nice things these days. Really, how else do you explain it?

 Even after Dart was injured against the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night, there was hope that there wouldn't be a "devastating outcome." But after further tests, that is exactly what it turned out to be.

 This was supposed to be the season the Giants made the jump after seven wins in the past two seasons combined. Dart looked primed to become one of the league's better quarterbacks, especially if he was more efficient out of the pocket and protected himself better.

 It all looked so promising with the way he played while dismantling the Cowboys the first week. And then it all came to a crashing halt five plays into the second game of the Giants' season, when he was high-lowed by Rams edge rushers Byron Young and Josaiah Stewart .

 Just like that, everything changed.

 ESPN's Giants reporter Jordan Raanan, national NFL reporter Jeremy Fowler, analytics writer Seth Walder and fantasy football writer Michael Florio get into the implications of Dart's injury and its effect on the Giants going forward.

 

 

 Is the Giants' 2026 season lost? 

 Lost? It's not like they were winning the Super Bowl anyway. As one NFL assistant coach said after watching their first two games in primetime, they "still have a lot of holes" on their roster. 

 But with Dart, the Giants could've -- should've -- been a playoff contender. At the very least, the expectation was to be part of the "In the Hunt" graphic shown when outlining the playoff picture come December. 

 If Dart made massive leaps as a passer, the Giants would have been a dangerous out. Now they'll be lucky to flutter around .500 with veteran Jameis Winston as their starter. (He of the 36-53 career record as a starter.)

 The Giants believe in him, though.

 "Jameis is one of our guys who obviously is here for a reason," Harbaugh said. "He's a very good football player."

 He's just not anywhere near as dynamic as Dart and struggled mightily in Monday night's 28-6 loss to the Rams. -- Raanan 

 

 Should the Giants have serious concerns about Dart's viability as their QB of the future considering his injury history? 

 It seems premature to come to this conclusion. Sure, Dart spent an inordinate amount of time in the blue medical tent as a rookie. But the reality is he missed only two games with a concussion. 

 

 This injury to his knee has nothing to do with a reckless style of play or even his desire to run. It came on a normal third-down dropback. He was hit 3.1 seconds after the snap on a play that was out of sync from the start. 

 Harbaugh came to the Giants in part because he watched Dart's tape and was convinced this was his best chance among the available options to win. Nothing he saw from the summer or opener should sway him otherwise.

 The Giants organization truly believes Dart is going to be one of the league's best quarterbacks and, with the way he works and cares about football, the rehab and comeback won't be anything he can't handle. -- Raanan  

 

 How does the offense adjust under Winston? 

 It's going to look different. Winston doesn't have the same running ability as Dart. That much was obvious against the Rams when Winston rushed for 1 yard in three-plus quarters. That will hurt their traditional running game, too, since they designed an offense around Dart's athletic skill set. 

 But the Giants believe Winston is a capable quarterback who can win them games. They didn't want it to be over a 15-game stretch, but there is a reason they handed the veteran a two-year, $13 million extension earlier this month. 

 The problem is that the Jameis experience comes with fire quotes, plenty of chuckles and a wide range of play. It's not uncommon to see a spectacular tight-window throw down the field followed by a pass that sails 15 yards over a receiver's head. It will be on this veteran offensive coaching staff, led by coordinator Matt Nagy, to limit the latter. Don't ask Winston to do too much. Rely on the physical running game to downplay his proclivity for mistakes and interceptions. 

 Jake Haener , who joined the team mid-summer, will serve as Winston's backup for now. Don't be surprised to see veteran Brandon Allen re-signed, either. -- Raanan 

 

 Should New York consider signing or trading for another QB, or will it roll with Winston? 
 Yes, the Giants should consider it, but they are only as good as their options. And options are scarce. Jimmy Garoppolo is the most viable free agent option, but he has considered retirement, and it's uncertain whether either side is interested.

 

 The best play might be making a phone call to Minnesota, where J.J. McCarthy is buried on the depth chart. Some teams I've talked to believe that McCarthy could come at a value because he does not appear to be in the Vikings' long-term plans.

 And the Giants did heavy homework on the 2024 quarterback draft class. But for at least one week, the Giants can see what Winston will do with a full week of game-planning around his skill set. -- Fowler 

 

 What does ESPN's Football Power Index say about the Giants' hope to stay in contention? 

 It says those hopes vanished. With Dart out, the Giants fell all the way to 31st in FPI's rankings -- better than only the lowly Dolphins. I'm surprised the fall was that severe. But the model was bullish on Dart, a young quarterback who had shown promise, so it seems the drop-off between him and Winston is substantial. Winston recorded a 17.2 QBR in relief against the Rams on Monday night.

 The Giants' projections have taken a tremendous hit. Heading into Week 2, sitting at 1-0 and with a healthy Dart, the Giants had a 43% chance to make the playoffs. One quarterback injury (and a blowout loss) later, that dropped to 1%. ESPN's FPI predicts the Giants to finish the regular season with five wins.

 The good news? The Giants now have an 8% chance to earn the No. 1 draft pick in April -- though Giants fans must be distraught that we're already talking about their draft slot in September. -- Walder 

 

 How does the change at QB impact Giants players in fantasy? 
 Winston is the next man up. While that has meant good things for his receivers in the past, his play looked rough Monday. Winston is purely an option for superflex leagues and is more of a depth QB3 than a starter.

 Given Winston's past tendencies to lock in and pepper his top wide receiver with targets, him throwing to Malik Nabers provides fantasy hope. While this news drops Nabers into more of the WR2 range for the rest of the season, he still brings upside given his immense talent ... just expect more weekly volatility as well.

 Isaiah Likely remains a TE1, even though his fantasy ceiling takes a hit here. While this news could mean the Giants become a more run-heavy offense, that would help keep Cam Skattebo afloat for managers. His fantasy value still takes a slight hit as there will be fewer consistent scoring chances without Dart, but he should see enough volume to remain in the low-end RB2 range. -- Florio

title: Why Aaron Glenn is encouraged by the Jets' progress
summary: New York is an overtime loss away from being undefeated after allowing the fewest yards through two weeks.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- Perhaps the strongest endorsement for New York Jets coach Aaron Glenn came more than a year ago, delivered by his previous boss.

 "If he can't [turn them around]," Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell said at the 2025 NFL spring meetings in Orlando, Florida, "nobody can."

 Despite a firestorm of criticism in the aftermath of their 20-17 overtime loss to the Green Bay Packers , Glenn has the Jets looking like a competitive team so far in his second season. It's overshadowed by a handful of questionable coaching decisions from the fourth-quarter collapse Sunday, but he is encouraged by the progress and insisted they won't allow the crushing loss to define their season.

 Glenn can prevent that from happening by beating the next opponent, which happens to be -- drum roll, please -- Campbell and the Lions. It's a delicious storyline, but Glenn, who served as Campbell's defensive coordinator from 2021 to 2024, can't let that distract him. His primary job is to refocus his team after blowing a 10-point lead.

 

 "It's my responsibility to get our guys to be able to close the door," Glenn said. "I take that, and it's something I will never run from."

 There are some positives to build on, which should make it easier to move past the Green Bay debacle. In two games, the Jets already have run more plays with a lead (68) than they did the entire 2025 season (66). They dominated the Tennessee Titans in the opener, never trailing, and they were only one timely play away from burying the Packers.

 The Jets have their best total yardage margin (plus-258) through two games since 1982, currently the third-best margin in the NFL. The defense, with Glenn calling the plays, is ranked No. 1 in yards allowed (197 per game). They have surrendered only 30 points, including 20 in the fourth quarter and overtime -- perhaps a troubling trend.

 Defensive tackle Harrison Phillips said they will make "a conscious effort this week to step up the intensity" in the latter portion of practice, hoping there's a carryover to the game.

 The Jets allowed the Packers to score on three of their last four possessions. Before that, they held Green Bay's vertical passing attack in check, though some of that could be attributed to  Jordan Love 's reliance on short passing because of a spate of offensive line injuries.

 The takeaway-starved defense, which has gone a record 19 consecutive games without an interception, recorded its first takeaway of the season -- a fumble recovery. There could've been more, but they recovered only one of five fumbles by the Packers.

 Glenn took that as a positive, saying, "We're attacking the football. We're punching the football out, and I do know this: Those things are going to come around for us."

 

 Offensively, the Jets haven't put up big numbers (40 points), but they're getting consistent quarterback play -- something that didn't happen last season. Geno Smith , who threw an NFL-high 17 interceptions last season for the Las Vegas Raiders , has yet to commit a turnover. Ditto, the entire offense -- the first time since 1971 they've had no giveaways through the first two games.

 "I still think we have a really good team, a team of high potential and we just went into a shootout with a [2025] playoff team," running back Breece Hall said after Sunday's game. "So I think we have everything we need."

 It wasn't exactly a shootout, but there's no doubt the Jets have been better than last season on offense. Smith already has more passing yards in his first two starts (462) than Justin Fields recorded in his last four (460) from last season. They're still lacking explosive plays, so it might behoove offensive coordinator Frank Reich to get wide receiver Garrett Wilson more involved. Wilson was targeted only seven times Sunday, just twice after his third-quarter touchdown.

 "Absolutely, that's a point of emphasis every time we go out: try to make sure we get him the ball, and we have to continue to do that," Glenn said. "There are guys on this team -- Breece, [ Mason Taylor ], [ Kenyon Sadiq ], especially Garrett -- that we have to make sure that we get those guys involved."
